US-Iran MoU is set to expire: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
20:28:21 UTC
05:28:21 KST

US-Iran MoU ends: What happens next?
Both sides accused the other of violating the June agreement shortly after it was signed.
The Memorandum of Understanding aimed at ending fighting between the US and Iran expired on Monday, with little sign that either side is willing to extend the agreement, which both sides have accused the other of violating for weeks.
“We have not yet made a decision to restart negotiations with the United States,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on Telegram on Saturday.
Meanwhile, mediators from Qatar and Pakistan continued to exchange messages with Iran. Araghchi added that Iran was working on a separate agreement with Oman to hash out new shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz, but emphasised that this was only possible if a political solution was reached.
On the US side, President Donald Trump told supporters in New York on Friday that the US would soon claim the critically important waterway for itself.
Here’s what you need to know about the expired MoU.
What is the MoU?
The agreement, signed on June 17 by Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, followed rare high-level talks hosted by Pakistan. It was meant to bring an end to more than three months of war that had killed thousands and crippled commercial movement in the Gulf, especially oil and gas exports relied on globally.
Leaving complex issues such as Iran’s nuclear programme to be dealt with later, the agreement sought not only to find an immediate diplomatic solution to halt the war with Tehran, but also to find an end to Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Iran and the US, the agreement said, “declare the immediate and permanent termination of military operations” and that a “final deal” would “confirm the permanent termination of the war on all fronts”. The agreement said this “final deal” would be endorsed by the UN Security Council and would be reached in a maximum of 60 days, which could be extended by mutual consent.
The US was to end its naval blockade within 30 days, remove its forces from near Iran after the “final deal” was reached and begin work on a reconstruction and development package for Iran of at least $300bn. Washington also agreed to terminate sanctions against Iran, issue waivers for Iranian oil exports and allow Tehran to access frozen funds. Iran, for its part, was to clear mines from the Strait of Hormuz and allow ships to pass “with no charge” for 60 days.
Tehran also reaffirmed it would not seek nuclear weapons and would negotiate on issues such as enrichment, the details of which would be laid out in a “final deal” to be backed by the UN.
Was the MoU successful?
Although the US and Iranian versions of the agreement differed slightly, much of the dispute since its signing has centred on more basic issues, such as whether it was a ceasefire or a more permanent agreement and what each side was supposed to do.
Whether the entire agreement was still in effect soon became disputed, and by June 27, Trump was calling Iranian strikes in the region “a foolish violation” of the deal. Iran said US strikes “violate Article 1 of the Memorandum of Understanding”.
On July 7, Trump said the agreement was “over,” and the US continued launching attacks on Iran, including on what Tehran called civilian infrastructure, killing at least 50 people. Iranian officials said the US had “violated and suspended” all its commitments and Tehran had “likewise suspended all our own commitments”.
Since then, the US has not fully lifted sanctions on Iran and Trump has scoffed at the idea of paying Iran for reconstruction, suggesting instead that Tehran pay compensation to families of protesters it had killed “over the last 50 years” as well as “all the people they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts”.
Reopening Hormuz has not materialised either, with Iranian and US officials continuing to insist their side controls the strait. Earlier this week, the Pentagon said it had fired on a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the strait because it “violated the US blockade against Iran.”
“The ceasefire stopped and was rendered obsolete after the US didn’t comply with the terms of the agreement, or the MoU,” Mostafa Khoshcheshm, professor at the University of Applied Sciences in Tehran, told Al Jazeera.
In particular, he added, Tehran views the US as having failed on its promises of releasing Iranian assets, lifting sanctions, removing its naval blockade and having Israel withdraw from southern Lebanon. “Now, formally, on paper, it is said the deadline has ended,” Khoshcheshm said.
What happens next?
Although the MoU expired on Monday, what that means exactly depends on which side you ask.
Iran’s Araghchi said on Friday that what was in the Islamabad MoU was “the end of the war, not a ceasefire”, according to the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA). He added that since the US violated the MoU and continued attacks, “there was no 60-day ceasefire that needed to be extended”.
The recent reshuffle in Iran’s national security apparatus suggests a tougher stance in future talks and less willingness to back down, particularly on control of Hormuz. Earlier this month, for instance, the former head of the IRGC, Mohsen Rezaei, was named as the new head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, its top security body. The move is meant to better synchronise military and civilian operations, analysts have told Al Jazeera.
Rezaei’s appointment, along with other recent leadership changes, “shows Iran believes it has the upper hand”, Khoshcheshm said. Any new talks would likely see Iran coming to the table with more demands, he said, from ending the war on Gaza, to lifting sanctions and a blockade of Yemen, even calling for the denuclearisation of Israel.
Few cards left to play for the US
As for the US, Trump and his administration have escalated rhetoric regarding the strait and economic warfare.
Trump on Friday announced plans to formally claim the waterway for the US.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” he said.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said on Friday that the US would apply measures that have “never been seen” on Iran.
But there are not many levers left for Trump to pull if he wants to exert more pressure on Tehran, Barbara Slavin, distinguished fellow at the Washington, DC-based Stimson Center, told Al Jazeera.
US stocks of interceptor missiles have been depleted, its strategic oil reserves drained and key military hardware, including aircraft carriers, have been kept at sea months longer than planned, meaning the US has few military options left to try. As for economic pressure, Tehran has shown it can inflict economic damage of its own by disrupting traffic transiting Hormuz, Slavin said.
“Iran is playing hardball here, clearly furious at the Trump administration for, in its view, not fulfilling the MoU signed back in June,” Slavin said. “They’re making the international economy and they’re making Donald Trump sweat.”
One way or another, Iran would likely be reimbursed for the war and gain a great deal of control over the Strait of Hormuz, Slavin said. This conflict, she said, “resolves through a deal, probably after our midterm elections, when there will be less of an impact on the vote”.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told reporters in Tehran on Saturday that the concessions Iran won in the MoU were “a source of pride and victory”.
“I can say with complete conviction that we truly emerged victorious in this war, both militarily and politically,” he said.

Britain’s Amy Hunt wins record 4th gold medal at European championships. ‘Mondo’ victorious again
BIRMINGHAM, England (AP) — Amy Hunt won a record fourth gold medal in a single edition of the European championships when Britain clinched victory in the mixed 4x100 relay on Sunday.
Hunt had already won two individual titles — the 100 and 200 — and added a third gold Saturday in the women’s 4x100 relay at Alexander Stadium.
The team of Jeremiah Azu, Dina Asher-Smith, Zharnel Hughes and Hunt won Sunday in a time of 39.97 seconds. Germany was second in 40.11 and Spain third in 40.42.
On the anchor leg, Hunt pulled away from Gina Lückenkemper to cross the line for gold.
“Oh my gosh, I’m over the moon,” Hunt told the BBC. “To finish it off with some of my best friends in the sport ... to do it all together is incredible.”
Asher-Smith won her career eighth European championships gold and became the competition’s most decorated athlete with her 11th medal, moving one ahead of the late Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska.
This was the debut of the mixed 4x100 relay in the European championships.
“It’s good to get to try something new,” Asher-Smith told the BBC, although she added, “I was absolutely terrified.”
Four in a row for Duplantis
Swedish pole vaulter Armand “Mondo” Duplantis earned his fourth consecutive European championship title by clearing 6.15 meters.
Duplantis is the world record holder — he vaulted 6.31 meters in March. That was his 15th world record. He first broke it in 2020 and has eclipsed his mark by 1 centimeter each time since.
The two-time reigning Olympic champion watched on as Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis (6.00) lost momentum after getting over 6.10 but knocking the bar off on his way down. Karalis took his second straight silver at the championships. France’s Baptiste Thiery (5.85) earned bronze.
Italy wins medal table
Bragging rights were on the line in the last event of the week-long championships when Britain and Italy were tied at nine golds each atop the medal table.
The Italians pulled out the victory in the men’s 4x400 relay final, and the home team settled for silver. That means Italy topped the table with 10 golds and an overall 22 medals, three more than Britain’s total.
Italy also topped the medal table two years ago in Rome.
In the penultimate event of the championships, the Dutch women’s 4x400 relay team won gold when star Femke Broeders-Bol held off Britain’s Emily Newnham down the stretch. It was the third straight women’s 4x400 relay championships title and Broeders-Bol’s sixth career gold at the championships.
In the women’s 1,500 final, Britain’s Georgia Hunter Bell improved on her silver medal from two years ago by crossing the line first in 4:07.78.
Larissa Iapichino had added to Italy’s gold tally by winning the women’s long jump, leaping 7.00 meters for the title.
Memorable marathons
Amanal Petros made sure there was no photo finish this time.
The German won the men’s marathon on Sunday morning by a whopping 7 seconds, less than a year after missing out on gold in a photo finish at the world championships in Tokyo.
Petros crossed the finish line in Birmingham in 2 hours, 9 minutes, 11 seconds — breaking the championships record in the process. Italy’s Pietro Riva took silver with his 2:09:18, three seconds better than Israel’s Gashau Ayale.
Last September, the Eritrean-born Petros settled for silver behind Tanzania’s Alphonce Simbu in the closest marathon in world championships history. Both men were officially clocked at 2:09:48, but it was determined that Simbu crossed the line a fraction sooner.
In the women’s marathon Sunday, Finland’s Alisa Vainio dominated the field to finish in 2:22:26, nearly five minutes ahead of silver medalist Lili Anna Vindics-Toth of Hungary. Britain’s Abbie Donnelly took bronze. Vainio broke Christelle Daunay’s championship record from 2014 by almost three minutes.

African Union rejects foreign interference, parallel governments in Sudan

Adel Abdelrheem and Rania Abushamala
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
The African Union Peace and Security Council on Sunday rejected foreign interference in Sudan's internal affairs and attempts to establish parallel entities or governments that could undermine the country's unity and sovereignty.
The position was conveyed during a meeting between Sudan's Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and an African Union Peace and Security Council delegation led by Algerian diplomat Mohamed Khaled at the presidential palace in the capital Khartoum, according to a statement from the Transitional Sovereignty Council.
Khaled, the council's rotating chair, described the meeting as "fruitful," saying it addressed several issues related to peace, security and stability in Sudan.
He reiterated the council's condemnation of any foreign interference in Sudan's internal affairs, saying such intervention "fuels the conflict."
Khaled also affirmed the council's rejection of attempts to create parallel entities or governments that could undermine Sudan's unity and sovereignty.
"The only path to achieving lasting peace in Sudan is through dialogue, national reconciliation and reaching a comprehensive political settlement that meets the aspirations of the Sudanese people," he said.
He welcomed steps related to a peace initiative and the government's return to performing its duties from Khartoum, describing the move as "pivotal" to restoring the functioning of state institutions and providing essential services to citizens.
Khaled called on the government and political forces to make the transitional process more inclusive and work toward a national consensus leading to a constitutional system through free and fair elections.
Earlier Sunday, Sudanese Prime Minister Kamil Idris told the council's delegation that a Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue would "begin soon."
Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) over plans to integrate the latter into the regular military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN estimates.

====================================================================================================

How AI is splitting Australia's education system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:55:17 UTC
04:55:17 KST

Why alternative schools are not rushing to bring AI into classrooms
In short:
One of Australia's largest alternative school systems has ruled out developing its own artificial intelligence (AI) tool.
Generative-AI tools have been created for public schools in New South Wales, South Australia and Queensland, with supporters saying it reduces workloads and helps students more study effectively.
But early research has cautioned against an over-reliance on the technology, and the NSW government has now launched a broad review into its impact on student learning.
The head of one of Australia's major alternative school systems has ruled out creating an artificial intelligence (AI) learning tool for its teachers and students.
Generative-AI learning tools have already been created for public schools in New South Wales, South Australia, and Queensland but concerns about the technology's impact on critical thinking are growing.
Steiner Education Australia CEO Andrew Hill said their schools would not be following suit.
"Anything which is going to compromise healthy growth of the brain, we would take a cautionary view towards," Mr Hill said.
Supporters of embedding AI in schools say it reduces teacher workloads and allows senior students to study more effectively.
But early research has suggested an over-reliance on AI reduces independent problem solving and critical thinking skills.
Last week, the NSW government announced it would consider banning take-home assessments as part of a broader review into AI's impact on student learning.
Complicated ethics
Data from the OECD suggests most Australian teachers have at least experimented with AI.
Loading...
In a 2024 education report, two-thirds of Australian teachers reported having used it in their work; the fourth highest proportion among the international organisation's 38 member countries.
Some teachers are boycotting the technology, unable to look past the public criticism that has accompanied the AI boom.
Mark*, a south-east Queensland state primary school teacher, scaled back his use of AI because he felt it brought a cold, lifeless feel to the classroom.
"I used it a bit last year to create things to read from, like an example paragraph to practise reading," he said.
"And then I noticed it has that AI voice. I really started to notice it, and I thought 'this isn't great', I don't want kids to learn how to read through this really sterile way of using language."
A growing number of students are pushing back against the technology too.
In June, high school and university students protested outside the construction site of a new data centre at the Sunshine Coast.
Students who attended cited anxieties around environmental impacts and diminishing future job prospects for young people.
Fears over cognitive 'offloading'
South-east Queensland teacher Lauren* said she was reluctant to role-model a technology that could be impacting her students' ability to think for themselves.
"I teach English and the humanities — those subjects exist to teach critical thinking skills.
"If we're outsourcing that to computers then what are we doing?"
In Queensland, the Department of Education uses a generative AI tool called Corella which is available to teachers and students in years 7-10, although students need parental consent.
A spokesperson for the department said Corella was built around a Socratic teaching method, which guides students "rather than instantly providing them with full, direct responses".
"This encourages critical thinking and problem solving … it is intended to support learning, not replace student thinking, effort or creativity," the spokesperson said.
"The department continues to monitor the rollout of Corella and developments in AI and education across jurisdictions."
The impact of AI on critical thinking skills has been the subject of a growing body of research.
A 2025 UK study which surveyed more than 600 people found young people with high dependence on AI scored lower in critical thinking tests than older people with lower AI dependence.
University of Queensland Education Psychology Professor Jason Lodge said cognitive "offloading" was the biggest risk of embedding AI deeper into schools.
"The brain in many ways is like the body. The harder you work it, the better it gets at doing what it does," he said.
"And AI provides shortcuts that mean some students are not doing the work that's necessary."
But he said those shortcuts could also be beneficial.
"If you're writing something, not necessarily in English class and grammar and spelling is not a key part of the lesson, then maybe it's OK if we're getting an AI tool to help with structuring grammar and correcting spelling," Mr Lodge added.
"There can be very beneficial offloading that allows students and teachers to focus on the more important parts of the lesson."
At the Samford Valley Steiner School, north-west of Brisbane, school director Andrew Curry said designing lessons without intellectual shortcuts had never been more important.
He teaches year 10 students trigonometry by taking surveying instruments called theodolites to measure angles at a nearby creek.
"They're creating a map with traditional techniques," Mr Curry said.
"[It] could be done with drones and AI in probably half the time, but the students wouldn't get all of that richness of learning in that time. They'd just get a map."
Super-powered teachers
Ali Kadri, chief executive of Queensland independent school the Islamic College of Brisbane, said students becoming dependent on AI would not be the fault of the technology.
"It's the fault of how some people are taught or some people teach," he said.
The 45-year-old is also a tech entrepreneur and is designing an in-house AI assistant for the college called Aladin; his answer to the comic book hero Tony Stark's digital sidekick Jarvis.
As well as generating learning materials, Mr Kadri claims Aladin will be able to predict the likely future performance of students based on past grades and attendance.
"If we identify the student is going to do worse than what they've been doing so far, then the machine learning model will trigger an alert … a staff member will then intervene and assign a strategy to address that issue," he said.
"I think it … gives teachers superpowers."
The Islamic College of Brisbane's head of junior secondary Vincent Parry said, although initially a sceptic, he had started to discover where AI could work in the classroom.
He said he was encouraging his students to use AI to simplify explanations they didn't understand, which was particularly helpful for students for whom English was a second language.
"Once you take control of it rather than let it take control of you, it's a very valuable tool," he said.
From teachers to support workers
Looking into the future, Ali Kadri sees a world where AI has changed the teaching profession entirely.
"At this point in time a student does not have to go to a classroom to get their question answered … they can go to an AI model, which is much more knowledgeable and smarter in information that an average teacher would be," he said.
"I think there is a world where education looks like a teacher going into a classroom full of students and instead of delivering content, they'll be mentoring and coaching students while they learn, study and thrive."
Samford Valley Steiner school director Andrew Curry said such a world might improve test scores but wouldn't help students.
"You might get results, but you wouldn't get understanding.
"And the difference is where is your focus? Is your focus on passing a test? On accessing uni? Or is your focus on the student actually understanding the content that's being presented to them?"
*Names withheld for privacy

12 more bodies are recovered in Zimbabwe’s ferry disaster, bringing death toll to 84
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — Authorities on Sunday searched for more bodies from an over loaded ferry that capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe last week as the death toll in the disaster rose to more than 80 people.
The ferry capsized in strong waves on Tuesday. Police on Sunday said the death toll had risen to 84, from 72 the previous day as more bodies were recovered. Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency has said 77 people were rescued.
Estimates had put the number of passengers as high as 153 on a ferry authorized to carry 90 people, but the latest official figures now suggest the number of passengers could be even higher.
Police in the southern African country said “search efforts are still underway in a bid to recover victims identified as missing.”
The aging ferry was traveling from the town of Kariba to rural and fishing communities in the country’s northwest, where roads are damaged and public transportation is scarce.
Among the dead are 18 children, with the youngest just 1 year old. According to police, 16 of the victims were aged 10 or younger.
Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, created by damming the mighty Zambezi River in the late 1950s and early 1960s. It stretches more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) and is up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.
Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with their border running through its middle.

Drone strikes, intelligence chief’s killing expose Libya’s fragile balance - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:50:13 UTC
04:50:13 KST

Drone attacks on energy facilities in western Libya and the assassination of a senior intelligence official in the east have renewed fears of instability as Libyan factions maneuver ahead of possible political negotiations.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
No evidence has emerged connecting the two sets of events, and no group has claimed responsibility for either. Their timing has nonetheless raised questions about whether Libya faces another brief outbreak of violence or a broader contest for influence.
Maj.-Gen. Fawzi al-Mansouri, head of military intelligence for Khalifa Haftar’s eastern-based forces, was killed in Benghazi on Monday night, August 10, when an explosive device detonated at his vehicle in the Hawari district, according to security officials and the eastern General Command.
Al-Mansouri was buried the following day at a funeral attended by senior military figures, including Saddam Haftar, one of Khalifa Haftar’s sons. A security committee has opened an investigation, but authorities have not publicly identified a suspect or motive.
The assassination eliminated one of the most senior officials in an eastern security establishment that has portrayed Benghazi and much of eastern Libya as having left behind the instability of earlier years.
Hundreds of kilometers to the west, attacks were hitting some of the country’s most important energy facilities.
Drone strikes began targeting facilities in Zawiya on August 9. The following night, a drone hit a gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a major fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5 million liters of gasoline when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.
Zawiya drone attacks continued through August 11
Another drone landed near a second tank without causing reported casualties or damage. Further attacks continued into August 11.
The National Oil Corporation said firefighters had contained the blazes and that the refinery itself was not damaged, although production was briefly disrupted. It warned that more attacks could force it to suspend operations.
The complex includes Libya’s largest operating refinery, which can process approximately 120,000 barrels per day. It is connected to the Sharara oil field and plays a central role in the country’s energy production and fuel-distribution network.
Libyan Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, who heads the internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli, condemned the strikes as organized crime and promised to hold those responsible accountable.
Another drone struck the South Zawiya electricity substation on August 12, setting it ablaze and causing widespread outages. Libya’s state-run General Electricity Company said more than 700 megawatts of the nearby power plant’s 1,300-megawatt capacity remained unavailable.
US energy company GE suspended work at the power station and withdrew its technical teams because of the security situation.
The attackers and their objectives remain unknown. Zawiya is divided among armed groups with shifting alliances, and tensions have grown between Dbeibah’s government and forces associated with Mohamed Bahroun, a powerful commander in the city.
Libya has been divided between rival centers of authority for more than a decade. Dbeibah’s government operates from Tripoli, while authorities backed by Haftar’s forces control the east. A 2020 ceasefire ended the last major nationwide war but failed to produce unified political, military, or security institutions.
The latest violence comes as Libyan leaders and foreign governments seek arrangements that could narrow the east-west divide.
Misbah Omar, a Libya-based analyst at the Institute for Integrated Transitions and a member of the Mediterranean Platform, said the attacks could be part of a larger contest, although no wider pattern has yet been established.
“If this assessment is correct, what we are witnessing may represent an initial phase in the restructuring of Libya’s political and security landscape - one aimed at allowing the main actors to consolidate or redefine their respective spheres of influence before moving toward a clearer political process,” Omar told The Media Line.
Zawiya's significance to the contest over western Libya
Zawiya is particularly important in any contest over western Libya. The city sits west of Tripoli at the junction of armed influence, energy infrastructure, migration routes, and economic networks.
The attacks raise the possibility that armed factions or their opponents are shifting their focus from direct clashes to the resources and supply systems that sustain military power.
“Such actions would represent a significant shift in the nature of the confrontation,” Omar said. “Rather than focusing exclusively on the armed formations themselves, pressure could increasingly be directed toward the economic and logistical networks that sustain their influence and operational capacity.”
Potential targets could include infrastructure, revenue sources, supply routes, and other assets that help armed groups maintain their position, he added.
Ibrahim Mousa Said Grada, a former Libyan ambassador to Sweden and former UN adviser, also described Zawiya as central to the struggle over political power and economic resources.
“This happened in Zawiya, a city that deserves to be described as afflicted and targeted because it has become a meeting point for the contradictions of politics, conflicts of interest, and disputes over the division of power and resources in Libya,” Grada told The Media Line.
The violence coincides with renewed US efforts to encourage cooperation between Libya’s rival authorities.
Massad Boulos, senior adviser to US President Donald Trump for Arab and African affairs, has promoted an initiative focused on institutional reunification and economic cooperation. He has met Haftar, Dbeibah, and other political and military figures across Libya.
Published accounts describe the initiative as an effort to reach agreements between Haftar’s eastern authorities and Dbeibah’s Tripoli-based government, with energy investment and economic development offered as incentives.
The plan remains controversial, and many of its details have not been made public. Critics warn that a power-sharing agreement could preserve the authority of Libya’s current leaders and armed factions rather than build representative national institutions.
Omar said the US approach seemed to favor a series of limited agreements rather than a comprehensive settlement.
“If this trajectory continues, the initiative could enter a more practical phase during the final quarter of this year and the beginning of next year, operating along two parallel tracks: economic and political, supported by corresponding security arrangements on the ground,” he said.
Grada was less optimistic about its immediate prospects.
“The Boulos initiative ‘appears’ to have been placed in a freezer during this scorching summer, so that it does not die or become buried altogether,” he said.
The recent attacks do not show that Libya’s factions have agreed on a new division of power. They could instead represent attempts by competing groups to improve their positions before negotiations, whose timing and structure remain unclear.
Al-Mansouri’s assassination creates another problem for the east. Grada said the loss of its military intelligence chief came at a sensitive time for Libya’s divided security services.
“At the same time, the absence of the head of military intelligence for the eastern Libyan forces coincides with the continuing dispute over the leadership of the General Intelligence Service, or external security apparatus,” Grada said. “This means an intelligence vacuum and state of confusion at a particularly dark and sensitive moment domestically and during a highly unstable and critical international environment.”
Foreign involvement adds to the uncertainty. Russia, Turkey, the US, European powers, and regional governments retain varying degrees of political, economic, and security influence in Libya.
“There is an increasing possibility that Libya could be transformed into an arena for proxy warfare between intelligence services and their military and media arms, as international and regional conflicts and rivalries expand and deepen,” Grada said.
The latest violence does not necessarily mean that Libya is heading back to nationwide war. Omar said a series of limited moves intended to change the balance of power was more likely than an immediate, large-scale confrontation.
“However, these developments should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence of an imminent comprehensive military confrontation,” he said. “A more plausible scenario may be a series of calibrated and limited moves designed to alter the balance of power gradually, while leaving room for negotiations and political accommodation.”
The next political agreement may depend as much on events outside formal negotiations as on what happens at the table. Control of territory, energy assets, and security institutions will help determine what Libya’s competing factions are willing - and able - to accept.
The Zawiya strikes and al-Mansouri’s assassination do not prove that anyone is carrying out a coordinated plan to redraw Libya’s balance of power. They do show how quickly an attack on an oil tank, power station, or security chief can unsettle a country whose rival authorities have never fully resolved the conflict between them.

Soldier dies in Spain’s Aragon wildfire

Soldier dies in Spain’s Aragon wildfire
- A Spanish soldier died while fighting a major wildfire in Aragon, with the region deploying its largest firefighting force ever, including French reinforcements and 1,000 firefighters.
- The wildfire has burned 16,600 hectares, forced over 1,000 evacuations, and threatened historic monasteries linked to Aragon's medieval heritage.
- Authorities reported progress in controlling the fire amid extreme heat and winds, linking the intense wildfires to climate change and recent European heatwaves.
AI generated
MADRID – A Spanish soldier died on Aug 16 while helping with efforts to extinguish a major wildfire in Aragon, the north-eastern region’s leader said, with local media reporting that his truck had overturned.
“I have conveyed my heartfelt condolences to the lieutenant-general of the Military Emergencies Unit (UME) for the death of a soldier in the Penas de Riglos fire,” Jorge Azcon said on social media platform X.
“All my love and support for his family, his colleagues and the whole UME at this time of deep pain,” he added.
Like its European neighbours, Spain has suffered several spells of extreme summer heat, contributing to ideal conditions for a string of wildfires.
Scientists say climate change, driven by humanity’s burning of fossil fuels, is increasing the length, frequency and intensity of such extreme weather.
The regional government had announced the largest firefighting deployment in Aragon’s history, including French reinforcements, to tame the blaze that broke out on Aug 10.
The flames have come close to the two monasteries of San Juan de la Pena, which are perched in mountainous, rugged terrain and are a symbol of the region.
The oldest monastery, linked by legend to the Holy Grail, has origins in the 10th century and contains the remains of the first kings of the medieval kingdom of Aragon, which were rescued on Aug 13.
A complicated week marked by unpredictable winds and high temperatures saw the flames spread across 16,600ha and prompted the evacuation of more than 1,000 people from surrounding villages.
‘Optimism and caution’
The regional government reported “a night of positive work” on Aug 16 as firefighters “managed to consolidate a large part of the perimeter”.
They would be reinforced with the arrival of 100 French firefighters and the participation of between 35 and 40 aircraft, it added in a statement.
Existing reinforcements from the army and other parts of Spain would take the total to 1,000 firefighters, which Azcon said was “the largest deployment of resources against a fire in Aragon’s history”.
“We’re facing the day with optimism, but also with total caution,” he wrote on X.
In the southern region of Andalusia, the authorities allowed more than 400 evacuees to return home after a wildfire that had raged for 10 days and affected more than 25,000ha was declared under control on Aug 16.
The authorities have said the number of affected hectares straddling the provinces of Huelva and Sevilla only alludes to the perimeter of the fire and does not mean that the entire area has been burned.
Andalusia’s leader Juanma Moreno said it was “probable that the burnt area is smaller than what we were estimating at the start”, pending satellite analysis.
In late July, a wildfire just dozens of kilometres west of Madrid became the largest in Spain’s recent history and triggered a national emergency. AFP

From evil spirits to the Illuminati: How we learned to love conspiracy theories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:46:09 UTC
04:46:09 KST

In the past month, I found myself twice very surprised during ordinary conversations with intelligent people. The first was with a woman in her 30s who attended the most prestigious universities and is clearly an impressive analytical thinker.
While discussing the oft-asked question of whether the war would resume, she analyzed the situation and explained the role played by the Illuminati.
The second person who surprised me was a sharp and intuitive Greek woman, albeit with a rather basic education. She told me her national ID card was about to expire and she had no intention of renewing it.
The government, she explained, wants all Greeks to switch to biometric IDs. She refuses because she heard that when your fingerprints are scanned, a drop of blood is secretly taken so your DNA can be stored in a national database.
I remembered these anecdotes this week when I heard from a Greek friend about a grim superstition common when she was a child; it was about why some women only manage to have one child. It then occurred to me that today's conspiracy theories are a reincarnation of the superstitions of yore.
Organize the chaos
Anthropologists and psychologists have long understood that alongside mythology, classic superstitions developed as primitive attempts to explain natural phenomena. Long before we knew about bacteria, meteorology or genes, we needed ideas to help us explain our problems. If crops repeatedly failed or a healthy baby died in the middle of the night, our minds demanded an explanation and used their ability to identify patterns even when the supporting data was scarce or ambiguous.
Thus we invented the evil eye, vengeful spirits and a variety of rituals. Superstitions provided an explanation, a villain or at least a focal point as the source of evil, and a feeling that if we only acquired secret knowledge and acted accordingly, we would increase our protection. And even if it didn't work 100 percent, at least we'd make the world logical again.
Eventually, empirical science entered the picture. Observation, data collection, experimentation and gradually technology lifted the fog. Evil spirits and intentions were replaced by the stuff of bacteria, tectonic plates, atmospheric pressure and gynecological problems.
Today, even if people don't understand some of their health problems or other natural phenomena, they can rely on the assumption that a body of scientific knowledge and the scientific method exist. And in principle, if a natural phenomenon occurs, science can answer for it.
But today, the main source of existential anxiety isn't the instability of nature but the opacity of human power. That is, when we're contending with the instability of nature, like wildfires, floods or extreme heat, deep human anxiety arises about those billionaires who are plundering the Earth and leaving us to roast as they build colonies for themselves on the moon.
Unknown mechanisms
I have a very successful friend who told me he's trying to sell tickets for 10,000 euros each that could be used as down payments for apartments on other planets. Another acquaintance explained to me, after in-depth reading on artificial intelligence, that we have 10 years, 20 at most, before billionaires destroy us all or we become slaves to AI.
That is, in ancient times, power was a much more tangible phenomenon. We might not have liked the king, we probably hated the feudal lord and detested the village priest, but we could point to them. We knew who owned the land, who collected taxes and more or less who wrote the laws. There were always intrigues and corruption – we know this from the Bible, Shakespeare and the tales of Robin Hood – but our minds could grasp the system of power and its internal dynamics.
Today, however, the interplay between money, technology and global politics exists in a terra incognita somewhere beyond the horizon, in a place a simple citizen's eye hasn't seen and perhaps can't see, because it's possible that power today is driven by mechanisms whose interconnections can't be understood in the old way.
And it may be that biology is failing us. Our minds evolved in a small-scale social context. Within the tribe, power was a personal attribute, and behind every exercise of power stood someone who could theoretically be identified. We're cognitively equipped with the technology that allows us to understand who heroes, villains and tricksters are (all our popular culture attests to this), but we struggle to intuitively grasp nonhuman systemic complexity.
One global Olympus
When we face systems that are difficult for us to imagine, the mind is more likely to play it safe and prioritize an erroneous explanation that protects it, over ignoring possible danger. That is, if I see a bush rustling and I run for cover, but it turns out to be just the wind and not a leopard, maybe it's embarrassing, but nothing bad happened.
But if I see a bush rustling, assume that it's just the wind and don't see the predator hiding there, I might have forfeited my ability to pass my genes on to the next generation. For these reasons, evolution favored people with an inherent bias to assume that an intentional agent was behind every unexplained event. These people had more children.
In ancient times, this mechanism might have led us to believe that a child born with a certain birthmark would cause miscarriages or the deaths of the child's baby brothers and sisters. Today, as we contend with the immense complexity of global institutions, the same mechanism causes us to knead the dough of these decentralized systems into a single mold; for example, in the form of a secret meeting between figures who conspire to run the world.
There is no real difference between the imaginary room where the Illuminati meet or where the people who take blood from innocent Greeks scheme, and the way the ancient Greek concept of Mount Olympus was formed. The Greeks imagined capricious gods sitting above the clouds fighting, betraying, deceiving and, in the process, changing human lives without warning. We observe market crashes, wars, inflation and policy changes and feel the invisible touch of distant omnipotent figures. Our suffering or random moments of luck become evidence of their actions.
Someone to blame
Thus, conspiracy theories play the psychological role that superstitions once did. When we feel that the world is impossibly complex, a conspiracy theory offers a narrative anchor, just as a superstition once explained natural phenomena beyond our comprehension. In both cases, the explanation is comforting.
Why is it comforting to believe that a dark group like the Illuminati runs the world, or that DNA is collected in a secret room in a government building?
First, because living in a world controlled by evil masters is slightly less troubling than living in a world driven by headless, chaotic and unmanaged complexity. If there is an evil master plan, there is someone to blame (Hollywood movies, where these villains are even punished, demonstrate this fantasy to us). The alternative leaves us completely helpless. Also, the feeling that we possess secret knowledge reduces the existential anxiety or humiliation that comes with this helplessness.
Many times, conspiracy theories develop where ignorance has taken root, intentionally or unintentionally. But the cases I've described here show that conspiracy theories don't signify stupidity, and they're certainly not always a sign of the limits of human intelligence.
They show that we can no longer read the map of power. Until a new kind of "science" enters the picture in the form of transparent governance, education for political and economic literacy, and true systemic responsibility, these theories will continue to emerge, expressing our refusal to surrender to the forces that crush us.

Details
As Astra writes, the fuel, including from India and Morocco, remains on tankers in Murmansk: oil companies want to sell it at a significantly higher price than Russian domestic prices because of the high delivery costs.

The St. Petersburg Exchange established a basis for trading imported gasoline at the Kola station in Murmansk Region back on July 29, but no deal has taken place so far. Regulators require imported fuel to be sold at domestic prices, but oil companies consider such a scheme unprofitable because of logistical costs.
According to Bloomberg, on August 5 Russia received its first shipment of Indian gasoline, totaling 42,000 tonnes. InfoTEC sources clarify that several major oil companies brought the imported gasoline into Russia, without specifying the volumes.

NEW DELHI: After earlier uncertainty, there are now clear indications that barrierless tolling on national highway (NH) stretches, coupled with e-notices for violations, is inculcating greater discipline among road users.At Choryasi toll plaza on NH-48 in Gujarat, the first to go live, e-notices fell from 1.7 lakh in May to 1.1 lakh in June and further to 92,240 in July. Mundka toll plaza in Delhi, which went live on May 10, recorded 1.69 lakh e-notices in June, with a marginal decline to 1.67 lakh in July.
Multilane free flow (MLFF), or barrierless tolling, is currently operational at five toll plazas. It was rolled out at Daulatpura on Delhi-Jaipur highway and Gharaunda on Delhi-Chandigarh highway in the third and fourth week of June, respectively. Manoharpura on Delhi-Jaipur highway was the latest to go live, on July 1.Data show that e-notices issued during the first month of MLFF operations at Daulatpura, Gharaunda and Manoharpura were significantly lower than those issued when the system was launched at Choryasi and Mundka. Daulatpura issued 33,038 e-notices in July, while Gharaunda and Manoharpura recorded 86,760 and 70,550, respectively.“As awareness about e-notices for toll non-payment spreads, road users are becoming more compliant. A large number of vehicle owners, particularly car users without active FASTags, are also falling in line,” said an official involved in NHAI’s tolling system.Failure to pay or challenge an e-notice within 72 hours can result in the vehicle owner being liable to pay double the toll. Türkiye, 7 countries condemn Israeli rejection of Trump’s Gaza plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:42:56 UTC
04:42:56 KST

Türkiye and seven other countries on Sunday condemned Israel's rejection of a roadmap for completing the implementation of US President Donald Trump's plan to end the Gaza conflict, saying the move jeopardises efforts to achieve lasting peace.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates condemned Israel's declared rejection of the roadmap, as well as its rejection of Palestinian statehood.
The ministers said the positions amount to “a direct repudiation” of Trump's Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, which was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803.
They said Israel's rejection jeopardises the plan's implementation and “fundamentally undermines the collective efforts undertaken to achieve a just and lasting peace”.
“Such rejection confirms that Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza and the rest of the Occupied Palestinian Territory,” they added.
The ministers said the roadmap, which has been accepted by Palestinian factions, was the result of extensive efforts by mediators, including Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye and the US, alongside the High Representative of Gaza and the Board of Peace.
They described it as a key step towards the decommissioning of weapons alongside the withdrawal of Israeli forces, deployment of the International Stabilization Force, transfer of administrative authority to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, and reconstruction of the enclave.
Call for sustained US engagement
The ministers warned that rejecting the roadmap amounts to an explicit refusal to proceed with the implementation of Trump's plan and threatens to derail US efforts to end the war and establish conditions for lasting peace.
They stressed the importance of “sustained and active US engagement” to ensure Israel's full compliance with the commitments and arrangements set out under the plan and roadmap and to prevent further obstruction.
The statement said Israel bears “direct and full responsibility” for consequences resulting from continued rejection, obstruction, delay or non-compliance, including any deterioration on the ground or disruption of efforts to end the war in Gaza.
The ministers also called for the full and immediate implementation of the plan to address the humanitarian situation in Gaza, ensure security and stability, and pave the way for reconstruction and recovery.
They reaffirmed their support for Palestinian self-determination and statehood, categorically rejecting any attempt to deny or prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state, including through unilateral actions.
“A just, lasting and comprehensive peace only will be achieved by the implementation of two-State solution, by the realization of an independent and sovereign Palestinian State based on the 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital,” the statement said.
The ministers also underscored the importance of the continued role of the Board of Peace and called on all parties to support its efforts to implement the roadmap and advance the second phase of Trump's plan.
They urged the board, with active US support and engagement, to take “immediate and concrete measures” within its mandate to preserve the integrity of the plan and prevent any party from obstructing its implementation.

Aussies have long held a narrative of the resilient “battler”. But recent history suggests the days of "she'll be right," may be behind us. Insight explores whether the little Aussie battler still exists or whether a culture of complaint has taken over. Watch Insight episode Wired to Whinge Tuesday 18 August at 8.30PM on SBS or SBS On Demand.
Semi-retired lawyer Walter Bilas says he is not a whinger but has dabbled.
"Whingeing shouldn't be disparaged. I think it's a right in any liberal democracy like Australia," he told Insight.
"There are laws there which have to be upheld; sometimes those laws don't function. People whinge when they don't function."
Having lived in Sydney's Inner west since immigrating from the UK a few years ago, Walter feels a sense of civic duty to the neighbourhood.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He acted on that sense of duty most acutely a few years, taking issue with what he describes as a "problematic nightclub".
"When the club shuts down in the early hours — or late at night, rather — you've got the antisocial aspects of people slamming car doors, people shouting, people urinating in the street, people leaving bottles, cans, et cetera ... "
He said it was taking a toll on himself and his neighbours.
"People wake up to mess in the morning ... People can't sleep — it stresses people out."
Walter took the neighbourhood's noise complaints, which included a petition signed by more than 150 residents, to the Inner West Council and Liquor & Gaming NSW.
He said there is an "art" to complaining that required one to be organised and to go to the top authorities about the problem.
Alison Flett never imagined her live music venue would cause such conflict when it first opened in 2021.
She had experience running similar venues and made sure every aspect was up to standard.
"It was DA-approved. My lawyers, my town planners, my advisers said, 'You'd be mad not to take this place over'," Alison said.
It was when new government-mandated COVID-19 restrictions — including rules around physical distancing — took effect that she says venues like hers were encouraged to make use of their outdoor spaces.
While this allowed Alison's venue to continue operating, it also meant locals were more exposed to noise; and in 2023, the complaints ramped up.
Alison said one letter from the council even informed her she was on criminal notice.
"I didn't really know what the criminal notice was, because as far as I was concerned, I was just running a live music venue — and that scared me as a young entrepreneurial lady."
The complaints triggered an investigation, which led to Alison having to change the venue's licence, install a noise limiter, pay fines and hold monthly meetings with the police.
"I was starting on the back foot [having reopened the business during the COVID-19 pandemic] but then lump in legal fees, fines, putting in noise limiters, investing time and money into making sure that the neighbours wouldn't complain ...
"It left me with no money and no choice but to close [in 2024]."
Complaining to get ahead?
As a retail worker at a Sydney optometrist, Lauren Leung has also been on the receiving end of complaints.
"After working in retail for a substantial amount of time, you get to notice a pattern with customers — and they tend to try to take advantage of your customer service."
She said customers adopted an attitude of, "I really want to get my money's worth out of this complaint" to get new frames or lenses and "they pick a fight or they often stay in the store for quite a long time".
Outside of work, Lauren wears the self-proclaimed title of whinger with smells often being a topic of complaint.
"I have a very good sense of smell. One particular major thing I get irritated by is people's smell on public transport — especially when you're crammed in like sardines."
As an engineering student, she said exam times are particularly difficult.
"You can smell people from across the room who've been cramming for exams ..." she said.
"You've really skipped that shower to get that extra 20 minutes of study time."
But she believes whingeing has its advantages and can be a means of gauging perspective.
"I whinge to see, 'Oh, are my thoughts and opinions within reason? Does everyone else think about this? Or am I out of line?'"
Why do we whinge?
Psychologist Sue Read, who has a neuroscience background, says there's a reason we whinge, and why many find connection in doing so.
"We are wired to whinge; we are wired to look for the negative," Read told Insight.
"We evolved in a time of scarcity; we are social animals. So being able to communicate what was wrong actually did help us survive."
But Read said that there can be "profound impacts" if we are constantly focusing on the negative — and if we're complaining without wanting to have an outcome.
"At one level, it keeps us in a heightened state of threat. So we're flooding our body with adrenaline and cortisol and stress hormones. We feel more defensive. We see more perceived injustices," she said.
"It makes it harder to access the higher-order prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for things like compassion, empathy, nuance and complexity."
We've 'gone soft'
Sydney business owner John Megalli prides himself on not whingeing. In fact, he has very little patience for it.
"I don't put my energy into whinging," he said.
"Because the more I put my energy into that, the more I don't grow."
John built a multi-million-dollar air-conditioning business from the ground up in western Sydney's Mount Druitt and believes whingeing limits our potential.
"You're looking in the rear-view mirror when you've got a massive screen in front of you — that you can move forward through — but you're still looking backwards.
"So, you're not progressing."
John believes whingeing is culturally common in Australia and we've "gone soft".
He said younger generations complain more due to a sense of entitlement and comparing themselves to others.
"We have it with our apprentices.
"After a year and a half of being an apprentice, they want to be the CFO."
Competitive suffering
When asked if there is more for us to complain about today, Read said it's relative and if we look at previous generations, "the things they really struggled with were often real-life survival".
"The way we live now is like only royalty could live in the past [with the exception of the lowest socioeconomic demographic]," she said.
Although people struggle with different things, the psychologist says we must be careful of "competitive suffering", the act of comparing or ranking one's suffering against others.
"This idea that we hold onto now that 'my pain is worse than anyone's ever in history' becomes a problem ... like I think 1850s for women [was] probably not a great time [neither was wartime in the 1940s] ...
"There is a problem when you think you're the only one who's ever experienced it, because that actually isolates us more."
Read says that constantly focusing on the negative does not make for a better life and that it is important to acknowledge your hardship, have compassion and seek support for it if needed.
'You have to complain to get things changed'
Walter said that after a year of complaining the community was relieved when Alison closed her venue and their "immediate problems had vanished overnight".
But the complaint campaign was only a temporary success as there is a new venue operating in the same space.
"We still occasionally hear rowdy behaviour on a Friday or Saturday night; so, the problem is still there," he said.
Walter still believes in the power of complaining to achieve a "sense of justice" and "fair dinkum" in the community.
"If we don't whinge, well, there's pent-up frustration, and we start taking the law into our own hands ... and that basically is corrosive ...
"You have to complain to get things changed, to get things done, to move the agenda forward effectively."
Alison says the complaints had more than a financial toll on her.
"My mental health had deteriorated so much that I needed to stop ..."
"I don't run that business anymore, and I'm really not in the music industry and not interested at all in going back. I took it very personally."
She wrote handwritten apologies to several locals when she closed her business.
Believing this to be a "very noble act of contrition", Walter contacted her to meet, and the pair had coffee where they shared and understood each other's perspectives.
"My eyes opened — I actually saw that it would have been pretty upsetting," Alison said.

U.S. Navy Orca Uncrewed Submarine Makes First 1,852-Kilometer Pacific Transit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:33:00 UTC
04:33:00 KST

In July, the U.S. Navy’s newest Orca XLUUV autonomous underwater vehicle traveled 1,852 kilometers across the Pacific Ocean, marking the vehicle’s longest known transit.
Naval News reported this.
The submarine reportedly traveled through the eastern Pacific.
It is unknown whether it carried a payload or weapons during the transit or which specific missions it performed.
In the future, Orca is planned to be equipped with the Hunter module, a payload that will allow it to conduct mine-laying operations in waters inaccessible to conventional submarines. Procurement of these modules is expected to be approved in late 2027 or early 2028.
The U.S. Navy received its first Orca in December 2023.
Orca XLUUV (Extra Large Uncrewed Undersea Vehicle) is an autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-duration operations in demanding environments.
Development of the uncrewed platform began in 2017, when the U.S. Navy awarded Boeing a contract to develop it. Shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls Industries later joined the project.
The U.S. Navy allocated $43 million for the project, with plans to build four prototypes. In March 2019, a fifth Orca was ordered.
The 80-ton, 26-meter-long vehicle features a modular design that allows it to be adapted more easily for different missions.
The vehicle’s propulsion system consists of a hybrid diesel-electric system combined with lithium-ion batteries. This combination is intended to allow the vehicle to remain at sea for several months at a time while traveling at about 3 knots (5 km/h).
A payload module can be installed in the vehicle’s stern section. The 10-meter-long section can accommodate a payload weighing up to eight tons. It is primarily intended for carrying naval mines.
The U.S. Navy also plans to equip the uncrewed platform with other modules for mine-clearing, electronic warfare and underwater surveillance operations.
Orca autonomous underwater vehicle. Photo: Boeing
Future payloads are expected to include a synthetic aperture sonar that will allow Orca to map the seafloor.
In addition, the U.S. Navy is interested in integrating various weapons systems into the uncrewed vehicle, including torpedoes, cruise missiles and even aerial drones.

At least six people dead from days of storms and record flooding in Indiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:27:22 UTC
04:27:22 KST

Days of storms and flooding in Indiana left at least six people dead as flood waters peaked in Indianapolis’s White River – and rains were expected to ease in the state capital region and other parts of the state on Sunday.
A four-year-old boy, two men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began on 11 August, state homeland security department spokesperson Liz Woods said.
Officials in Jennings county, in the southern end of the state, said the boy was killed on Tuesday when a tree crashed through his bedroom during strong winds.
“This is obviously unexpected,” Jennings county deputy chief Cody Low told the local ABC affiliate. “There’s nothing we can say that is going to make it any better. We’re going to push through this as a community.”
The other victims included a 19-year-old man whose body was recovered on Saturday. Officials in Delaware county, located east of Indianapolis, said Matthew Morey had jumped off a bridge into the rushing waters of the Mississinewa River with friends three days earlier.
Family and friends gathered earlier in the week at the bridge to remember the recent high school graduate, who was headed to Purdue University, and warn of the dangers of swollen rivers.
Delaware county officials also said they recovered the body of Stephanie Sallee and her dog in a cornfield on Saturday, not far from her car. They believe the 58-year-old had been driving on a flooded road when the vehicle was swept away. In a statement shared with local news outlets, her family remembered her as a compassionate and loving person who adored her grandchildren and other young relatives.
In Indianapolis, flooding from the White River peaked early on Sunday morning, with high water levels expected to hold for a few hours before beginning to recede, according to the city public works department.
The agency said it would reopen the city’s floodgates on Sunday and that emergency shelters remained open after hundreds of homes along the river and its canals were evacuated. First responders used boats to rescue people stranded by rapidly rising flood waters.
Recovery efforts, meanwhile, started in earnest as northern parts of the state began drying out.
“I must admit it is a good morning,” Christine Altman, president of the Hamilton county board of commissioners, said during a Sunday briefing. “It’s not raining, and the water is receding.”
She said the county, located just north of Indianapolis, escaped without any loss of life, though officials were assessing whether a significant bridge damaged in the flooding could be repaired or if it needed to be completely replaced.
Heavy rain and flash flooding were still possible across portions of the central part of the state throughout the day, the National Weather Service (NWS) warned.
The NWS urged residents to check river and weather forecasts and “stay out of dangerous, fast moving waters” as heavy rain has led to significant flooding along most rivers and creeks across central Indiana. Roads and bridges across the state have also been seriously damaged or washed out entirely by the powerful rushing waters.
Nearly 130,000 utility customers statewide remained without power by midday Sunday, down from a peak of about 300,000, according to Woods and the online utility tracker PowerOutage.us.
Heavy rains have hammered Indiana over the past week, causing rivers to crest and setting new records.
The White River crested at more than 24 feet (7.32 meters) in the communities of Anderson and Noblesville, surpassing records set in 1913.
Indianapolis mayor Joe Hogsett said the flooding was the worst the capital city has seen in more than 30 years.
Governor Mike Braun’s office said more than 350 evacuations and scores of rescue and welfare checks have occurred elsewhere in the state, including at a senior mobile home community north of Indianapolis.
Donald Trump on Saturday approved Braun’s request to the president for federal disaster assistance to help with flooding response and recovery efforts.
The drenching rains and destructive flooding were among the effects of severe storms that have wreaked havoc across the US midwest and beyond in recent days.
Tornadoes, heavy rains and flash flooding brought serious damage to communities from Illinois to western Pennsylvania.

The Trump administration is considering reimposing human rights sanctions on Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes over what US officials view as a "consistent pattern of abuse" involving press freedom and individual rights, the Financial Times reported Sunday.
De Moraes has been accused of leading an "oppressive campaign of censorship" and authorizing arbitrary detentions, according to the newspaper.
The latest tensions involve the judge ordering police raids targeting a journalist and the journalist's sources, a move American officials reportedly view as "impinging on free speech rights."
Critics within the administration described de Moraes as an "enemy" who has specifically targeted supporters of US President Donald Trump and conservative activists in Brazil.

The White House and State Department declined to comment on the report, while Brazil's Supreme Court had yet to issue a statement, according to the Financial Times.

Kushner meets Hamas leaders in Egypt to push Trump’s Gaza plan

Kushner meets Hamas leaders in Egypt to push Trump’s Gaza plan
After meeting with the US envoy, Hamas says it called on the Board of Peace to ‘compel’ Israel to accept the plan.
Hamas leaders have met in Egypt with US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, Jared Kushner, who is seeking to push a peace plan for Gaza that Israel has rejected.
A Palestinian source told Al Jazeera on Sunday that Hamas’s leadership briefed Kushner on Israel’s ceasefire violations in Gaza. The source also stated that Kushner said the US rejects any plans to displace Gaza’s residents.
Recommended Stories

Another official familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that Hamas and Kushner met in the town of Alamein “with the objective of translating the roadmap’s obligations into concrete, verifiable steps”.
“These are actions that maintain the ceasefire; begin to transfer all governing responsibilities to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza; ensure that Hamas has no role in Gaza’s future administration,” the source, who is neither a member of the Board of Peace nor a US official, said.
“There can be no ambiguity: Hamas must relinquish governing authority and all weapons and military infrastructure. And Gaza can never again be a source of terror for Israel,” the source added.
Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya attended the talks. Also present were Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, Qatari diplomat Ali Al Thawadi and a senior Turkish official, US outlet Axios reported. Board of Peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is also a member of the board, joined Kushner in the meeting.
Kushner’s visits to Israel and Egypt are an effort to narrow differences over Trump’s latest roadmap for Gaza, which Netanyahu said last week was “unacceptable” for Israel.
‘Compel’ Israel to accept Gaza plan
In a statement issued on Sunday, Hamas said it emphasised its “acceptance” of the roadmap for the second phase of Trump’s plan during the meeting with “delegations from the mediators and guarantors of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza”.
“Hamas and the resistance fully adhered to the first phase of the ceasefire agreement,” it said. Israel, however, “failed to implement this phase, escalating its military operations on the ground and deepening the humanitarian catastrophe, and has explicitly rejected the roadmap”, Hamas added.
Hamas said “it called upon the mediating parties and the Board of Peace to fulfil their responsibilities and compel the [Israeli] occupation to implement all its obligations in the first phase, end all violations, halt the killings and incursions, agree to the roadmap for the second phase of President Trump’s plan and begin developing a timetable for its implementation”.
The US has for years refused contact with Hamas, which it classifies as a “terrorist organisation”. But the Trump administration has increasingly been comfortable with direct contact in hopes of ending Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Hamas’s al-Hayya also met separately with Egypt’s Rashad on Sunday, according to the Reuters news agency.
Kushner, meanwhile, met with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi after meeting with Hamas. The Egyptian president’s office said that aside from Gaza, the two discussed Egypt-US relations. El-Sisi highlighted the strategic partnership between the two countries and praised their ongoing cooperation across shared interests. Kushner, in turn, commended the close coordination with Egypt and expressed appreciation for el-Sisi’s role in advancing regional peace and stability.
Israeli strikes continue
On Sunday, the foreign ministers of eight nations – Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia – condemned Israel’s rejection of the roadmap for Gaza, branding it a “direct assault” on US-led peace efforts and Palestinian statehood.
Warning that Israel now bears full responsibility for derailing the plan, they urged Washington to step in and enforce compliance, while insisting that only a two-state solution on 1967 borders can bring lasting stability and calling on the Board of Peace to move swiftly against any further obstruction.
A senior Israeli official said that Kushner and Board of Peace envoy Mladenov were scheduled to meet with Netanyahu on Monday. The official said Israel was concerned about Washington’s demand to end targeted assassinations of Hamas fighters in Gaza.
Trump announced the roadmap last month, saying it was a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas had agreed.
The roadmap calls for the immediate cessation of military operations in the enclave. It foresees Hamas disarming as Israeli troops withdraw, and Gaza is rebuilt under a new civilian Palestinian administration.
Hamas said it had agreed to the plan to avoid a resumption of the war, but added that implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawing its forces and halting attacks.
After scaling back its attacks in the besieged enclave earlier this month, Israel has resumed air strikes on Gaza in the past few days, despite an October 2025 “ceasefire”.
At least five Palestinians were injured on Sunday after an Israeli strike hit a tent encampment in Khan Younis, medics said. A separate air strike hit an apartment in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, wounding several people, medics said.
Israeli fire has killed more than 1,250 Palestinians in Gaza since the “ceasefire” took effect, according to Palestinian official sources. The death toll since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 is now above 73,300.

Moroccan security forces arrest nearly 300 migrants trying to reach Spain’s Ceuta

Moroccan security forces arrest nearly 300 migrants trying to reach Spain’s Ceuta
CASABLANCA, Morocco (AP) — Hundreds of migrants trying to reach the Spanish exclave of Ceuta by land and sea were arrested by Moroccan security forces, Moroccan state television reported Sunday, as authorities tightened security along the border following calls for a new mass crossing.
Moroccan state broadcaster Medi 1 TV said 294 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were arrested Saturday while attempting to enter Ceuta. Authorities also arrested 61 Moroccans accused of facilitating the migration attempts, the broadcaster reported.
The attempted crossings followed a surge in social media posts calling on migrants to make their way to Ceuta, a Spanish city on Morocco’s northern coast. In response, Moroccan and Spanish authorities beefed up security presence and limited movement toward the area.
The latest attempt comes two weeks after tens of thousands of would-be migrants, driven by poverty and misinformation, rushed toward Ceuta in one of the deadliest migration crises to hit the region. At least 90 people died on both sides of the border, according to official numbers, while human rights groups reported higher figures.
The interior ministry did not respond to AP’s questions about the latest arrests or the number of security personnel deployed around the border to prevent a new migration push.
A senior Moroccan diplomat previously said that more than 20,000 Moroccan security personnel are deployed along the border with Ceuta each day, at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. The diplomat was not authorized to be publicly named speaking about the issue and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Thousands of migrants from across Africa and beyond travel to Morocco each year, fleeing conflict, poverty and instability and seeking a route into Europe. Many attempt to reach Ceuta or Melilla, another Spanish exclave on Morocco’s northern coast, hoping eventually to make their way to mainland Spain and better economic opportunities.

Strikes kill 19 in Ukraine and Russia

Strikes kill 19 in Ukraine and Russia
- Strikes by drones and missiles killed 16 people in Russia and Ukraine, hitting civilian areas and infrastructure, with major attacks in Rostov, Kryvyi Rih, and Kyiv.
- Ukraine’s steel plant and Kyiv’s outdoor book market were damaged, causing operational halts and cultural losses, while Zelensky called for more air defence support.
- The conflict’s drone warfare is spilling over into neighbouring countries’ airspace, with NATO intercepting drones, and Ukraine targeting Russian logistics to weaken its war economy.
AI generated
KYIV – Strikes killed 16 people in Russia and Ukraine, the authorities said on Aug 16, as waves of drones and missiles pummelled civilian infrastructure on both sides.
With fighting at the front at a near standstill and talks frozen, the warring countries have significantly stepped up long-range attacks deep behind each other’s lines, pushing the civilian death toll to its highest levels since the war’s first months in 2022.
In Russia, swarms of Ukrainian drones killed five people in a residential area of the southern Rostov region, regional governor Yuri Slusar said. Three more people were killed in the Belgorod, Kursk and Moscow regions, along with four others in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.
Moscow’s regional governor Andrey Vorobyov described the assault as “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory”. Russia’s defence ministry said it had intercepted 822 drones across the country overnight.
Kyiv market hit
In Ukraine, a barrage of Russian drones and missiles killed two people and wounded 14 at ArcelorMittal’s steel plant in Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown.
The plant, one of Ukraine‘s biggest steel producers, said it partially halted operations after the strike damaged its core production facilities.
Another strike hit Kryvyi Rih on the evening of Aug 16, killing one person.
Strikes also hit other regions, killing two people in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, one in the border region of Sumy and another in Donetsk in the east.
In Kyiv, a popular outdoor book market at Pochaina, long the place to find rare and antiquarian volumes, was struck.
Bookseller Dmytro Semenukha saw all four of his stalls burn to the ground.
“There used to be a store. And books, and flags of all the countries, all the countries. Tons of everything. And that’s it,” the 45-year-old told AFP.
In a social media post on the overnight raid, Zelensky said that “wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure”.
Over the past week, he said, Ukrainian cities had been pummelled by “more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles”, as he renewed his appeal to allies for more air defence.
Spillover to Europe
Russia has carried out near-daily missile and drone strikes across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in early 2022.
It has recently intensified attacks using hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles, exploiting Ukraine‘s air-defence shortages after the US-Israeli war against Iran diverted supplies.
“When North Korean ballistic missiles destroy infrastructure and claim lives here in Europe, European interceptors cannot simply be allowed to sit in storage,” Zelensky said.
Kyiv has recently renewed claims that Moscow is receiving more missiles and troops from its ally North Korea.
Countries bordering the conflict have faced increasing spillover from the drone war. After the overnight raid, Romania’s defence ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet had shot down a drone that breached its airspace near the borders with Ukraine and Moldova.
