In Spain’s Ceuta enclave, hundreds of migrants stage protest, demanding asylum
- Hundreds of migrants in Ceuta protested demanding asylum and refusing to return to Morocco, living in harsh conditions while waiting for a chance to move to mainland Europe.
- Ceuta’s healthcare system is under strain with outbreaks of diseases and injuries rising, though officials deny a collapse and warn against xenophobia.
- Migrants come from poor or conflict-affected countries, seeking better lives despite the risks, with many expressing exhaustion and uncertainty while awaiting aid or asylum decisions.
AI generated
MADRID - Hundreds of migrants who recently entered Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta staged a protest on a popular urban beach on Aug 16, urging Spanish authorities to grant them asylum instead of sending them back to Morocco.
They were among the estimated 5,000 to 8,000 who remain in Ceuta after the mass border crossing two weeks ago that saw over 72,000 people surge into the tiny territory of about 80,000. The vast majority returned voluntarily in the following days.
With the city’s resources overstretched, most migrants were living in precarious conditions on El Trampolin beach or the city’s outskirts while awaiting a chance to journey on to continental Europe.
“We’re sleeping next to the sea, with cold and bad smells. We’re suffering a lot,” said Ayoub Elarroud from Morocco’s Tetouan, adding that police were blocking migrants from going to the city centre.
The protesters held up Spanish flags and banners reading “We don’t want to go back to Morocco” and “We are also human”, while chanting slogans such as “We’re tired” or “We need a solution”.
On the rocky shores behind them, some migrants washed their clothes while others fished with makeshift bamboo rods.
Earlier this week, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said migrants who had entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the enclave, travel to mainland Spain or obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability.
Health services under pressure
The head of Ceuta’s medical board, Enrique Roviralta, told Onda Cero radio that the city’s limited healthcare workers were exhausted and criticised what he described as a slow response by the central government.
Roviralta added that diseases such as infectious diarrhoea and scabies were breaking out, and violence-related injuries such as broken noses or stab wounds were rising.
On Aug 16, Health Minister Monica Garcia rejected suggestions that local health services had “collapsed”, but acknowledged they were under pressure.
“To associate migration with illness is unjust and xenophobic,” she told reporters in Ceuta, adding there was a moderate risk of epidemic outbreaks for migrants and a low one for residents.
Most of the Moroccan migrants interviewed by Reuters said they were driven by poor working conditions in their country, despite many holding higher qualifications.
Mohammed Ouanzar, a 39-year-old automation specialist from Fez, said average monthly salaries of 3,000 dirham (S$413) made it impossible for him to buy a home or start a family.
“Once I reached Spanish soil, I felt like I was born again,” he said. “I’d rather die than return.”
Hicham Chikir, 25, said most people were eager to work in Europe. “If anyone is bad, the police can send them back,” he added.
Refugees exhausted
Emmanuel, a 30-year-old electrician who fled conflict-ridden northeastern Nigeria, said he decided to embark on a perilous four-month journey across Niger, Algeria and Morocco because his children had stopped going to school over fears of being kidnapped.
“I’m fighting for a better life for them,” he said, adding that he would take any job he was offered.
Mohammad Ismail Hossain, 34, left Bangladesh over two years ago following the 2024 mass uprising. He traversed India, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria, Egypt, Libya and Algeria - mostly on foot - and saw many companions die of thirst in the desert.
Ousmane from southern Senegal said he was seeking asylum because he suffered persecution over his sexual orientation but had yet to obtain a reply from the local NGOs he had contacted.
“The worst thing is waiting all day with nothing to do, checking my emails constantly,” he said. REUTERS

BBC asks US court for help with testimony from the Trump family in defamation suit
Trump is seeking US$10 billion in damages from the UK broadcaster, alleging that a documentary edited a speech he gave on January 6, 2021
Britain’s BBC asked a US court for help in getting documents and testimony from members of US President Donald Trump’s family in connection with his US$10-billion defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster, a court document showed.
Lawyers for the BBC argued that Ivanka Trump, her husband Jared Kushner and Donald Trump Jnr have “personal knowledge” and are likely to have records relevant to elements of Trump’s claims against the broadcaster, according to a filing on Friday in federal court in Florida.
The broadcaster has been unable to serve subpoenas because the three have Secret Service protection and other security staff around them, the filing says.
Trump filed the lawsuit in December seeking US$10 billion in damages from the BBC, accusing it of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices.
The allegations centre on the way a 2024 documentary edited a speech Trump gave on January 6, 2021, before protesters attacked the Capitol in Washington. The lawsuit accuses the BBC of “splicing together two entirely separate parts of President Trump’s speech” to “intentionally misrepresent the meaning of what President Trump said”.
It added that the editing was “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 US presidential election.
The BBC has apologised to Trump for the misleading edit but said it had not defamed him.

The investigation remains ongoing. The identity of the deceased had not been released as of Sunday, pending confirmation by the Fayette County Coroner’s Office. Police have urged anyone with information about the shooting to contact investigators.

Li on Saturday said the ministry’s publicity budget has been slashed for a second consecutive year.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The ministry’s proposed publicity budget of NT$59.43 million was also deleted from last fiscal year’s general budget, while an additional NT$280 million budget request was rejected, he added.
Li said he initially found it hard to understand why the ministry has been targeted in the past few years, as the ministry’s budget accounts for less than 1 percent of the general budget.
He said he believes it is part of the opposition parties’ plan to “eliminate the nation by eliminating its culture,” he said, quoting poet Gong Zizhen (龔自珍), who wrote: “To destroy a nation, first erase its history; to destroy a people, first destroy its culture.”
“To silence a nation’s voice, first cut its media communications budget,” Li said, calling it a “horrendous” plan by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP).
About NT$1 billion from the ministry’s budget was cut, which undermines Taiwan’s ability to communicate with the international community and harms local cultural workers and organizations, he said.
A budget cut for two consecutive years has severely impacted subsidized people and organizations, while freezing and slashing the already modest PTS budget would mean funding cuts for struggling production teams that rely on PTS grants, he said.
Taiwan Creative Content Agency had already signed contracts for all activities in the second half of the year, he said, questioning how it could continue operating after its funding was slashed.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Rosalia Wu (吳思瑤) said the KMT suppressed Taiwanese culture during the martial law era, and now KMT and TPP lawmakers have become Chinese collaborators by acting as “executioners of culture.”
In response, KMT Legislator Lo Chih-chiang (羅智強) yesterday questioned whether Li was defending public policy or his job.
Saying that the PTS-affiliated English-language channel TaiwanPlus was set to receive almost NT$10 billion in funding over eight years, calling its performance lackluster, “shouldn’t such a disaster be subject to review?” he asked.
Rather than reform plans and demonstrating the effectiveness of ministry programs, Li had chosen to politicize the issue by accusing lawmakers of seeking to “destroy the nation and erase its history,” Lo said.
KMT Legislator Lo Ting-wei (羅廷瑋), who serves as the convener of the legislative Education and Culture Committee, criticized Li for calling the budget cuts an attempt to “‘destroy the country, people and culture,’ as if questioning the Ministry of Culture were equivalent to harming Taiwan’s culture.”
“The culture ministry is not synonymous with culture itself, nor is the DPP the sole representative of Taiwan,” he said. “The responsibility of those in power is to create a better environment for culture to thrive, not to claim ownership of it. Nor should they hide behind culture whenever they face scrutiny and portray all critics as enemies of culture.”
TPP caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) called Li’s remarks “fearmongering,” saying that the legislature reviewed the budget and exercised oversight lawfully.
The ministry still has more than NT$28 billion under the latest budget allocation, he said, adding that Li should step down if the ministry could not deliver results.

Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine running
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:56 UTC
01:41:56 KST

The Japanese yen has slid back towards 160 to the dollar, despite last month’s extraordinary US-Japanese intervention. Traders are betting that its role as a cheap funding pipeline for global finance would continue. Earlier this month the US President Donald Trump stepped in to help Tokyo stabilize its currency.
“Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor,” Trump explained. More help is likely to be on its way.
However, this is less a rescue of the yen than an attempt by US secretary of the treasury Scott Bessent to preserve a cash spigot that benefits the US. Japan’s ultra-cheap money has become a global funding utility: bankers borrow yen, sell them for dollars and buy higher-returning US assets, notably tech shares. Rising US stock markets support collateral and investment. Japan’s “carry trade” is one of the reasons Wall Street can lever hundreds of billions into artificial intelligence (AI). Research suggests AI sucks up more than 1 percent of US GDP.
Washington wants to keep this tap open, but not at the cost of a collapsing yen or US treasury sales. This column predicted this in April, warning that Tokyo’s monetary choices had bound US markets to the yen trade. What Bessent did was to sell at least US$10 billion in euros and buy yen to arrest its slide to a 40-year low. Not telling the Europeans said it all: allies matter to Washington only when they are useful.
Traders are probing US resolve. Rising oil prices, driven by US-Iran tensions, stoke Japan’s inflation and weaken the yen. Suppose it slides back to 164 yen to the dollar? Tokyo might respond with aggressive rate rises. This would be unlikely, as it would choke off the investment cycle that Japan is trying to create. It could also trigger a chaotic market unwind: higher rates shrink the gap between investors’ returns and yen borrowing; a stronger yen also makes yen-denominated debts costlier to repay; investors then sell US assets to buy the yen needed to close their positions. That strengthens the yen further, inflicting bigger losses and forcing more US asset sales. A currency correction could quickly become a Wall Street rout.
If Bessent dislikes that option, he hates the alternative: Japan selling its US$1.1 trillion treasury pile to buy yen. Dumping US debt would drive yields higher – and leave Washington with a costlier interest bill. Instead, Bessent has allowed Japan to borrow dollars against its treasuries and use those dollars to buy yen. He has used a Federal Reserve lending facility to help – and wants its US$60 billion daily limit substantially increased. This would give Tokyo room to stabilize the yen without having to choose between abandoning its reflationary program and selling treasuries.
If Bessent gets his way, the Fed could turn a substantial portion of Japan’s trillion-dollar hoard of US government securities into cash. Argentina showed Bessent would put US firepower behind currencies, spending billions to prop up the peso. Japan is the bigger challenge. He is asking traders: Are you sure that you want to return to 164 yen to the dollar? He has form as a currency trader. Bessent made George Soros a billion dollars in 1992 by selling pounds and forcing sterling from the European exchange rate mechanism. In 2013, he helped George Soros make another billion dollars betting against the Japanese currency. Margaret Thatcher famously said that “you can’t buck the market.” Scott Bessent is saying you can — as long you rewrite its rules.

The new rules, which take effect on Sept. 15, expand the power of authorities to restrict travel on national, industrial and technological security grounds, question travelers about their reasons for leaving and inspect electronic data. Taiwanese who do not support the ruling party should not dismiss the warnings as fearmongering or propaganda. Beijing applies its “anti-secession” laws indiscriminately, an official said recently while presenting a report on proposed amendments to combat China’s efforts at transnational repression. Chinese
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

The group, led by former Polish prime minister Beata Szydlo, also met Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), a gesture spanning Taiwan’s political divide. For most Taiwanese observers, this was a pleasant, if minor, diplomatic event. It was much more than that — and the timing matters. Within the same fortnight, Hudson Institute senior fellow Ken Moriyasu said in the Washington Examiner

National Human Rights Commission criticizes caning proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:56 UTC
01:41:56 KST

Judicial caning, one of three referendum proposals approved by the Legislature, violates international human rights standards enshrined in Taiwan’s legal system, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) said yesterday.
In a statement, the NHRC said that while it understood public concern over serious crimes and the need to strengthen crime prevention, criminal policy should be based on constitutional and human rights principles as well as scientific evidence.
The commission said that caning constitutes corporal punishment involving elements of humiliation and degradation, making it incompatible with protections under the UN’s International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).
Photo: CNA
As the ICCPR has been incorporated into Taiwan’s legal system, the NHRC said that government agencies and courts are expected to uphold the protections outlined in the covenant.
The referendum proposal, initiated by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), asks: “Do you agree that the government should enact laws to establish a special penal system (caning), pronounced by a court and executed in accordance with the law, for sexual assault crimes, child abuse and major or complex aggravated fraud to deter continuous criminal activities?”
It passed 52-51 on Friday last week, along with two others that concern the use of traffic fines and the abolition of Taiwan’s non-nuclear energy policy.
If approved by the Central Election Commission (CEC), the three referendums could be held alongside the Nov. 28 local elections.
According to the CEC, it is scheduled to review the three proposals at its Aug. 21 commission meeting and announce whether they qualify as referendums.
Under the Referendum Act (公民投票法), the Legislature must send approved proposals to the CEC within 10 days. The CEC must determine whether they meet the legal requirements for a referendum and, if approved, announce the referendum questions and other relevant information at least 90 days before polling day.

DPP scorns premier’s frozen salary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:55 UTC
01:41:55 KST

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Chung Chia-pin (鍾佳濱) yesterday said the opposition parties’ move to freeze Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) salary was illegal and unconstitutional.
The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan on Friday last week passed the central government’s annual budget and approved a proposal by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) to freeze Cho’s salary from September through December, the first such instance in Taiwan’s constitutional history.
Weng accused President William Lai (賴清德) and Cho of acting unconstitutionally and illegally, saying: “To deal with a rogue government, we would rather starve it to death than fatten it up.”
Photo: CNA
Chung yesterday said the Legislative Yuan’s oversight powers over political appointees are limited to “holding them politically accountable.” When it comes to substantive disciplinary action involving violations of the law or dereliction of duty, the constitutional system clearly divides responsibilities in which courts handle legal violations, while the Control Yuan can issue corrective measures or initiate impeachment proceedings for dereliction of duty, he said. Impeachment cases are then referred to the Public Functionary Disciplinary Sanction Commission, which can impose penalties including suspension from duty, leave of absence, suspension of pay, or a reduction in salary or rank, he added.
“Unlike career civil servants, political appointees do not enjoy tenure protections and may be required to take political responsibility or step down with the head of government,” Chung said.
By bypassing the Control Yuan’s impeachment process and the commission, the opposition lawmakers are using the budget-review process to directly “freeze” the salaries of individual political appointees, allowing the Legislative Yuan to encroach on the Control Yuan’s powers through control of the budget, he said.
Former Constitutional Court Justice Huang Hung-hsia (黃虹霞) said yesterday that although the Legislative Yuan has the power to review the budget, it cannot use that authority to punish specific public officials.
Doing so could exceed the legislature’s budgetary powers, infringe on executive authority and undermine the separation of powers, she said.
Freezing the premier’s salary is unconstitutional, she said, emphasizing that the Legislative Yuan cannot place itself above the Constitution and become a "super-Constitution" that is itself not bound by constitutional rules.

US pulls last aircraft carrier in western Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

US President Donald Trump’s war against Iran is stretching the limits of US aircraft carriers and leaving the western Pacific without one of the key US warships as China shows more signs of aggression.
The USS George Washington is departing the Pacific and expected to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East amid growing concerns about mental health and supply issues aboard the long-deployed carrier. The Lincoln has had its time at sea extended from its original May return date to support operations against Iran.
The lack of a US carrier in the Pacific might be short-lived if the US Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. However, it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some US sailors ragged, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the western hemisphere, analysts say.
Photo: AFP
“The administration says that the Pacific is supposed to be the most important behind the western hemisphere,” said Greg Poling, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Instead, the US is “doing the exact opposite” of its previously expressed goal of pulling out of the Middle East.
US allies in the Pacific are unsettled over the unpredictability of the Republican administration, while Beijing “is quite happy with US distraction, with the frustration of US allies and partners,” Poling said.
Beijing sees the US military presence in the region as a threat to China’s rise and an obstacle to its ambition to seize Taiwan. However, the US has argued that the Pacific region is too important economically to lose.
No one expects China to invade Taiwan because a US aircraft carrier has left the region. However, the carrier’s absence gives the Chinese another opportunity to show its strength, said Bryan Clark, a former US Navy submariner who is a defense analyst at the Hudson Institute.
“They’re using this as part of the narrative to demonstrate to the Philippines, to Japan, to Indonesia and others that the US is not the big dog in the western Pacific anymore,” Clark said. “They would just prefer that countries in the region decide that China is the bigger power and the US is not able to guarantee their security anymore.”
China conducted naval exercises last week with Indonesia and recently has shown signs of aggression toward Japan and the Philippines, two key US allies that also have territorial disputes with Beijing.
China carried out military drills this month near the Scarborough Shoal (Huangyan Island, 黃岩島) in the South China Sea. Taiwan, China and the Philippines have claims over the shoal. Last month, a Chinese guided-missile destroyer conducted a live-fire exercise off Japan’s southernmost island of Okinotori.
US Admiral Frank Bradley, head of the US Special Operations Command, has been trying to reassure regional allies of Washington’s commitment. He was in Manila on Thursday, telling his Filipino counterparts that US special operations forces are ready to step up joint exercises to strengthen the countries’ alliance. He also is expected to travel to Japan.
“We have the ability to project force, the United States, anywhere on the globe,” Bradley said. “And when the threat in the region of the Middle East has been attended to, we will redeploy and reorient, and be able to project that force wherever else it might be required.”
“I also feel very confident in the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ ability to protect their sovereignty here and for us to remain close with them,” he said.
Evan Sankey, a policy analyst at the Cato Institute who focuses on US policy toward China, said aircraft carriers provide psychological assurance to US allies.
The absence of carriers in the region “adds to the general sense that the US is distracted by events in the Middle East,” Sankey said.
Trump has relied heavily on aircraft carriers to support military operations during his second term. For example, the USS Gerald R. Ford returned home in mid-May after an 11-month deployment, the longest since the Vietnam War, during which it supported the US fight against Iran and the capture of former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
The Ford had experienced a fire in a laundry space that forced the carrier to turn around and return to the Mediterranean Sea for repairs and left hundreds of sailors without places to sleep. Meanwhile, the Lincoln has spent a record uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days. Democratic lawmakers have been calling for investigations and greater visibility into conditions aboard the ship.
Warships and their crews can only handle so much, said Robert Farley, who teaches national security and diplomacy at the University of Kentucky and often writes about aircraft carriers.
“People don’t get enough rest. It’s psychologically exhausting, and R&R [Rest and Recuperation] is part of keeping the crew healthy,” Farley said. “Sometimes it’s framed as: ‘These people haven’t had a vacation,’ but we are dealing with well-known limits on the capacity of a crew to operate at top efficiency over time, and that just declines.”
The squeeze on the nation’s aircraft carriers stems from the lack of preparation and planning for the Iran war, Clark said.
“If we were going to mobilize to do this kind of conflict, and we anticipated it might go this long, we might have done some changes to the carrier schedule to make sure more would be available,” Clark said.
Clark said the US Navy has 11 aircraft carriers and typically deploys two or three at a time. However, it could soon deploy four if the USS Theodore Roosevelt leaves San Diego for the Middle East, allowing the Washington to return to Pacific.
However, the massive warships would need maintenance, likely causing a bottleneck at the nation’s only two carrier shipyards.
“We’ll end up with a maintenance debt that needs to be paid for the next few years,” Clark said. “We’ll probably have less carrier presence than we’ve had in the previous years, because carriers will be lined up to get into the shipyard.”
Michael Swaine, a senior research fellow in the Quincy Institute’s East Asia Program, questions the future need for aircraft carriers as warfare rapidly changes.
Carriers can be more easily targeted with drones and missiles, particularly by an adversary such as China, while smaller ships and submarines can be as effective in striking targets as the fighter jets that launch off a carrier, Swaine said.
Top US Navy officials have indicated a desire to move away from a heavy reliance on carriers. US Fleet Forces Command Admiral Daryl Caudle in February said that he wanted to convince commanders to use smaller, newer ships and other assets instead of consistently turning to huge aircraft carriers.

Beijing has plowed billions of dollars into its space program in the past few years to achieve what Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) calls the country’s “space dream.” Monday’s rare launch failure involved a Long March 7A carrier rocket, which lifted off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China’s southernmost province of Hainan at 8:02pm, state news agency Xinhua said. Morocco arrests at least 111 migrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:51 UTC
01:41:51 KST

Moroccan police on Saturday arrested at least 111 people as they tried to enter Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, amid tightened security on both sides of the border after social media posts called for another mass migrant crossing.
The attempted crossing came two weeks after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, sparking tensions within the EU and fueling anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died in the attempt to reach European soil.
Those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city opposite Ceuta, a source in the Moroccan Ministry of the Interior said.
Photo: AP
Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse groups of migrants gathered on hills about 3km from the border, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
The Moroccan ministry ordered their journalists to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation, EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE reported.
In Ceuta, Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police heavily patrolled the enclave’s main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after the deadly crossing attempt on July 30.
Madrid has since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police from mainland Spain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The Spanish Ministry of the Interior said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.
“We’ll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of July 30 from happening again,” Spanish Minister of the Interior Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Thursday.
About 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, Grande-Marlaska said.
Hundreds were sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.
Grande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the enclave, travel to mainland Spain or obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability.
Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he added.
Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring “the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin” calling for a mass crossing on Saturday, warning it would prosecute organizers and participants.
There was reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Spain’s other North African enclave, Melilla.
Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra. However, witnesses said that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes toward Fnideq.
One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the border.
Many of the young people who entered Ceuta on July 30 were fishing, swimming or washing at Tarajal beach on Friday.
Driss Sadik, a 22-year-old from Fez who said he swam for five hours to reach Ceuta, urged others not to follow his example.
“The important thing I would advise people trying to cross: Don’t cross now, my brothers. You’re only going to suffer,” he said.
The warning was echoed by Adil Jamil, 17.
“Those who enter aren’t going to benefit from anything. There will just be more and more of us, and they won’t find a solution for all,” he said.
Jamil said that the mass border crossings were “planned by the people” who pick a date, gather in Fnideq and cross together to find strength in numbers.
“If I had stayed with my parents, I would’ve died slowly. But if I risk my life, arrive and build my future ... it will be better,” he said.

Bangladesh win hailed as biggest Test triumph
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:49 UTC
01:41:49 KST

Former players and fans yesterday hailed Bangladesh’s first Test win in Australia as the country’s biggest achievement in the five-day game, saying it could be a turning point for their cricketing ambitions.
Bangladesh sealed a historic nine-wicket thrashing inside four days in Darwin, marking their first Test victory on Australian soil and only second against their formidable opponents.
“This is, I think, the biggest achievement for Bangladesh cricket in Test matches,” former captain Akram Khan said. “It was something we dreamed of, but perhaps none of us expected Bangladesh to dominate and win like this. We are extremely happy and proud.”
Photo: EPA
Akram said the big win was built on a complete team performance rather than individual brilliance.
Fast bowler Hasan Mahmud laid the foundation with a career-best 6-55 as Australia were bowled out for 198 on the opening day.
Bangladesh then took charge through Tanzid Hasan’s maiden Test century, backed by important contributions from captain Najmul Hossain Shanto and all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz.
“This is the biggest win so far for Bangladesh in any format,” Najmul said. “Going forward we want to do something special in the future.”
Fresh from fielding a video call from Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Najmul said he was determined to make sure his team played just as well in the second Test, which starts in the North Queensland city of Mackay on Saturday.
Former spinner and national selector Abdur Razzak said the victory strengthened Bangladesh’s case for more Test opportunities against Australia.
This was just the seventh Test match between the teams.
“If you look at this Test and our position in the World Test Championship, there is no reason why we should not get more opportunities,” he said.
Razzak credited years of investment in domestic first-class cricket and Bangladesh’s Test program for the team’s progress.
Former Bangladesh women’s captain Rumana Ahmed said the team’s emphatic all-round display made the win especially significant.
“Hasan Mahmud was back in the team after a long time and he did very well, taking six wickets in the first innings. That was a major factor,” she said. “Tanzid’s hundred was historic for him as well. The batters took responsibility and scoring more than 400 in the first innings was extraordinary.”
The result was all the more remarkable because Bangladesh had been bowled out for just 54 by a Cricket Australia XI in a warm-up match days earlier.
Rahman congratulated the team on a video call with the players.
“We’re all eagerly waiting to welcome you home,” he wrote on social media.
Die-hard fans also savored the win.
“As a cricket fan of Bangladesh we don’t get occasions to celebrate very often,” Sefat Hasan Sumaiya said. “Winning against Australia in Australia seems surreal. It feels like a national festival.”
Another fan, Sahadat Ahmed Bhuiya, called it one of the defining victories in the nation’s cricket history.
“Winning a Test in Australia within four days is a huge achievement,” he said.

The pain is most noticeable in the produce section, where the past six months have been marked by a succession of price spikes in tomatoes, lettuce and apples. Before that, it was coffee, beef and, for a real throwback, eggs. These events can feel idiosyncratic: The lettuce crop was hit by a heat wave in Arizona (driving up prices before Cyclospora drove them down); beef prices were pushed up by the New World screwworm cattle parasite; and Florida’s tomato crop was hit by a cold snap.
However, it is no coincidence that these “one-off” force-majeure-type episodes suddenly seem so frequent and quickly reflected in prices. A litany of bad policy decisions from US President Donald Trump has made the producers and purveyors of these products more susceptible to the shocks that nature inevitably hoists upon us. And once passed on, corporations are loathing bringing prices back down after the shock fades.
Illustration:Yusha
Each new episode heaps pressure on households, which report becoming more price sensitive about their groceries. It is death by a thousand cuts for an American public that has been digging into savings to sustain spending after more than five years of high inflation. Those on lower incomes have been further burdened by a cutback in federal food assistance through Trump’s signature budget package.
It helps explain why Americans feel despondent about the economy, despite strong corporate profits and a booming stock market, and why the cost of living — the single most important issue among a plurality of adults — is once again the focus of November’s midterm elections. In the more puerile online world of GOP talking heads, the issue is manifesting itself as an acrimonious and viral burrito debate, which is simultaneously ludicrous and revealing.
Take the tomato example, a factor in the burrito saga (see: salsa). When the cold snap hit Florida’s tomato crop this year, it affected a sector that was already contending with a 17.1 percent duty on most Mexican tomato imports. Although the tariffs went into force last year, the knock-on effects have percolated slowly. According to the US Department of Agriculture’s analysis, the tariffs led Mexican farmers to plant fewer tomatoes (including switching to other crops). When Florida’s tomato-growing regions experienced a series of damaging freezes from late December through February, the supply chain was less able to replace the lost domestic output.
Even in areas where tariff errors were short-lived, consumers have felt enduring pain from policy volatility. The absurd 50 percent levy on Brazilian products last year initially sent coffee prices soaring. The Trump administration belatedly exempted coffee and tea from its “reciprocal tariffs,” but retail prices did not respond accordingly. Consumer coffee prices in the consumer price index (CPI) are still up about 25 percent from the end of 2024. The import-heavy spices business offers another example: After the Supreme Court invalidated many of Trump’s tariffs, McCormick & Co notched a surge in its gross profit margin, due in part to tariff refunds. There was no corresponding sign of price cuts on its earnings call or in the CPI.
With apples, the administration’s immigration crackdown might have contributed to what is now a 10 percent price jump in the past year. Apples are overwhelmingly produced in the state of Washington, but are known for their labor-intensive harvests. As immigration raids roiled communities around the country, reports described an environment of fear around Washington’s orchards, and trade group US Apple flagged skyrocketing labor costs. Many crops have also been affected by higher fertilizer and transportation costs, pushed up by the US-Iran war.
For all its salience among consumers, food inflation typically gets thrown out in economists’ and policymakers’ calculations of what they call “core” inflation — an egregious mistake. The original rationale was that, like energy, food prices were extremely volatile, making it hard to see where inflation was heading. That was true in the 1970s, when a focus on core inflation became popular.
It is not really true any longer of food: The grocery category (“food at home,” in Bureau of Labor Statistics jargon) is no more volatile than the nondurable goods category included in core inflation, research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City shows. The farming business is still subject to shock-inducing droughts and pests, but well over half the prices we pay for food at home comes from packaging, shipping and retailing.
We also eat out more than we did in the 1970s, and restaurant prices include very large labor costs. Most importantly, food costs loom large in households’ inflationary psychology, and economists believe that inflation expectations are self-fulfilling. Consumers might not notice changes in the price of dishwashers, since they buy one every decade or so, but they instantly take note of the tomatoes, bread and cold cuts that they buy twice a week.
Food inflation, in that sense, provides hints not just of where inflation has been, but of where it is going. It is running at 3.1 percent on a year-over-year basis — not dumpster-fire bad, but well above the 1.7 percent average of the 2010 to 2019 period, before the pandemic snarled supply chains and the Trump administration’s policies then reignited pressures.
The GOP influencer burrito debate is a curious, if misguided, example of the food-inflation zeitgeist. Andrew Kolvet of Turning Point USA shared on X what he described as the view of a college student: “A burrito shouldn’t cost US$20.” Podcast producer Joel Berry countered with: “Last night, my wife made homemade burritos for our family of 8 and it cost less than US$20 total for everyone. I’m beginning to think the affordability crisis is really an ‘I don’t know how to cook’ crisis.”
Burritos are actually at the intersection of high ingredient prices (tomatoes etc.) and higher restaurant prices (labor shortages). And yes, Trump deserves part of the blame.
Core inflation including food is about 2.6 percent, where it has hovered for about two years, thanks in part to a constellation of policies perfectly tailored to make every Florida freeze and cattle parasite worse on consumers than it would have otherwise been. That is not horrible, but the lack of a downward trajectory is — core inflation with food is stuck. No wonder Americans are frustrated with their food bills and increasingly blaming their politicians.

AI could intensify Chinese election interference: DPP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:45 UTC
01:41:45 KST

Beijing has established a comprehensive election interference industry supply chain for Taiwan, using artificial intelligence (AI) to target specific groups, impersonate people with highly realistic and tailored language and social media ecosystems with deepfake videos before elections, the Democratic Progressive Party’s China Affairs Department said yesterday.
The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) continues to expand its efforts to influence politics and society in Taiwan by combining economic and military threats, launching cyberattacks and spreading misinformation, the department said.
This can be seen from incidents such as when Taiwanese K-Pop singer Chou Tzu-yu (周子瑜) was criticized by Chinese Internet users after she appeared on a South Korean TV program holding the Republic of China flag and identifying herself as Taiwanese in 2016, the proliferation of disinformation and public-opinion manipulation in local elections in 2018, “united front” information warfare ahead of the 2020 presidential election and the period following then-US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022.
Photo courtesy of the Democratic Progressive Party’s China Affairs Department
AI has enabled the CCP to more effectively interfere with Taiwanese elections, the department said.
The CCP is expected to continue to use AI to broaden its interference, the department says.
Beijing could use AI to produce political messages that targets are likely to believe by analyzing people’s personal data, political inclination, social media activity and online behavior, the department said.
AI could be used by the CCP to mimic Taiwanese vernacular, tap into local issues, manage fake social media accounts, impersonate public personalities and infiltrate online group chats, it said.
False audio recordings, videos, endorsements and scandals could be generated using AI hours before voting, leaving officials without time to deal with them, it said.
The election interference supply chain functions by collecting voters’ data and issues widely discussed in public in Taiwan, the department said.
“Messages are subsequently distributed through China’s collaborators in Taiwan, their social media accounts and other content platforms,” the department said. “They then adjust their targeting strategies by the data collected.”
The department said the use of AI has significantly lowered the cost of producing disinformation, with the most dangerous aspect being the ability to generate false content that people would easily believe at a speed faster than it can be debunked.
“We want to remind people to find the original source of the information that they come across and verify it with credible news media and fact-checking agencies,” it said. “Don’t rush to believe information with unknown sources or sensational statements and those without original content.”

Luxury Chinese shoppers look a little bit different after the slump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

China’s luxury-spending slump has comfortably turned the corner, but what has emerged looks markedly different to the pre-pandemic heyday. Brands hoping to capitalize on the recovery would need to adjust to a new set of consumer priorities.
First, the good news. The world’s second-largest high-end retail market after the US is finally expanding again. Although it tripled in size in the five years to 2021, the sector shrank a year later as a result of the sweeping lockdowns that brought major cities such as Shanghai to a standstill — and again in 2024 after a property rout sapped consumer confidence, Daxue Consulting said. However, strong earnings from Cie Financiere Richemont SA to Ralph Lauren Corp suggest a rebound that took hold in the final months of last year has gained momentum. McKinsey & Co reckons China’s luxury industry would grow by as much as 6 percent a year to 2030.
European and US luxury houses and their investors are counting on Chinese consumers’ renewed appetites, but they need to manage their expectations. Although the pace of growth might be faster than other regions, it pales in comparison with the double-digit rates of the boom years.
The reality is that Chinese shoppers’ spending power on high-end products has peaked, at least for now. They are not the force they were in 2019, when Bain & Co estimated that China accounted for 90 percent of the growth in the luxury industry globally. As a result, they would also struggle to make up for the impact of the Iran war on the important Middle Eastern markets, where luxury sales have been hammered.
Structural changes to the economy make a return to those days unlikely. Beijing continues to prioritize export-led growth over policies that would meaningfully boost personal consumption, while a tough job market is putting additional pressure on younger shoppers. These factors have reshaped consumer behavior in two important and potentially lasting ways.
The relationship between China’s rising middle class and luxury has changed. During the gogo years, consumers stretched themselves financially to buy entry-level products such as leather handbags from high-end labels. However, shoppers are now more price sensitive and increasingly choosing higher-value-for-money products. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the growing preference for prestige beauty, which is more affordable than traditional luxury staples such as leather goods. The latest earnings results bear this out.
L’Oreal SA sales in North Asia were up 4.5 percent in its most recent quarter, a marked improvement from last year’s flat results. The performance was driven by 10 percent growth of the Luxe division — which includes Lancome, Kiehl’s and Helena Rubenstein — in China, chief executive officer Nicolas Hieronimus said in an earnings call last month. The mass market, on the other hand, had “turned negative,” he added.
It is a similar picture at Estee Lauder. High single-digit growth in the quarter ended March was led by prestige brands such as La Mer and Estee Lauder Supreme. Beiersdorf AG said there was “strong momentum” in China for the La Prairie line. By contrast, Chinese demand was flat at LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, even as its beauty emporium Sephora did well.
It all tallies with the idea that younger consumers have become more cautious and selective with their spending. A survey from consultancy Oliver Wyman and the Tax Free World Association found Chinese travelers expressed a much greater propensity to buy beauty and luxury apparel rather than higher-ticket items such as watches and leather goods.
Secondly, fewer Chinese are venturing overseas. Compared with 2019, when the majority of luxury purchases were made abroad, most buying now happens domestically.
Households are still bruised by the five-year-old housing slump, which would take time to resolve. This matters enormously in a country where about 70 percent of wealth is tied up in property. Last month, the authorities officially designated real estate as “durable goods” in the same category as automobiles and air-conditioners. It was an honest assessment of its diminished place in the Chinese economy: No longer a seemingly inexhaustible store of net worth, but an asset that depreciates with age.
For years, high-end retailers could count on China to deliver extraordinary growth almost regardless of what they sold. That era is over. The recovery taking shape is more measured and discerning. The winners would be ones that recognize that the old Chinese luxury shopper is not coming back.

China wants to block drone bill: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:43 UTC
01:41:43 KST

The Legislative Yuan is slated to hold cross-caucus negotiations on 14 versions of a draft uncrewed vehicle act on Thursday, amid rumors that Beijing is pressuring some Taiwanese politicians to block passage of a special bill proposed by the Ministry of National Defense to procure military drones and uncrewed vessels.
A source in Beijing said the Chinese Communist Party has been using its United Front Work Department and Taiwan Affairs Office to pressure Taiwanese politicians who are friendly toward Beijing, pushing them to block the Executive Yuan’s proposed special act to fund military uncrewed vehicles.
The proposed legislation would allocate up to NT$210 billion (US$6.55 billion) from August next year through December 2031 to procure coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, coastal attack drones and small uncrewed surface vessels designed for attack missions.
Photo: CNA
The source said staff units of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have conducted several wargame simulations of Taiwan’s plans to build up its drone forces in coordination with the US.
Beijing reportedly believes the deployment could significantly undermine the PLA’s strategic advantage in the Taiwan Strait and weaken its strategic deterrence against Japan and the Philippines. The PLA has recommended to the Chinese Central Military Commission that Taiwan’s drone buildup be blocked.
Beijing could accept a version of the legislation focused on “demilitarization,” but wants the budget to be subject to annual, item-by-item review and approval, the source said.
They said blocking the Executive Yuan’s special budget could also pressure the administration of President William Lai (賴清德) to find alternative ways to complete its planned military buildup, giving the Chinese military more time to develop countermeasures.
The Legislative Yuan’s Economics, Foreign Affairs and National Defense, and Finance committees on July 27 jointly reviewed the 14 versions of the legislation. After nearly six hours of discussion, lawmakers failed to reach agreement on the bill, including its responsible authority, spending cap and implementation period. The bills passed the committee stage, but must undergo cross-party negotiations before being considered by the full legislature.
The Legislative Yuan on Friday approved NT$63.4 billion in uncrewed vehicle spending, including a six-year NT$44.2 billion industrial development program proposed by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and NT$19.2 billion in drone procurement budgets proposed by government agencies.
Executive Yuan Secretary-General Xavier Chang (張惇涵) on Saturday said the opposition should support the administration’s special act if it supports the armed forces.
He said opposition lawmakers previously blocked drone-related spending, adding that the upcoming negotiations would show whether they truly support the country’s drone development and national defense.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) yesterday said the opposition had supported the NT$63.4 billion in related spending.
Hsu said the KMT’s proposed legislation would invest NT$240 billion over six years in the uncrewed vehicle industry, more than the NT$210 billion proposed by the Executive Yuan.
The KMT favors funding the program through annual budgets rather than a special budget, Hsu said, adding that this would allow the legislature to review procurement results, industrial policy and progress toward domestic production each year.
She said the KMT supports drone development and greater defense autonomy, but wants greater scrutiny of how the money is spent, what equipment is purchased, who produces it, how much is manufactured domestically and whether the equipment meets the military’s operational needs.

Crown-of-thorns to be removed to protect park reefs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

The National Park Service’s Marine National Park Headquarters has stepped up efforts to remove crown-of-thorns starfish in Dongsha Atoll National Park and South Penghu Marine National Park to protect coral reefs.
The world has experienced four mass coral bleaching events due to the impact of global climate change.
The outbreak of crown-of-thorns starfish — which consume coral reefs like locusts would — has affected coral reefs globally, accelerating the risk of coral reef ecosystem collapse.
Photo courtesy of the National Park Service’s Marine National Park Headquarters
The headquarters said it has stepped up the monitoring and removal of crown-of-thorns starfish in the two national parks.
Latest data showed that 133 crown-of-thorns starfish have been removed, with South Penghu Marine National Park’s Dongji East Waters Recreation Area having relatively more crown-of-thorns starfish.
To prevent the “coral-reef killers” from spreading and damaging the coral reef ecosystems, the headquarters in May initiated a marine patrol to remove the starfish.
The headquarters asked tourists visiting Penghu and local business operators to jointly safeguard the ocean of the four islands of Southern Penghu by reporting crown-of-thorns starfish sightings.
To prevent adult crown-of-thorns starfish from proliferating and jeopardizing coral reef ecosystems, monitoring at fixed survey stations has continued this year with the scope and frequency of underwater patrols increased, the headquarters said.
The strategy of “early detection and prompt removal” was adopted to effectively control the density of crown-of-thorns starfish and reduce the risk and scale of outbreaks, it said.
Fourteen large-scale patrols have been conducted, with professional divers carrying out starfish removal operations under safe and compliant conditions, the headquarters said.
A total of 133 crown-of-thorns starfish were removed, most of which were medium or small-size starfish with a body length ranging from 15cm to 25cm, amounting to 89 individual starfish, it said.
No significant coral bleaching events were detected in areas where removal efforts were done, the headquarters said.
The headquarters would continue to follow up on the removal of crown-of-thorns starfish and monitor the ecological environment, it said.
Waters of Dongji Island (東吉嶼) would be prioritized for starfish removal, while close monitoring would continue for the other islands, the headquarters said.

Michael Mazza on Taiwan: The US Coast Guard to the rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing.
Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets. If Chinese coast guard vessels, for example, far outclass their Philippine counterparts, should the Philippines respond with warships? Can Taiwan stop Chinese fighter jets from crossing the Taiwan Strait median line without shooting them down? Such steps could be construed as escalations, invite Chinese escalation in turn, and put allies and partners like the US in a difficult position: whether to engage in military confrontation with China or let a friend blow in the wind.
Beijing has used this approach to great effect. Since 2013, the People’s Republic of China has literally built a string of islands across the South China Sea, used “fishing boats” to enforce sovereignty claims, continually pushed boundaries in deploying military forces near Taiwan, and engaged in “law enforcement” activities in far distant waters. It can now project power far from its southern shores and claim effective control of numerous contested reefs and islets, and it has normalized the daily military coercion of Taiwan.
The US has had no real answer for this slow-motion onslaught. It has used freedom of navigation operations (FONOPs), in an attempt to uphold broadly held views of international maritime law. It has also maintained and further invested in its forward presence in the Western Pacific, which plays an important role in deterring outright aggression. But the fact is that the American approach has done little to change facts on the ground: operating in the interstitial space between peace and war, China continues its creeping advance.
The US’ approach may now be changing. In an incident near Second Thomas Shoal last month, a Philippine sailor was injured after a Chinese coastguardsman struck him with a wooden baton. Help, it turned out, was not far off. “In fact, there was a US Coast Guard vessel in the region at the time this happened,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio revealed a few days later, “and it actually helped stand between the two sides and allowed the injured individual to be rescued and brought back for medical treatment.”
The following week, the American Institute in Taiwan published a photo of US and Taiwan Coast Guard vessels sailing side by side. According to AIT, the two agencies are closely coordinating on multiple joint maritime objectives.
In mid-July, the US Coast Guard announced that its Expeditionary Cutter Squadron, historically known as Patrol Forces Southwest Asia, an expeditionary cutter squadron of six fast response cutters, was in the process of relocating from Bahrain to Guam and the Pacific Islands. This marks a significant boost to Coast Guard capabilities in the Western Pacific. “Coast Guard forces have always adapted to meet urgent national needs,” said the Commandant of the Coast Guard, Admiral Kevin Lunday. “Our expeditionary cutter forces provide Combatant Commands with uniquely capable maritime assets, leveraging the Coast Guard’s military and law enforcement authorities to advance US national security objectives in the Western Pacific and Western Hemisphere.”
This new deployment gives Admiral Samuel Paparo, Commander of Pacific Command, new tools he can use in creative ways to complicate life for China. When an American cutter interposed itself between Chinese and Philippine vessels in the South China Sea, it acted proactively to put the onus for further escalation on the Chinese baton-wielders. And when Taiwanese and American cutters linked up in unspecified waters, though presumably near Taiwan, it sent a powerful signal: Taiwan’s exercise of maritime legal authority is legitimate. The operation also conveyed a message narrowly targeted at China: next time your Coast Guard shows up in the Western Pacific for a “special maritime traffic law enforcement operation,” the US Coast Guard may be there, too.
Put simply, these activities constrain China’s freedom of action and limit the effectiveness of its gray zone operations. Where there is contestation, advances are harder to secure. If effectively integrated with other tools — including military forces, legal argumentation, diplomacy, and public messaging — American cutters could finally turn the tide on China’s insidious gains in Asia.
Michael Mazza is senior director for research at the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security (formerly the Project 2049 Institute) and a senior non-resident fellow at the Global Taiwan Institute.

Average annual personal income rises to record level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

Taiwan’s average annual personal income last year rose to a record NT$763,000 (US$23,810), with earnings increasing across all age groups on the back of strong economic growth, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said over the weekend.
People younger than 30 earned an average NT$587,000, up 5 percent from NT$559,000 in 2024, the DGBAS’ survey of household income showed.
Average annual income was NT$770,000 for those aged 30 to 34, NT$860,000 for ages 35 to 39, NT$959,000 for ages 40 to 44, and NT$886,000 for ages 55 to 64.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
Those aged 45 to 54 earned an average NT$982,000, the highest among all age groups, up 4.03 percent from a year ago, while people aged 65 or older saw the lowest income at NT$502,000, up 2.03 percent year-on-year, the survey showed.
DGBAS Counselor Lee Chia-hang (李佳航) said continued economic growth, a stable labor market, lower unemployment and increases in the minimum wage helped lift incomes across all groups, although income growth remained stronger among the highest-income households than the lowest-income group.
The DGBAS’ survey also found that average household disposable income rose 3.9 percent to a record NT$1.21 million last year from a year earlier, while the median increased 3.4 percent to NT$1.018 million.
After adjusting for household size, average per capita disposable income increased 7.4 percent to NT$450,000, while the median rose 3.2 percent to NT$367,000.
By region, Hsinchu City retained the nation’s highest average household disposable income at NT$1.604 million, up 6.7 percent from a year earlier, while neighboring Hsinchu County climbed to second place with NT$1.569 million, overtaking Taipei, where the figure stood at NT $1.554 million.
The DGBAS attributed the Hsinchu area’s strong performance to its concentration of high-tech industries centered around the Hsinchu Science Park, which has benefited in the past few years from growing business opportunities related to artificial intelligence.
Among Taiwan’s six special municipalities, Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Taichung all recorded average household disposable incomes above the national average, while Tainan and Kaohsiung fell below the average at NT $1.044 million and NT$1.206 million, respectively.
The survey also showed average household consumption expenditure increased 3.6 percent year-on-year to NT $920,000, while average household savings rose 4.9 percent to NT$290,000.

Ceremony held for Paiwan cultural alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

Academia Sinica’s Institute of Ethnology and the Kaviyangan community in Pingtung County’s Taiwu Township (泰武) yesterday formalized a cultural alliance through a traditional Paiwan masanvetjek ceremony, pledging to regard one another as siblings (vetjek).
The Tjerelai family of the Kaviyangan community also donated 36 reels of audio recordings to the institute’s collection. The recordings document key moments in the community’s history and serve as an important resource for preserving and passing on its cultural heritage.
The connection between the Institute of Ethnology and Kaviyangan Village dates back to their shared effort to safeguard a national treasure — the “mulitan” ancestral pillar, Academia Sinica President Chen Chien-jen (陳建仁) said.
Photo courtesy of the Academia Sinica via CNA
Since the joint curation of the “Returning Home: Recalling kaviyangan’s Records of Art” exhibition in 2020, the two sides accumulated six years of collaboration in holding physical and online exhibitions, building trust and deep fellowship, he said.
Yesterday’s new alliance was formed according to Paiwan tradition, and it marks a major milestone in returning knowledge to the sovereignty of the tribe.
The alliance ceremony was led by the Zingrur family, traditional leaders of the Jiaping people, and they entered the venue while tribe members shouted, intoned ancient chants and fired guns, to perform an emayam (blessing and verification of gifts) ritual.
Photo courtesy of Academia Sinica
The Zingrur family bestowed upon the Institute of Ethnology the house name Vavulengan, implying the pinnacle of academic prestige, as well as symbolizing the peaceful dwelling of the mulitan ancestral spirit pillar within the vavulengan family house.
Following the ritual, an official announcement of the alliance was made to the ancestral spirits and the tribe.
After the alliance was formed, the Jiaping donated 36 volumes of mamazangiljan ti ljaljangalan a lja zingrur oral history recordings to the institute.
The collection was personally recorded in the 2000s by Chou Lin Yi-chih (周林義治, 1923 to 2017), a younger brother of the tribe’s 17th-generation leader.
The contents cover the tribe’s founding history, shifts in traditional rituals, and historical experiences of traditional leaders in exercising regional diplomacy, which serve as crucial oral history and cultural memory for the Jiaping Tribe.
Institute of Ethnology director Jou Yuh-huey (周玉慧) said once the oral recordings enter the public cultural preservation system, the cultural vitality of indigenous people in contemporary society can be sustained through research, archiving and reinterpretation.
Chou Lin’s granson Chou Cheng-chun (周政君) said that the voice recordings left behind by his grandfather serve as an important memory repository for future generations to understand the history and culture of the Jiaping Tribe.
They also bear the strength of the tribe as it faces the changing of times and safeguards its cultural autonomy, he said.
The event concluded with the Paiwan traditions of zemiyan (a circle dance) and papukizing (a ceremony of becoming family).
The Jiaping Tribe also presented a large wooden kadang (spoon), symbolizing sharing meals from the same hearth, and both sides expressed commitment to maintaining their sibling bond and continuing to promote cultural preservation, knowledge inheritance and tribe-centered cultural revitalization.

Proactive support needed for teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

The death of an elementary-school teacher in Kaohsiung on Tuesday last week has drawn renewed attention to the pressures educators face in the workplace. The 53-year-old teacher died after falling from his residential building. According to a teachers’ union, the teacher’s wife said he had been experiencing considerable work-related stress. The also said that he had previously sought assistance in workplace disputes and had later been asked to consider transferring to another school. The school denied that any forced transfer had occurred and said it had followed appropriate procedures and regulations.
Although no direct causal relationship between the workplace disputes and his death has been established, the case raises an important question: Are existing systems doing enough to support teachers before workplace conflicts become overwhelming?
The question is particularly relevant as concerns grow over school bullying, parental complaints and challenges to teachers’ professional authority. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) has proposed measures to enhance school safety and provide teachers with better legal protections, including legal consultation, financial support for lawsuits, easier police access to schools in serious incidents and funding for schools to hire legal counsel.
The measures are welcome, but are largely reactive. Legal aid is useful only after a conflict has escalated into a formal complaint, investigation or lawsuit. What teachers need is reliable institutional support when difficulties first emerge.
Similar concerns have been raised in South Korea, where teachers have reported increasing difficulty in maintaining classroom discipline because of fears of parental complaints and administrative consequences. Such experiences suggest that teacher protections should not be understood simply as protection from legal liability. They should also address the cumulative stress created by prolonged disputes, uncertainty over professional authority and the feeling that teachers must manage serious conflicts on their own.
The Taipei City Government should adopt a more comprehensive approach. Alongside legal assistance, schools need clearer and more independent mechanisms for protecting teachers’ professional judgements and mediating disputes early.
Mental health support should also form an essential part of this system. Teachers experiencing prolonged workplace stress should have timely and confidential access to counseling and psychological support. Such services should not be treated merely as emergency interventions after a crisis, but as preventive support available throughout the conflict-resolution process.
Other countries have adopted systems to support teachers. In the UK, Education Support, an independent charity, provides teachers with a free and confidential 24-hour helpline for advice and emotional support. In addition, some schools offer Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs) that give staff access to counseling and mental health services. Teachers can arrange sessions outside working hours, including evenings and holidays, to discuss work-related stress, burnout or personal difficulties.
Legal protection matters, but it is only one part of the solution. The Kaohsiung case shows that prevention, institutional backing, early mediation and accessible mental health support are crucial for protecting teachers. A sustainable education system cannot depend solely on teachers’ personal resilience. It must provide structures that allow them to exercise professional judgement with confidence while ensuring that help is available before workplace pressures become unmanageable.
Li Hong-lin is a professor at the General Education Center of National Taiwan University of Arts.

Notes from Central Taiwan: From vaccines to drones: The anatomy of Taiwan’s political forgetting
Unknown

16:41:32 UTC
01:41:32 KST

The Tzu Chi Foundation, the globally known Buddhist charity, announced on July 21, 2021 that it had signed a deal to purchase 5 million doses of the Pfizer-BioNTech (BNT) COVID-19 vaccine. It said that the vaccine doses would be donated to the government’s COVID vaccine program. In October the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) made a public announcement thanking the Buddhist foundation and others for the 889,200 doses of the BNT vaccine they had collectively donated.
FRAUD
Earlier this month, the public was stunned to learn that prosecutors had indicted former Changhua Bar Association chairwoman, Chen Yu-hsuan (陳昱瑄), and others on suspicion of defrauding Tzu Chi of over NT$1.06 billion by falsely claiming to have special channels for purchasing BNT vaccines. According to investigators, the suspects had neither the ability nor the means to obtain the vaccine as they had claimed.
Photo courtesy of the Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office via CNA
According to local media, prosecutors said that Tzu Chi had stated that the manufacturer’s quote was US$205 million (US$41 per dose), but Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密, also known as Foxconn Technology Group, 富士康科技集團), who were also buying and donating vaccines, had a budget of approximately US$175 million (US$36 per dose). The difference was US$30 million, or roughly the equivalent of the NT$1.06 billion commission paid by Tzu Chi to the fraudsters.
The alleged fraudsters, posing as brokers, had apparently inserted themselves into Tzu Chi’s vaccine acquisition program. They told the charity that they could procure the vaccines, took the money on trust and did nothing because the vaccines were coming anyway through other channels. Incredibly, it seems Tzu Chi neither did due diligence when first approached, nor did it follow up to see whether any purchases had taken place on its behalf. It apparently remained completely unaware it had been victimized until investigators stumbled onto the scam while pursuing another case, according to media reports.
This story has blown up as a major political issue, particularly in the Taipei mayoral campaign, as it revisits a past of Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) attacks on the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and its vaccine policies, including accusations of corruption and cronyism. These accusations have gone down the rabbit hole of political forgetting, though they follow the pattern of the KMT whenever the DPP makes a pro-Taiwan move instead of supporting the People’s Republic of China (PRC). That pattern of forgetting is also a feature of the public’s reception of KMT attacks on Taiwan and the DPP.
Photo courtesy of the Changhua County Public Health Bureau
Readers may recall that during 2021 there were numerous donations of vaccines by Japan, the US and other countries. However, as a recent editorial recounts in the Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times), political and business figures associated with the KMT and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), began to promote the German-made BNT vaccine. The apparent attention of this program was to stop the use of any vaccines but BNT.
However, the “Greater China” distribution rights for BNT vaccine were obtained by Shanghai-based Fosun Group (復星國際). Though Taiwan secured a contract for 5 million doses of BNT in early 2021, the PRC halted the sale. (It is astonishing that the repeated betrayals of local KMT interests by the PRC never affects KMT willingness to support the PRC.)
To fill in the gap, private organizations stepped in. However, as the government observed at the time, private groups cannot bear the legal and compensation responsibilities if health problems with the vaccines should arise. Hence, the vaccines had to be given to the government. Private groups had to obtain government authorization and a special import permit to bring in vaccines. Because of these requirements, former Minister of Health and Welfare and then-head of the Central Epidemic Command Center, Chen Shih-chung (陳時中), a DPP appointee, repeatedly reminded these organizations that brokers who claimed to have procurement channels were likely scammers.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Politicians from the KMT and TPP camps attacked the DPP for “blocking vaccines” and killing Taiwanese. The Liberty Times recalled that then-chairman of the TPP, Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), said that “at the height of the pandemic, the government blocked BNT from entering the country in order to ‘protect high-end vaccines.’”
Indeed, Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), then-chairman of the KMT, sued Chen Shi-chung and the director of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for corruption, saying that they had profited from these high-end vaccines. The KMT also accused the DPP of using dangerous, untested vaccines on young people, since older people had priority for vaccines. As Brian Hioe pointed out at Taiwan Insight, the KMT was “hoping to make inroads with a demographic that has drifted away” from the party. The KMT also attacked the Astra-Zeneca vaccine, though major figures in the KMT quietly had themselves vaccinated with it.
Chiang’s complaints follow the typical pattern of KMT attacks. Chiang said that the KMT had always supported the development of domestically produced vaccines, but it supports “safe and effective” vaccines that adhere to international standards and acquire international certification, not vaccines whose growth is artificially accelerated.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
DRONES
Sound familiar? Just substitute the word “drones” for “vaccines.” The KMT has one pattern of attack, which it always uses: accuse the DPP of corruption whenever it is doing something Taiwan-centered, say that the DPP approach is too expensive, while simultaneously putting its hand on its heart and piously proclaiming that it has always supported whatever program it is attacking. The last two decades offer many examples of this playbook.
For then-legislator and current Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), the vaccine issue became an important line of attack on the DPP. He said the DPP was “constantly blocking vaccines and protecting high-end vaccines,” and asked the public: “Do you believe Tzu Chi or the DPP?”, as if the two were in conflict.
The pro-China parties’ attack on the DPP thus accused it of killing people to make money for vaccine makers it was connected to, which the Liberty Times said had powerful effects on the 2022 local elections. The attacks continued into 2023, as a recent Taipei Times editorial observed, impacting the 2024 elections. A legislator at the time, Chiang Wan-an sat in on closed meetings on government vaccine procurement, and knew what was really going on.
As the Liberty Times pointed out, this was the same playbook that Chiang is now using in the tainted oil failure of the Taipei and Taichung city governments — accusing the central government of forcing people to consume toxic oil, when in fact KMT-led governments were responsible.
The brazen fraud against Tzu Chi has completely destroyed Chiang’s accusations from the COVID era and vindicated Chen Shi-chung’s warnings about fraud. DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has had a field day accusing Chiang Wan-an of hypocrisy and lies. A CMmedia piece last week said that the DPP hopes to use the KMT’s now-exposed vaccine attacks as leverage in the elections in Taipei, Hsinchu and Nantou.
Hopefully voters will finally make the connection between drones, tainted oil, vaccines and a hundred other items.
KMT politicians just this week were complaining that the public should have been better informed about the Internet slow down drills. KMT Legislator Ko Ju-chun (葛如鈞) said without better clarity the drills were essentially treating the public as “guinea pigs.”
Sound familiar?

Heat, water scarcity driving stranded-asset risks: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:41:30 UTC
01:41:30 KST

Extreme heat and unreliable water supplies are threatening asset valuations across a growing number of sectors as everything from labor productivity to energy costs gets impacted, an analysis by Moody’s released on Friday showed.
“Heat and water are no longer separate perils moving on separate timelines,” Moody’s managing director and head of catastrophe modeling for insurance solutions Mohsen Rahnama said. “They are converging, and doing so quickly.”
For investors, “both perils translate into operational risk, earnings volatility and stranded-asset exposure,” he said.
Photo: Bloomberg
This year is on track to be the hottest recorded in human history. In Europe, the fastest-warming continent, heat has exposed huge gaps in the region’s preparedness as its infrastructure buckles. Economists are already warning that disruptions to harvests, commodity supplies and the ability of humans to function would hit inflation and GDP.
Heat and water risk are starting to “weigh on values” in the real estate sector, Rahnama said.
Such impacts, left unpriced, “can quietly erode cash flows and portfolio returns” for firms in sectors spanning agriculture, the manufacture of apparel and of semiconductors, he said.
The upshot is that investors need to adapt to a “new risk landscape” created by extreme weather conditions, as the impact of heat and water scarcity morph into permanent risk features, Rahnama said.
“Reinsurers, banks and investors are watching these same trends closely, given their reach across regions and their role in how capital moves in response to physical risk,” he said.
In the US, Moody’s said a sample of about 159,000 water-intensive facilities revealed that close to 49,000 might face high or very high water stress in the decades ahead.
Most are concentrated in Texas and California, while more than 60 percent of the facilities reviewed are used for heavy manufacturing and processing.
About one-quarter are used for producing food and drinks, while 14 percent are for mining and quarrying, the report said.
Such risks can be hard for insurers to capture, due to the slow-moving nature of the damage done.
“Traditional indemnity cover sits awkwardly with chronic risk,” Rahnama said.
However, “losses from heat and water stress build slowly, are hard to model precisely, and tend to strike many policyholders in a region at once, overwhelming the usual diversification,” he said.
