Sevastopol explosion on 13 August: death of traitor to Ukraine confirmed
The Book of Executioners project has confirmed that Robert Shaheiev, the former commander of the Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine's only submarine, who betrayed his oath to Ukraine and switched allegiance to Russia, was killed in an explosion on 13 August.
Source: The Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and those who betrayed Ukraine, citing data from Russia's Federal Tax Service
Details: Unofficial reports of a possible assassination attempt on Shaheiev in Sevastopol had emerged earlier, but his death had not been confirmed. The traitor's taxpayer identification number was later found to be listed in a registry of invalidated individual numbers, providing the first official confirmation of his death.
The Book of Executioners notes that in 2014, Shaheiev surrendered Ukraine's only submarine without a fight to the Russians during the occupation of Crimea, broke his oath of allegiance, and went on to serve in Russia's Black Sea Fleet.
For reference: Robert Mansurovich Shaheiev was born in Prymorskyi, a settlement in Ukraine's Autonomous Republic of Crimea, on 21 February 1977.
His service as a professional in Ukraine's Armed Forces began in 1999. His final contract, signed on 26 June 2009, was for five years. He held the rank of Captain First Rank.
Shaheiev was appointed commander of the Zaporizhzhia, a large submarine at the Ukrainian Navy's Naval Operations Centre, by Order No. 201 of the Ukrainian Navy Command on 15 October 2013.
During Russia's occupation of Crimea in spring 2014, Shaheiev ignored orders to relocate his unit to Odesa. He was required to report to his new duty station, military unit A2238, by 12 May 2014, but failed to do so. He refused to take the Zaporizhzhia to mainland Ukraine and declared his intention to serve in the Russian military.
On 17 May 2014, Shaheiev was relieved of his duties as the submarine's commander and placed at the disposal of the Ukrainian Navy Command under an order issued by the Chief of the General Staff.
After signing a contract with the Russian armed forces, he assumed the position of deputy commander of the 4th Separate Submarine Brigade of Russia's Black Sea Fleet.
Shaheiev had been charged with desertion and treason under Articles 408.1 and 111.1 of Ukraine's Criminal Code.
Background: An explosion occurred in occupied Sevastopol on the morning of 13 August, killing a military serviceman. The explosive device was believed to have been placed in a rubbish bin. Reports on Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels suggested that the person killed may have been Shaheiev.

The US-Iran battle of attrition: 'Chance of agreement was always slim'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:19:31 UTC
23:19:31 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump’s ceasefire with Iran in June was intended to lead to a broader agreement to end the war and curb Tehran’s nuclear program, during a negotiating period set at 60 days. But the deadline, which had been scheduled to expire Sunday, has effectively been abandoned, and the war has turned into a contest of willpower and economic endurance with no end in sight.
There have been no public reports of American strikes against Iranian targets since late July, . However, the effective collapse of the agreement underscores how much Trump is struggling to end the war he began in February alongside Israel, and how far he is from the ambitions of the June agreement, including the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Officials inside the White House are well aware that they will pass the deadline without reaching an agreement, and that the confrontation has largely become an economic war, two American sources familiar with the details of the negotiations told The New York Times.
The current strategy bears a surprising resemblance to previous American efforts, which lasted for years, to isolate Iran in the hope of forcing it to abandon its nuclear ambitions. That policy produced mixed results, and some analysts doubt that even heavy economic pressure alone will force Iran to change course. In fact, this was the approach Trump tried to take during his first term. His treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said last week that he was about to impose unprecedented financial sanctions.
The vague wording that led to the agreement’s collapse
The June memorandum of understanding was seen by many as a significant achievement for Iran, giving the regime badly needed sanctions relief while talks on difficult concessions, such as uranium enrichment, were deferred to a later stage. However, Iran’s leaders chose to escalate the situation again rather than consolidate the gains they had secured from the agreement, according to Nate Swanson, an Iran expert at the Atlantic Council, a Washington think tank.
Ships were able to sail freely through the Strait of Hormuz before the war. Iran’s insistence that the wording on the issue in the memorandum of understanding remain vague gave it control over the shipping lane, leading to the agreement’s collapse. Iran began firing on ships sailing in lanes outside its territorial waters, and American forces responded with strikes in southern Iran, setting off a cycle of attacks and counterattacks across the Middle East.
Iran is now refusing to reopen the strait until the U.S. fulfills its ceasefire commitments, such as releasing frozen Iranian assets abroad, according to Ali Vaez, an Iran expert at the International Crisis Group. The Trump administration, by contrast, is demanding that Iran first end the naval blockade. “Neither side is really willing to complete the agreement. Both think that within days or weeks the other side will be more desperate for a deal, and that way they will be able to extract more from it,” Vaez said. “That is why we are once again trapped in this test of attrition.”
The reopening of the strait has gradually become Trump’s central focus in the confrontation, even though he originally declared that the war was intended to strengthen the Iranian people so they could topple the existing regime, severely damage its missile capabilities and prevent Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons. There are very few indications that Iran and the U.S. have held in-depth discussions on Iran’s nuclear program since the June ceasefire, let alone formulated an agreement acceptable to both sides.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said over the weekend that Iran had not yet decided whether to resume talks with the U.S., but noted that the 60-day deadline was no longer relevant, given that the June agreement is effectively no longer in force. “We did not have a ceasefire that now needs to be extended,” Araghchi said. “We had an end to the war, which has now taken on a new status.”
'The chances were slim from the start'
Former U.S. officials who worked on Iran issues told The New York Times that the chances of a new nuclear agreement between the U.S. and Iran within 60 days were always slim, even though the framework included the possibility of an extension. A previous agreement, reached under former U.S. President Barack Obama, required about two years of complex talks. Trump withdrew from that agreement, known as the JCPOA, in 2018.
The Trump administration hoped the June agreement would at least lead to the opening of the Strait of Hormuz. But in order to close the deal, it relied on vague formulations that strengthened the validity of Iran’s claim to future control over shipping traffic in the strait, analysts said. “It was a flawed document, rushed out before it was ready,” Swanson said. “Beyond that, they did not solve the most urgent problem in the immediate term, which was the issue of the strait.”
Now, the U.S. and Iran appear to be bogged down in an open-ended struggle — neither all-out war nor defined peace. In an effort to force Iran to accept American terms, the Trump administration has restored sanctions on Iranian oil and reimposed the naval blockade. Iran’s collapsing economy, which led to mass protests that were brutally suppressed earlier this year, is a central consideration for the country’s decision-makers. But Swanson argues that the current deadlock is likely to push Iran toward escalation rather than reconciliation.
Trump’s declaration and Iran’s demand
While very little progress has been made on the commitments detailed in the agreement, Trump and his Iranian counterparts have continued to exchange threats. During an event in Garden City, New York, on Friday, Trump again appeared determined to change the narrative, threatening that “American ownership of the Strait of Hormuz” would soon be declared.
It was unclear how serious Trump’s declaration was. But such a move could include the deployment of ground forces and would almost certainly require a prolonged naval presence, steps that run counter to the “America First” values of Trump supporters who seek to end prolonged military conflicts overseas. Trump is also known for floating undeveloped foreign policy ideas to divert attention and criticism, as he did when he surprised the world last year by proposing that the U.S. take control of the Gaza Strip — an idea that never materialized.
The White House did not respond to questions about whether the administration had drawn up practical plans to seize control of the Strait of Hormuz. Trump’s aides also did not respond to questions about the approaching deadline.
Iranian army commander Amir Hatami responded Sunday to Trump’s statement and said: “The U.S. president says he wants to declare the Strait of Hormuz part of his country. After seeing the reactions, he announced that he was joking. The expulsion of the Americans has been implemented, and they are no longer permitted to enter the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Oman or the Strait of Hormuz. Everyone should know that there is no way American bases can return to their previous state, and Iran will never allow it.”
Hatami also said: “The Strait of Hormuz is a divine gift to the Iranian people and will not return to its previous state. Any price we pay to preserve the Strait of Hormuz is worth it. We will defend it with all our strength.” Earlier, a quote attributed to him was also published, saying Iran is offering a $30,000 reward for the capture or killing of an American soldier.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi wrote on social media: “Recognize reality once and for all. So far, you have suffered severe strategic defeats. The Strait of Hormuz was Iranian, is Iranian and will remain Iranian.”

US mulls copying Russia’s air defense tech – Military Watch

US mulls copying Russia’s air defense tech – Military Watch
The US is looking to Russia’s air defense technology as it develops a new generation of mobile radars following losses suffered during the war with Iran, Military Watch has reported. New THAAD radars are reportedly set to gain a mobile sensor platform function similar to those built into Russia’s S-300 and S-400 systems from the outset.
According to a report published earlier this week, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) destroyed more than $3 billion worth of American air defense radars during the first week of the war on the Islamic Republic launched by Israel and the US in late February.
The losses reportedly included lower-value radars such as the AN/TPS-59, valued at around $70 million, as well as an AN/FPS-132 radar and two AN/TPY-2 X-band mobile radar systems from the THAAD anti-ballistic missile system, each valued at more than $1 billion. The destruction of the radars dealt a major blow to the situational awareness of US forces and their allies, the military-focused magazine noted.
The reported approach would potentially move away from the traditional Western concept of a self-contained air defense battery, according to the report. Instead, radars would serve as nodes in broader networks, allowing a mobile sensor to detect a target and relay data to remote launchers while remaining physically separate from the interceptors, the magazine noted.
The concept is reportedly in line with Russia’s networked air defense architecture and with the US Integrated Air and Missile Defense Battle Command System (IBCS), which is designed to connect different sensors and weapons.
According to Military Watch, the destruction of the radars reportedly forced the US and Israel to rely more heavily on ship-based sensors and an AN/TPY-2 radar stationed in Turkey.
Earlier this month, The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian strikes had caused up to $13 billion in damage to US military assets and facilities in the Middle East. Since the start of the US-Israeli war on the Islamic Republic, Tehran has carried out more than 2,000 air, missile, and drone strikes, damaging at least 20 sites in eight countries used by the US military. Iran has also damaged or destroyed more than 42 US military aircraft, several while parked at air bases.

US Military YouTuber Paid His Own Way to Cover Ukraine's Front Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

For Justin Taylor, refusing to be paid was the whole point.
The American YouTuber, who spent six years as a US Army infantry officer before leaving active duty in 2024, traveled to Ukraine for two weeks to report from the front line – and covered every expense himself.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The trip, organized with help from UNITED24, Ukraine’s state fundraising platform, and AIR Brands, the influencer arm of Kyiv-based AIR Media-Tech, produced a video that has since drawn more than a million views.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“I didn’t receive a single dime from UNITED24, and I prefer it that way,” Taylor said in an interview. “Then I can say, I’m not getting paid to say this.”
For a creator whose channel is built on explaining military topics to viewers with little or no service background – Taylor estimates only about a quarter of his largely American and English-speaking audience has any military experience – that distinction mattered. Going into a war he had already spent years covering and commenting on from a distance, he said it would have felt “hypocritical” to keep talking about it without seeing it firsthand.
Ukraine Disables 7 of 10 Largest Wildberries Warehouses
“I really wanted to get that experience of going over there,” he said, “and also do what I could with my platform to help Ukraine defend itself.”
From NATO’s eastern flank to Ukraine’s front
Taylor’s interest in the region predates the full-scale invasion. During his time in the army, his unit rotated along NATO’s eastern flank, giving him a firsthand view of the alliance’s posture near Crimea even before Russia’s 2022 assault. By the time he left the military and turned to content creation full time, he said continuing to discuss the war only through secondhand reporting no longer sat right with him.
The trip came together fast. A handful of contacts who had made similar trips connected him with UNITED24; less than a week after his initial outreach, he said, arrangements were largely locked in – itinerary, press credentials and all.
Of his two weeks in the country, Taylor said close to a week was spent near the fighting itself: interviewing troops, observing drone operations, and, by his account, waking up to the sound of the war rather than reading about it. He described one night in Kyiv, his last before heading back through Poland, when machine-gun fire outside his window marked an attempt to shoot down incoming drones.
“There wasn’t a point while I was over there that the area around me wasn’t getting hit, even in the larger cities,” he said, recalling nearby towns – including one he described as effectively destroyed – pockmarked by drone debris and explosions.
What surprised him
What struck Taylor most, he said, wasn’t the war’s scale but its improvisation – Ukrainian units coordinating fire support over Zoom or requesting ammunition on WhatsApp, using commercial phones instead of the heavily encrypted, specialized systems he’d grown used to in the US military.
“There wasn’t anything that they wanted to do that they couldn’t do,” he said, arguing Ukraine had matched the battlefield effectiveness of far more expensive Western systems using consumer technology – a drone tied to Starlink, in one example he cited. His takeaway, he said, was that Western militaries had something to learn from that approach rather than dismiss it as makeshift.
He also said the trip reordered his sense of Kyiv’s position in the war. Arriving as Russia was consolidating its drone forces and ramping up production, Taylor said he initially sensed Ukraine losing momentum. Looking back nearly a year later, he argued that the edge has swung back toward Ukraine, pointing to long-range strike capabilities – he cited the Flamingo cruise missile – that he said Russia has yet to counter.
A case for continued US involvement
Much of the interview turned to the argument Taylor said he has almost daily online: that the war, and NATO more broadly, remains a US interest even for Americans who feel disconnected from it. He drew a parallel to Cold War-era deterrence, arguing that countries without a NATO security guarantee – he named Georgia and Moldova alongside Ukraine – have ended up with Russian troops on their soil, while NATO members have not.
“The reason we never had to go to war with Russia isn’t because it’s never going to happen,” he said. “It’s because we spent the entire Cold War providing deterrence.”
Taylor, who turned 30 during the trip and celebrated in Kharkiv, said he intends to return, framing a potential second trip around how the war has changed in the year since his first visit. He has not set dates.
Asked about the response to his coverage, he described it as broadly positive, if not universal – an outcome he attributes to avoiding sensationalism. “I’m not trying to blow anything out of proportion for views,” he said. “I’m genuinely trying to explain how things actually are in that moment.”

Study warns of measles risk with 1.7 million Australians vulnerable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:04:01 UTC
23:04:01 KST

Warnings of possible measles outbreak as study finds 1.7 million Australians are vulnerable
In short:
A study has found an estimated 1.7 million people are susceptible to catching measles, according to 2019 data.
The paper, to be published today, says susceptibility is high for key groups of Australians born from the late 1970s onwards.
What's next?
Travellers at a higher risk of bringing the disease into Australia are being urged to get another jab, as are adults in at-risk age groups.
An estimated 1.7 million Australians are not protected against measles, putting the country at risk of more outbreaks, according to new analysis from the peak immunisation research organisation.
The National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance (NCIRS) study found almost 7 per cent of the population was susceptible to measles in 2019.
The paper will be published today in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health.
Lead author Zoë Croker said susceptibility was high for key age groups of Australians born from the late 1970s onwards.
The number of people susceptible included Australian babies who were not yet eligible for measles immunisations.
"The concern is that there will be more measles outbreaks that will be harder to contain," Ms Croker said.
"We'll start to see more cases and a higher chance of there being a death associated."
'A warning sign'
Ms Croker said the world-first study combined blood samples testing measles immunity, with vaccination data and it represented the most comprehensive national estimate currently possible.
The analysis found overall measles immunity was 93.3 per cent, which epidemiologist Adrian Esterman said Australians must take as a "warning sign".
"[That] is not good enough. That means that we are at risk of getting major measles outbreaks,"
"We don't really want it to get any worse."
The World Health Organization has a target of achieving 93-95 per cent vaccine coverage to establish herd immunity and prevent the spread of measles.
Australia achieved measles elimination status in 2014 but continues to have imported cases in overseas visitors and returning residents.
There were very few measles cases in Australia during the pandemic. However, numbers have increased in the past two years.
Who is at risk and why should we be worried?
Anyone who is not fully vaccinated is at risk. Babies and young children are particularly at risk because they are not routinely vaccinated until they are 12 months old. So are those with reduced immunity and unvaccinated pregnant women because they cannot be immunised while they are pregnant.
The paper identified the key age groups with higher levels of susceptibility to measles, which included infants and young children and people aged 42-49 years, 31-33 years and 25 and 26 years.
Ms Croker said those groups were highly susceptible because of generational gaps in immunisation programs.
"The biggest gaps are in people born around the year 2000, as well as those born in 1993, 1994 and 1995, which was when that second dose of measles-containing vaccine was introduced," she said.
"Close behind are people in the early vaccine era, so born in 1977 to 1983 … they're more likely to only have a single dose of measles-containing vaccine."
Ms Croker said people born during or since 1966 may also be more susceptible because they may have missed vaccination altogether or only be partially vaccinated.
Loading...
However, she said some of these people may have life-long immunity from childhood measles infections.
Professor Esterman, from Adelaide University, said the numbers were daunting.
"We are at that stage where we need to be worried,"
"We do not want our coverage rates to drop any more than they are now.
"If a single infectious person goes into a room with a group of people who haven't got immunity, they will infect, very quickly, 12 to 15 of them. It's the most infectious disease we know about."
Overseas travellers urged to get another jab
Travellers are a higher risk of bringing measles into Australia, according to National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance (NCIRS) associate director Frank Beard.
"We'd strongly encourage people in the current climate of increasing global outbreaks of measles to check … records of measles vaccination," Dr Beard said.
"If they haven't had good evidence that they previously received two doses at any time, then we strongly encourage them to get vaccinated again."
Professor Esterman said those aged between 20 and 40 years old were catching measles during overseas travel.
"Almost all of those cases are coming from people who've gone to Asia, so it could be the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, where they have quite large measles outbreaks … they come back and bring it with them," he said.
"There's a huge role here for GPs. If a patient is going overseas and talks to a GP about what they need in terms of protection, the GP should immediately ask them, what's your measles status like?"
Dr Beard said he would "strongly encourage" all adults in the at-risk age groups to consider getting another measles vaccine.
'We'll see more outbreaks'
Ms Croker said measles would circulate more throughout Australia if herd immunity dipped below 93 per cent.
"It means that our public health system is less likely to be able to chase down every case and we are at a greater risk of measles then becoming more prominent in Australia."
Professor Esterman fears Australia will fall below the threshold for herd immunity, which will lead to "more and more outbreaks".
"It does mean that there will be some pockets of the Australian population which have got much lower coverage than that, and that's where you start seeing these small outbreaks occurring," he said.
"It's in those pockets of the population which have got lower coverage rates.
"This is telling us that there's something wrong, which we need to do something about."
The latest immunisation data shows childhood vaccination coverage declined for a fifth year in 2025.
Ms Croker said her paper may "underestimate" susceptibility to measles, given childhood immunisation rates have dropped in recent years.

Beyond bloodline: How donated milk is saving India’s most vulnerable newborns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:02:50 UTC
23:02:50 KST

Doctors strongly challenge the widespread belief that most mothers simply do not produce enough milk.
The first thing a mother wants to do after bringing a baby into the world is often the simplest: hold the child close and feed it. But for some newborns, that first feed never comes.Their mothers may be critically ill, separated from them, unable to breastfeed immediately or, in the most heartbreaking cases, no longer alive.For a premature baby weighing just a few hundred grams, however, waiting for circumstances to change is not always an option.This is where another mother can step in.Human milk banks in India are built around a quiet act of generosity: a lactating mother donates milk her own baby does not need, and through a carefully regulated medical system, that milk reaches a newborn whose own mother cannot provide it."Milk bank helps one mother save the baby of another mother," said Dr Poonam Sidana, director of neonatology and paediatrics at CK Birla Hospital, Delhi.The idea may sound straightforward. But behind every bottle is a mother who has agreed to share something deeply personal and another family placing its trust in a system to provide their fragile newborn with the safest possible nourishment.
When a mother is not there
Dr Satish Tiwari, founder and convener of the Human Milk Banking Association of India and professor of paediatrics, has spent decades trying to expand that system.He traces the movement in India to 1989, when the first human milk bank in India and Asia was established at Sion Hospital in Mumbai by Dr Armida Fernandes.
By the mid-1990s, Tiwari had begun exploring milk banking while working on maternal and child nutrition and malnutrition."What we realised was that milk banks are needed not only in Mumbai or Surat or Udaipur, but it is a requirement all over India," he said.The babies who need donor human milk, he explained, are often those who have been separated from their mothers for reasons beyond anyone's control.A newborn may be admitted to a NICU at 500g or 700g, born at seven or eight months of gestation and too weak to breastfeed. The mother may have to return home while the baby remains in hospital."Mother may not be available for months when he is admitted in a neonatal care unit," Tiwari said.Then there are babies whose mothers have died."There may be the death of the mother. So the mother herself is not available for the baby," he said.There are also abandoned newborns and babies whose mothers are temporarily unable to breastfeed.In such situations, the conventional fallback has often been formula or other substitutes. But for a vulnerable premature baby, doctors say human milk can make an important difference."If you feed on mother's milk, which is through the milk bank, then the child's improvement or the child's outcome as far as his life is concerned becomes much, much better," Tiwari said.
The babies for whom every feed matters
For premature and low-birth-weight infants, the issue is not simply about calories.Their digestive and immune systems are still developing, making them especially vulnerable to infections and serious complications.Sidana said the strongest evidence for donor human milk is in premature and low-birth-weight infants, particularly in reducing the incidence of necrotising enterocolitis, or NEC, a severe condition that can damage the intestine and, in serious cases, lead to infection and death."Donor human milk is believed to bring down the incidence of necrotising enterocolitis and some infections more than formula does in premature babies," she said.Human milk also contains bioactive and immune components that formula cannot replicate.But Sidana is clear about the hierarchy: when a mother can breastfeed her own baby, that remains the ideal."A mother's own milk, preferably via breastfeeding, is the best option since it is optimal for her infant and has the required nutrients and immunity that facilitate his or her growth and resistance to infections," she said.Donor human milk becomes the next option when that first choice is temporarily or permanently unavailable.Dr Sakshi Goel, senior consultant in obstetrics and gynaecology at Madhukar Rainbow Children's Hospital, Delhi, described it as a "transitional or supplemental resource" for newborns at risk."It should not take away from the importance of establishing and continuing with lactation," she said.
The mother who gives
That distinction is important because milk banks do not exist simply to distribute milk. They also help mothers breastfeed and, when possible, produce enough milk for their own babies.Tiwari strongly challenges the widespread belief that most mothers simply do not produce enough milk."The concept that mother is not able to make enough milk, basically we feel it is a misconception," he said.In most cases, he explained, breastfeeding is a physiological process. Difficulties can arise because of delayed initiation, poor positioning, inadequate feeding or the early introduction of formula or bottle feeding."If we start top milk or powder milk, then the mother's milk, it goes on decreasing," he said.That is why milk banks and lactation centres first try to understand why a mother believes she does not have enough milk."If there is some fault, we try to manage that fault in the feeding," Tiwari said. "And then we convince the mother that she has more milk as compared to the requirement of her child."Only when a mother has enough milk for her own baby does the conversation turn to donation."She cannot only feed her child, but she can also donate the milk," he said.For many mothers, that can become an unexpectedly emotional decision.They are not donating something abstract. They are expressing, collecting and handing over milk their bodies produced to nourish their own child.But in a regulated system, they know where it is going: to a newborn who needs it.
How does a mother donate?
The process begins not with a bottle, but with a conversation.Goel said a mother who wants to donate should approach a reputable human milk bank or Comprehensive Lactation Management Centre rather than trying to donate informally.The centre counsels her, reviews her medical history and determines whether she is eligible."After that, the mother goes through the essential screening and testing and is given instructions on how to express, collect and store her milk," Goel said.The milk is then collected through the recognised channel and subjected to the necessary processing and safety checks.Tiwari said milk banks initially relied heavily on mothers delivering in the same hospital. But awareness has slowly widened the donor pool."Now we have that type of mother also," he said of women who hear about milk banks and voluntarily approach them.Some centres have even begun using milk collection vans to travel between hospitals and homes.There is no commercial transaction involved."There is no monetary benefit to the mother who is donating," Tiwari said. "Similarly, we do not charge any mother for getting milk also.""Neither we give money or monetary benefit to the donor nor to the recipient. It is totally voluntary."That word — voluntary — is central to the idea. A mother is never expected to compromise her own baby's nourishment. She gives only what is surplus.
Medical journey before reaching baby
The emotional generosity of donation is matched by a rigorous safety system.Donors are screened for communicable diseases and other health risks. Their medications are reviewed, as are lifestyle factors that could make the milk unsafe."We take three or four precautions," Tiwari said.Mothers are screened for illnesses such as hepatitis B and C and other infections that could potentially be transmitted to a recipient. They are also assessed for medicines that could harm a baby."If she is on some psychotropic drugs or some anti-cancer drugs or if she is on some habit-forming drugs, then we have to take care of that also," he said.Smoking and alcohol consumption are also considered."All these factors are considered, and screening is completed before collecting the mother's milk," he said.The donated milk then goes through processing and testing.According to Sidana, India's standards include Holder pasteurisation, in which milk is heated to 62.5°C for 30 minutes and then rapidly cooled.Samples undergo microbiological testing, and pasteurised milk is released only when cultures do not show bacterial growth.Pasteurisation does mean that donor human milk is not biologically identical to fresh mother's milk."Pasteurization processes modify various parts of human milk, especially a number of heat-sensitive enzymes and immune factors," Sidana said.But, she added, it preserves the nutritional composition and many of the biological qualities of human milk while significantly improving safety.For a highly vulnerable premature baby, that balance matters.
Why informal sharing is not the same thing
The instinct to help another mother can be powerful enough to encourage direct sharing through friends, social networks or online groups.But doctors caution against confusing generosity with safety."A regulated milk bank is run in accordance with a proper medical and quality-control system," Sidana said.There is donor screening, testing, pasteurisation, storage and traceability.With informal sharing, those safeguards may disappear."There might be doubts about the health condition of the donor, medications that were taken, how the milk was stored, and whether it comes from the right source or is contaminated," Sidana said.The warning is particularly important for premature and sick newborns whose immune systems are already fragile."The problem does not lie in people who generously donate the milk," she said. "There is a problem of the lack of screening, control over the sources, storage practices, and testing for milk intended for very vulnerable neonates."
More needy babies than donor mothers
The need for donor human milk can be greater than the available supply.Tiwari said many milk banks are still unable to meet the complete requirements of the hospitals where they operate.Goel said there is no reliable real-time evidence pointing to a single nationwide shortage because availability differs considerably between hospitals and regions. But demand can exceed local supply, especially where large numbers of premature or medically fragile newborns are being treated.When that happens, the most vulnerable babies are prioritised."The main point is fair allocation of resources while at the same time helping mothers with the establishment and maintenance of their own milk supply," Goel said.This is one reason awareness matters so much.At JIPMER, a July 2025 PIB release noted that the Amudham Thaipaal Maiyam's average voluntary milk collection had grown from about 400ml a day in its early years to around 1,000ml a day, with at least 20 babies, particularly premature infants, benefiting every day.But Tiwari believes India still has a long way to go.He said his association reaches doctors, medical students and hospitals through conferences, talks and awareness campaigns. NGOs and organisations such as Rotary have also helped with equipment, infrastructure and publicity."We are doing publicity on media. We are doing mouth-to-mouth publicity by the mother who has received the milk for her baby," he said.
Small act with enormous human meaning
Human milk banking is ultimately a story about mothers.One mother may be sitting beside her own healthy baby, expressing milk her child does not immediately need.In another ward, another mother may be sitting beside an incubator, watching a tiny chest rise and fall and wondering whether her baby will make it through the night.
Tiwari's message is simple."Mother's milk is best for any newborn child," he said.And for mothers who have more milk than their own babies need, he wants hesitation to give way to awareness."Most of the mothers, they have more milk as compared to the requirement of her child," he said. "Mother or the relatives or the grandparent, they should not hesitate in donating the milk."There is no grand ceremony when a bottle of donor milk leaves a milk bank.It is labelled, tested, pasteurised, stored and eventually carried to a NICU.But inside that bottle is something much larger than milk.It is the generosity of one mother reaching a baby she may never see.And for a newborn who has arrived too soon, whose mother is too ill, or who has lost the person who was meant to feed them, that generosity can become a lifeline.

Slovakia’s STV Machinery Produces Two Prototypes of New BMP-1 Hull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:02:34 UTC
23:02:34 KST

Slovak company STV Machinery is preparing for serial production of new armored hulls for BMP-1 infantry fighting vehicles.
The Future Army publication reported this.
The first several dozen hulls are planned for production in 2026-2027.
STV Machinery has already produced two prototypes. The first was intended for testing final assembly and weapons installation, while the second is being used for physical and load testing.
The company operates at the site of the former ZŤS defense plant in Dubnica nad Váhom. During the Czechoslovak era, Soviet BMP-1 and BMP-2 vehicles were produced there.
Development of the new hull began in 2024 at the request of Czech company STV Group. As part of the project, the companies fully digitized the design, prepared new production documentation and developed welding equipment.
The new hull was created based on the BMP-1 design, which remains widespread around the world, but was adapted to modern requirements. In particular, the manufacturer plans to use modern armor materials used in Western armored combat vehicles.
“We are currently actively preparing for serial production of the first several dozen units,” said Pavel Beran, director of special projects at STV Group.
The company is also developing vehicles for different powerplant configurations. Customers will be able to choose between different engines, including powerplants manufactured in the West.
At the same time, STV Group does not disclose information about potential customers for the new vehicles. According to Beran, the company does not disclose details about specific customers or contract terms for security reasons and due to commercial confidentiality.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Slovak company STV Machinery had already received its first order from a foreign customer for serial production of BMP-1 hulls.

Death toll from Zimbabwe capsized ferry accident rises to 84
Rescue workers recovered more bodies on Sunday following a ferry capsizing accident that occured earlier this week on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, bringing the death toll to at least 84. The search continues, as authorities fear the number of casualties could rise even further.
The death toll after an overloaded government ferry capsized on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba has risen to 84 after more bodies were retrieved on Sunday, the police said.
The passenger ferry, a vital means of transport for rural villagers, overturned on Tuesday in choppy waters on the vast lake on the border with Zambia.
The police "reports that the death toll is now 84 after the recovery of four bodies from the lake this afternoon", a statement said.
"The police confirm that search efforts are still underway in a bid to recover victims identified as missing," it said.
Officials said earlier in the week the boat was authorised to carry 90 people, but had 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children onboard.

The five-year plans that turned into lifetimes: Windrush elders’ stories ‘open door’ for young people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

There are faces young and old around a table in Hackney library as people share a meal of curry goat, rice and peas and sorrel cake. There are photos of the smiling faces of Windrush elders scattered around. They will soon become permanent fixtures of the Hackney Archives.
There is a feeling among the group that somebody is missing. Lessept Saunders, the founder of the Hackney Caribbean Elderly Organisation, died in April aged 107. He had been the second-oldest known living man in London and the oldest contributor to Stories of Windrush. Saunders was part of the Windrush generation, having arrived in London from Jamaica in 1944 after hearing stories about higher wages and hope from returning friends who had served in the second world war.
“Saunders had a five-year-plan, like many of the elders who came to the UK,” says Paul Anderson, the CEO of Voyage Youth, a social justice charity leading the archival project. “They would tell themselves ‘I’m only going to be here for five years and go back’ but many were not able to do that. The cost to travel back home was such a barrier that many just stayed.”
Stories of Windrush is one of the first projects in the UK to document first-hand accounts from Windrush elders collected entirely by young people. The accompanying book and photographs and its digital counterparts will have a permanent place in the Hackney Archives.
Zainab Awonoki was 15 when she first started working on the archive four years ago. “I never grew up with my grandparents so speaking to elders has been so eye-opening,” she says. Despite learning briefly about the Windrush generation in her Hackney secondary school, it was only through the archives that she learned about the struggles these elders had faced. “Hearing their stories first hand lets you see that they practically fought for us to actually stay here. It tells our elders that they’re not alone with their past and trauma.”
Research has found that giving young people access to archives can improve educational attainment and increase awareness of local decision-making. It seems to resonate with Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, who wrote a foreword for the book. She wrote: “For all those who form part of the Windrush generation, and many who have been subject to scandalous impositions by state agencies, we must not forget their lives, their struggles, their achievements and their legacy are worth celebrating.”
Claudette Barned arrived in the 1960s from Jamaica at the age of nine and was immediately struck by the freezing temperatures in Clapton, east London. Today, the 74-year-old fans herself in the scorching heat, wearing a pink summer dress and recently having dyed her hair blue. “My mother passed away before I could ask her about history,” she says. “Talking to the young people means that when we die our stories are shared and when they’re old they can repeat the cycle.” Now retired, she has not forgotten the loneliness of her first few years in England. She socialises at elderly clubs with other Windrush elders and has passed on her Caribbean traditions to her grandson, who has nicknamed her “Reggae Grandma”.
Through the archives, Anderson hopes to address the youth unemployment crisis, starting with Hackney’s children who experience some of the highest rates of child poverty in England. He says: “For many, it opened a door they had not known was there: a route into the heritage sector, a reason to consider higher education, and a genuine change of pathway into a field where African and Caribbean communities remain significantly under-represented, despite so much of the history held within it being their own.”
Yvonne Straughn was born in Barbados in 1941 as the only girl among five brothers. “I was rebellious,” she told the young archivists, recalling how she would refuse to do chores unless she was paid. At 85, her rebellious spirit seems to live on. As Anderson describes the legacy of the archives, she is quick to remind the elders that none of them will be around to see it.
Straughn’s tale is a classic Windrush story. In 1966 she arrived in England to work in a hospital, treating patients who were often hostile to the sight of a black nurse. Awonoki says it is a big responsibility to be entrusted with stories such as Straughn’s, particularly in the rollback of diversity initiatives. “You need their stories to realise this isn’t something new,” she says. “The older generation had a massive impact on life. They gave us the Equality Act and now we’re talking about getting rid of it?”

‘Absolutely manic’: hot weather puts unprecedented pressure on Greater Manchester police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

On England’s hottest day of the year so far, Ashton-under-Lyne in Greater Manchester was thronging with pedestrians, many clutching ice-creams or cold drinks as they passed through the town centre.
Officers from Greater Manchester police were also out in force, some in plainclothes, some stationed by a facial-recognition van, apprehending wanted suspects and stopping persons of interest. In total, officers made 54 arrests across the borough of Tameside as part of Operation Avro, GMP’s blitz on local crime which runs in a different district each month.
For the past two months, the demand on officers here has been greater than ever, and GMP received a record-breaking 152,000 contacts from the public in July – the highest number ever recorded by the force in a single month.
The World Cup is likely to have played a part, but the main driver, officers said, was the continued hot weather, which is putting an added strain not just on health services but also on the criminal justice system.
And GMP is not alone – according to data from the National Police Chiefs’ Council, which includes all the Home Office’s forces, British Transport Police and Police Scotland, emergency call volumes increased by about 11.5% year on year during July.
Digital contact with the public also increased. Online reports submitted through Single Online Home, the platform used by most police forces, increased by about 10% year on year.
The Met Office has confirmed that July was the hottest and the driest month on record, while heatwaves have continued into August. “These factors bring people outside, there’s an increase in alcohol consumption, an increase in people going into reservoirs, into water,” said Tameside’s neighbourhood chief inspector, James Grundy. “So that does increase the demand for police.”
Grundy said there had been an increase in calls on everything from off-road bike use to antisocial behaviour and people taking disposable barbecues to locations prone to wildfires.
“It is challenging,” Grundy said. “Obviously we have to attend incidents based on the threat, harm and risk, so we have to prioritise certain incidents over others, which means that some people don’t often receive the level of response that they deserve. We have officers that are pulled from different areas to support that demand on the frontline at times.”
“At the moment in Greater Manchester police every day is a busy period,” said the Tameside neighbourhood police sergeant Rob Froggatt. “Every day police officers are being run ragged.”
He said his neighbourhood officers were often pulled on to response policing when those teams needed more support in order to do their jobs safely. “It’s a fine balance,” he said, “but I’d say we deal with it quite well.”
Tameside response officer PC Daniel Bragg has been in his job for seven years, and said with the exception of perhaps New Year’s Eve, this summer had been the busiest he had ever known.
“Over the last few months, obviously with the World Cup, the sun, it’s just non-stop,” he said. “Due to the football you have more people jumping in cars after pubs, so we had a lot more crashes. When it gets warm, naturally with older people you have a lot more deaths occurring.”
Bragg said domestic incidents and mental health crises were also two big drivers of 999 calls. “It was absolutely manic again last week, non-stop,” he said, adding that senior officers were being sent out on jobs in order to meet response targets.
Officers attended 14,991 grade 1 incidents (where there is an immediate emergency) in July, achieving an average response time of seven minutes and 54 seconds, and 10,266 grade 2 (serious incidents lacking immediate danger), with an average response time of one hour and two minutes.
In the last month, Bragg said, the team had been responding to up to 40 calls in a night shift; typically that number would lie somewhere between 10 and 20.
“You’re doubling or quadrupling that in one night,” he said. “You are out of the station from 9 o’clock when a job comes in, and then you’re coming back in at 7 o’ clock really, just going job to job.”
With more hot summers on the horizon, Bragg said: “I do think if it continues like this over the years to come, there would have to be a change just in terms of staffing. It’s kind of impossible to police what we’re policing at the minute.”
“When I look at the three-month period and compare it to the same three months last year, it’s been a really significant increase,” said the Tameside district superintendent, Arif Nawaz. “We’re looking at around an extra 572 grade 2 incidents and an extra 272 grade 1 incidents. So that effectively means my response teams have to deal with an extra seven grade 1s and 2s every single day.”
As well as the weather, Manchester’s rapid development brought more people to the city, which in turn placed additional strain on policing, Nawaz said. “The economic development around Manchester is brilliant for the region but it’s also contributing. The Co-op Arena is a new site attracting 20,000 people each event. That’s in addition to the AO Arena. So that’s just one simple example of something that’s great for the economy, but there’s a policing demand.”
The repeated heatwaves were, Nawaz said, “a very serious issue that as a society we need to consider, as a police service we need to consider”.
“The government’s looking at it as well, so who knows what the future will bring?” he added. “Clearly it is in our thinking around how we prepare ourselves for this.”

Interest rate dilemma for central banks as inflation rises but growth slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

As the Middle East crisis drags on into its sixth month, central banks sit in a tricky position. Oil prices remain at elevated levels, stoking inflationary pressures while also threatening to weigh on growth.
The US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and the European Central Bank are still smarting from the criticism of their inaction in 2022, when inflation soared above 10% in the UK and eurozone and over 9% in the US.
Central banks were plagued by accusations that they moved too slowly to confront inflation in the months after the Ukraine war started, when post-pandemic consumer spending was already stoking prices on everything from food to construction materials.
Now they are asking whether the continuing throttling of fossil fuel shipping through the strait of Hormuz will mean another year of target-busting prices growth.
The Federal Reserve seeks help
Last month US inflation edged lower to 3.4%, down from 3.5% in June and 4.2% in May, largely in response to easing petrol prices following the US memorandum of understanding with Iran.
Since the Bureau of Labor Statistics collected the data, the price of a barrel of Brent crude has risen again to about $90 – a figure that will push up the price of energy and transport across the US in the second half of the year.
Fed officials are asking whether US inflation will climb back towards 4%, double its target. The US central bank’s new boss, Kevin Warsh, has instigated an all-embracing review of its operations based on the advice of 15 outsiders that he says are among the most eminent experts and economists of the age.
Many analysts have applauded him for recognising that a series of inflation shocks dating back to the arrival of Covid-19 have undermined the integrity and durability of central bank forecasting.
Mohamed El-Erian, an economist and professor at the Wharton Business school, said Warsh recognised that many of the shibboleths of monetary policymaking had proved flawed.
“The key issue for me is having someone there who’s committed to long-overdue Fed reforms. This is essential for future Fed effectiveness, credibility and political independence,”he said.
Chief among the tools Warsh has already ditched is forward guidance – the explicit signalling of the likely future path of interest rates. He also declined to join other Fed policymakers in creating dot plots on a graph showing how the economy and inflation are expected to develop over the next couple of years.
Among Warsh’s 15 appointments to five subject committees is Mervyn King, the former governor of the Bank of England. Lord King is considered a founding father of inflation forecasting, but has since argued that central banks should take more account of uncertainty in how people react and ditch a heavy reliance on economic models that claim to predict likely outcomes.
In his 2022 book Radical Uncertainty, he described forward guidance as “silly” when no central bank knows what the interest rate will be in six months or two years’ time.
El-Erian calls forward guidance “spurious accuracy”. What financial markets and the public need to know is the “reaction function”. In other words, how the central bank will respond to different economic developments.
Charlie Bean, a professor at the London School of Economics and a former deputy governor of the BoE, said that Warsh’s changes mean that Fed watchers don’t have guidance on either the path of rates or the central bank’s likely reaction to events.
“Warsh is getting in a bit of a mess in the way he is not giving a guide to where rates are going and also not talking about how changes in the economy will affect rates,” said Bean. “It means he is not saying anything of substance.”
The Fed held rates in July and financial market betting expects a hold again in September, though a rise is thought possible. Markets anticipate at least one, and possibly two, quarter-point increases by the middle of next year, taking the Fed’s target rate from its current 3.5-3.75% range to 4-4.25%. Will market betting prove reliable? Nobody knows.
The Bank of England suffers a post-Covid hangover
While the BoE is widely considered to have acted consistently since the start of the Iran war – saying it will raise the cost of borrowing should there be any signs of persistent inflation. However, the decision to hold the Bank Rate steady at 3.75% so far this year could come under pressure.
The UK consumer price index (CPI) dropped to 2.6% in June, but some analysts expect it to rise to 2.9% or even 3% when July’s figures are published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday this week.
A majority of the nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) are wary of increasing interest rates when it will have little effect on global oil prices, aware that higher borrowing costs could depress an already weak UK economy.
Bean says the MPC is also under pressure from even more fundamental trends, including high and rising government debt.
The difficulty arises when governments are highly indebted and a central bank wants to raise interest rates to control inflation. A rise in the cost of borrowing increases the government’s debt financing bill. Central banks must decide whether to cripple the government’s finances or let inflation remain high for a longer period above its target.
This is a problem for the Fed’s Warsh, too – after the US paid the highest borrowing costs to sell 30-year bonds since 2001, in an debt auction this month.
Neil Shearing, chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, says he has argued for many years that central banks will preside over high inflation for as long as western governments cannot control their debt-fuelled spending.
“The conceit is that central banks need to maintain 2% as their target, while at the same time tolerating a slightly higher level of inflation,” he said.
Making matters worse, most inflationary shocks come from global events that restrict the supply of essential goods. Interest rate rises dampen consumer spending with little effect on the price of imported goods.
Nevertheless, financial markets predict the BoE will raise rates this year, possibly from as early as its next meeting in September on the path to pushing rates as high as 4.25% by late 2027.
The ECB goes rogue
Unlike the Fed and BoE, the ECB has raised the cost of borrowing this year. Critics say it moved too quickly. While the eurozone’s central bank has freed itself from forward guidance, critics say the ECB remains confused about how to react when inflation begins to climb.
It raised interest rates in June after only a modest rise in inflation caused by the Middle East war and rising oil prices. Many economists said the move was too early when much of the eurozone economy continues to be devastated by the energy shock that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Shearing said: “The ECB was clearly fighting the previous war and prematurely raising rates. The underlying picture in the eurozone is one of weakness.”
He is among many analysts who believe financial markets are wrong to expect the ECB will raise its main deposit rate by a quarter-point to 2.5% at its next meeting in September and possibly act again with a further quarter-point increase next year.
Shearing says that while high oil prices put pressure on inflation, they act as a brake on economic activity, as a rise in interest rates would also do. A rate rise would be like kicking the economy when it is already down, and the ECB wouldn’t win any plaudits for doing that.

College women are increasingly marrying men without degrees as college demographics shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:00:21 UTC
23:00:21 KST

A recent study published as a working paper by the National Bureau of Economic Research indicates that the widening gender gap in college graduation is reshaping American marriage patterns. As women increasingly outpace men in higher education, college-educated women are maintaining stable marriage rates by more frequently marrying higher-earning men without degrees. This shift leaves women without college degrees with a shrinking pool of economically stable potential partners, which corresponds to a sharp decline in their marriage rates.
People tend to marry partners with similar educational backgrounds, a pattern sociologists and economists call assortative mating. Over the past fifty years, United States college campuses have shifted from enrolling a majority of men to enrolling a majority of women. Today, about 1.6 million more women than men attend four-year colleges in the United States.
This demographic shift raised questions about how college-educated women would adapt to a relative shortage of similarly educated men. The study was partly inspired by conflicting narratives about modern dating. “Two puzzles,” explained study co-author Benjamin Goldman, an assistant professor of economics and public policy at Cornell University. “One is the salience of commentary (e.g., here) about how it’s become difficult to date as a highly educated woman, alongside the fact that marriage rates have been stable for women with four-year degrees.”
“The second is how those marriage rates have stayed stable, given that there used to be many more college-educated men than women, and now the reverse is true,” Goldman continued. At the same time, men without college degrees have experienced decades of economic stagnation. Their average earnings and labor force participation have dropped. The authors of the working paper designed their research to understand how these twin developments interacting together might affect the marriage prospects of women across different educational backgrounds.
To examine long-term changes, the researchers analyzed data from the Current Population Survey and the American Community Survey. They focused on American men and women born between 1930 and 1980. The sample was divided into four groups based on whether individuals had completed at least four years of college.
The authors first tracked overall marriage rates at age 45 for these different cohorts. They observed that the ratio of college-educated men to college-educated women dropped from 1.8 in the 1930 birth cohort to just 0.8 in the 1980 birth cohort. Despite this growing scarcity of college-educated men, the marriage rate for college-educated women only declined slightly, moving from 77.7 percent to 71.0 percent.
In contrast, the marriage rate for women without college degrees fell dramatically. For the 1930 birth cohort, 78.7 percent of these women were married at age 45. By the 1980 cohort, only 52.4 percent were married.
To understand the mechanics behind this divergence, the researchers applied a mathematical model to estimate the changing value or surplus of different marital pairings. They found that the share of college-educated women married to men without degrees quadrupled. In the 1930 cohort, just 2.3 percent of all women were college-educated and married to a man without a degree. By the 1980 cohort, this figure reached 9.6 percent.
The data indicates that college-educated women increasingly partnered with a specific subset of men without degrees. The men who married college-educated women experienced an increase in average real earnings from $61,400 to $68,400 over the studied cohorts. Meanwhile, average earnings for all other men without degrees fell from $56,400 to $46,100.
This combination of economic decline and increased competition from college-educated women substantially reduced the pool of available high-earning partners for women without degrees. “The genders are not in zero-sum competition,” Goldman told PsyPost. “Troubling trends for men, like falling behind in school and the labor market, affect the marriage and family opportunities available to women, especially less-educated women.”
The researchers noted that these shifting partnership dynamics ripple across the socioeconomic spectrum. “As fewer men go to college, college-educated women have started marrying high-earning men without degrees, leaving fewer stable partners for non-college women,” Goldman added. The share of men without a college degree who earned above the national median and were not already married to a college-educated woman plummeted. That figure fell from 72.9 percent in the 1930 cohort to 35.3 percent in the 1980 cohort.
The researchers then looked at recent geographic data to see if local economic conditions mirrored these historical trends. They analyzed American Community Survey data from 2017 to 2021, focusing on adults aged 40 to 49 across 2,351 geographic areas with an average population of 140,000. They measured the employment-to-population ratio for men without college degrees in each area. The analysis controlled for local college attendance rates among women.
The geographic data supported the historical findings. In areas where men without degrees struggled to find work, marriage rates for women without degrees were substantially lower. A 7.6 percentage point drop in the employment rate for men without degrees corresponded to a 4.2 percentage point drop in the marriage rate for women without degrees. For college-educated women, the same drop in men’s employment was associated with only a 2.4 percentage point decline in marriage.
To account for the possibility that married couples simply move to areas with better job markets, the authors conducted a third analysis. They used data from the Opportunity Atlas, which links adult outcomes to the specific geographic areas where individuals grew up using anonymous tax and census records. This phase of the research categorized individuals by their parents’ income rather than their adult education level. The researchers compared individuals from families in the top 25 percent of income to those from the bottom 25 percent.
This analysis yielded similar patterns. A four percentage point decrease in employment for men from lower-income backgrounds corresponded to a 5.3 percentage point drop in marriage rates for women from similar backgrounds. For women from higher-income backgrounds, the same decline in men’s employment was associated with a 2.1 percentage point drop in marriage. In communities where lower-income men experienced higher rates of joblessness, incarceration, or mortality, the marriage gap between higher-income and lower-income women was substantially wider.
Readers might be tempted to assume that men’s declining employment directly causes women to avoid marriage. The study observes strong statistical relationships between these variables, but it cannot rule out other factors that influence family formation. “The evidence isn’t causal; it doesn’t prove that improving working-class men’s well-being would restore marriage rates to 1950s levels,” Goldman said.
Cultural norms surrounding marriage have shifted dramatically over the past fifty years, which likely plays an independent role in declining marriage rates. “But both over time and across areas of the United States, education gaps in marriage rates clearly emerge for women in environments where men struggle with non-employment, incarceration, and early-life mortality,” Goldman noted.
The research primarily focuses on opposite-sex pairings. This approach captures the vast majority of historical marriages but does not account for shifting dynamics in same-sex relationships. Additionally, the working paper was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, an organization that circulates papers for discussion and comment. These working papers do not undergo the formal peer review process typical of academic journals.
Future research could explore how specific policy interventions might alter these trajectories. “I’m hoping to answer the causal version of this question: do interventions that raise men’s economic standing improve their marriage prospects?” Goldman said.
Another avenue for exploration is how the institution of marriage itself might influence men’s economic stability and labor market success. Understanding these dynamics could provide a more complete picture of how class disparities and family formation intersect.
The study, “Bachelors Without Bachelor’s: Gender Gaps in Education and Declining Marriage Rates,” was authored by Clara Chambers, Benjamin Goldman, and Joseph Winkelmann.

WATCH Ukrainian press gang tear-gas crowd trying to save man from conscription

Unknown Publisher

WATCH Ukrainian press gang tear-gas crowd trying to save man from conscription
Ukrainian conscription officers reportedly sprayed civilians with tear gas in Odessa after they tried to stop a press gang from seizing a man for military service.
According to the Novosti Odessa Telegram channel, several people approached a vehicle carrying draft officers during an alleged attempt at ‘busification’ – a pejorative term denoting a practice whereby draft officers snatch military-age men in public and drag them into vans to take them to conscription centers, often using violence against those who resist.
A video posted online by the outlet shows several people trying to pull away a young man whom the press gang was presumably after, while pushing the draft officers back into their vehicle. The officers then appear to spray tear gas at the crowd before hastily driving off amid expletives and angry shouts of “get out of here.”
The outlet said the incident took place on Saturday evening in a busy residential neighborhood roughly midway between the city center and Odessa’s Black Sea port.
Kiev has increasingly relied on violently enforced conscription amid battlefield losses and Russian advances, with reports of ‘busification’ emerging almost daily.
The campaign has fueled tensions across Ukrainian society, with multiple reports of draft officers brawling with relatives and passersby trying to free would-be conscripts from press gang vans.
While officials insist mobilization is unavoidable in the conflict with Russia, many citizens see the system as rife with state-sanctioned corruption and as disproportionately targeting the poor.
Recruits and their families have also accused authorities of systematic abuse, ignoring exemptions and drafting men medically unfit for service. Meanwhile, military-age men have resorted to various means to avoid the draft, from fleeing the country illegally to setting military recruitment offices on fire or hiding in their homes for months.
Saturday’s incident is not the first reported case of draft officers using tear gas on civilians. Earlier this month, a video purportedly showed a press gang assaulting a young couple in a taxi and repeatedly spraying them with what appeared to be tear gas while trying to drag the man from the vehicle. In late June, a press gang reportedly used tear gas on a 12-year-old girl caught up in an attack on a vehicle carrying draft officers.
Some Ukrainian officials have grown increasingly critical of how the forced conscription is being carried out. Kiev’s human rights ombudsman, Dmitry Lubinets, recently blamed abuses on systemic Defense Ministry failures that had fostered a culture of impunity. In a Telegram post on Saturday, he cited the case of a Ukrainian scientist and archaeologist who was forcibly conscripted despite being entitled to a draft deferment, the documents for which were still being processed. Lubinets called the situation “outrageous,” saying that “blind busification” and mobilization “for the sake of a tick must be eradicated.”
Moscow has argued that growing public resistance to forced conscription shows that the Ukrainian government has lost its legitimacy and can only survive through increasingly authoritarian measures. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova recently described the situation as “absolute lawlessness.”

Transcript: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Aug. 16, 2026
