Egypt could join Mecca defence pact, Turkey's Erdogan says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:35:33 UTC
20:35:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt could join Mecca defence pact, Turkey's Erdogan says
Egypt could join the military alliance recently formed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said, a week after the three countries signed a defence agreement that some analysts have likened to an "Arab NATO".
In an Al Jazeera interview due to air on Sunday, Erdogan said it was "possible" that Cairo could join the 'Mecca pact', adding that the alliance was open to participation from other countries in the region.
The agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city on 14 August by Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan’s Prime Minister, Shehbaz Sharif.
It includes a defence clause similar to NATO's Article 5, which stipulates that an attack against one of the countries is an attack against them all.
Egypt has in recent months joined Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in an informal grouping that has coordinated closely amid the turmoil of the Iran war and Israel’s destabilising actions across the region.
But Cairo has fallen short of formally joining the military alliance. Egypt's foreign minister Badr Abdelatty on Friday said the possibility was being considered "very seriously" but that it requires careful study on its impact on "Egypt's constitution and legal commitments".
Joining the pact would mark a significant departure from Cairo’s long-standing preference for strategic hedging and avoidance of binding regional military blocs.
While Egypt has cultivated security ties with a range of powers, analysts argue that formally committing to a collective-defence alliance could risk entangling the country in conflicts beyond its control.
Erdogan's comments echo statements made by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan this week, who expressed hope that Egypt might join the alliance after addressing "a few technical issues".
Turkey's regional agenda: Syria, Gaza and Lebanon
Erdogan also addressed a range of regional issues, including the US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz and the conflicts in Syria, Gaza and Lebanon.
On Syria, he pledged Turkey’s support for the country’s stability and reiterated his long-standing intention to visit Damascus. In a separate interview on Saturday, Turkey’s ambassador to Syria, Nuh Yilmaz, said Erdogan could travel to the country before the end of the year. The president had initially planned to visit in April, but the Iran war delayed the trip, Yilmaz added.
Erdogan said Syria’s Kurds would have a “share in peace and stability”, adding that Ankara would seek to improve relations with Kurdish communities across the region.
Turning to Gaza, Erdogan said Turkey “cannot leave Gaza alone” and would provide whatever support was necessary. He said Hamas had upheld its commitments under the October ceasefire agreement, while accusing Israel of continuing the war. Turkey has helped mediate efforts to end the conflict alongside Qatar, Egypt and the United States.
On Lebanon, Erdogan said he was deeply concerned by Israel’s continuing attacks, adding that he had appealed to the United States to help bring the war to an end during President Donald Trump’s recent visit to Ankara.

Europe's tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in rural Poland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Europe's tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in rural Poland
1 of 3
- Published
A statue of the Virgin Mary believed to be Europe's tallest has been formally unveiled in a small Polish village.
The 55.6-metre (182ft) concrete figure is roughly two double-decker buses longer than Rio de Janeiro's smaller - if more prominently placed - Christ the Redeemer monument, though it still pales in comparison to a 98m Virgin Mary erected in the Philippines.
The ecclesiastical sculpture in rural Konotopie was consecrated by a local bishop in a ceremony on Saturday, a day chosen to coincide with the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
Its inauguration comes at a time when the influence of the Catholic church on public life in Poland has declined.
The icon's remote location - in a field miles from any of Poland's population centres - is largely due to it being commissioned by a millionaire couple who live locally.
Two helicopters circled to drop rose petals over the Virgin Mary, which stands in a large crown with open arms, during Saturday's ceremony.
Bishop Krzysztof Wętkowski, who consecrated the statue, told those congregated that "many contemporary people look only to the earth, focused on themselves", whereas the figure beckoned "to raise our gaze upwards to God and heaven", according to Polish news agency PAP.
While Poland remains an overwhelmingly Catholic country, many younger Poles in urban areas have increasingly turned away from the church and its traditions.
Among the attendees on Saturday was Lech Wałęsa, who led the movement to end communism in Poland and would go on to become the country's first democratically elected president.
Wałęsa famously wore a Virgin Mary pin badge while campaigning and credited his Catholic faith as playing a major role in his fight against communism.
"I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary," the 82-year-old told the Associated Press.

Four Renaissance paintings stolen from museum in Italy

4 Renaissance paintings stolen from museum in Italy
Four paintings of "extraordinary value" which date back to the Renaissance have been stolen from a museum late Saturday in Sicily, Italy.
Three panels of the San Gregorio Polyptych and a double-sided panel of The Madonna and Child, all attributed to Antonello da Messina dating back to the 15th century, were stolen from the Regional Interdisciplinary Museum of Messina, according to Italy's Ministry of Culture.
The polyptych, which is a painting divided in various panels, was originally composed of at least five different sections and had been damaged after an earthquake in 1908. The painting of The Madonna and Child is listed in the Christie's auctioneer website as having sold for more than $300,000 in 2003.
Minister of Culture Alessandro Giuli expressed his "dismay and regret" at the theft and said the pieces had "extraordinary value for our cultural heritage."
The mayor of Messina called the theft a "heinous criminal act," and said he was "deeply outraged" by the act, in particular because it took place during the city's traditional celebrations honoring the Virgin Mary.
"We hope that those responsible will be identified and that our artworks will be returned home," Federico Basile said in a social media post. "Messina will not let its history be stolen."
The theft comes just months after the Italian state bought a work called "Ecce Homo" by Antonello da Messina at a New York auction for nearly $15 million.

Officials said that the attacks caused "significant damage to the network’s infrastructure" and warned that continued targeting of substations and transmission lines could trigger further blackouts.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks, and Libyan authorities have not publicly identified a perpetrator. However, analysts have linked the attacks to escalating competition among western Libya’s rival armed groups for control of Zawiya’s strategically important refinery, fuel networks and associated smuggling economy.

====================================================================================================

Andy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxury | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:33:42 UTC
20:33:42 KST

I don’t think I have ever written before about a British strike directly related to the climate emergency. But that’s exactly what began late last week in north London, with a zeitgeisty connection to Andy Burnham’s fixation on buses: picket lines outside depots and massed walkouts, while the temperatures in the relevant parts of the capital and its suburbs hovered at about 34C (93F).
Last Friday, more than 1,500 drivers employed by the transport giant Arriva began a planned run of 26 stoppages through to October, affecting bus routes spread between London and Essex. Everything is being led by the union Unite, whose recent grievances include alleged company union-busting and assaults by the public on staff. But the fundamental basis of the dispute is at the heart of the national condition: the near-impossibility for millions of people of working through another insanely hot summer.
Most of Arriva North London’s buses, says Unite, have old-fashioned air cooling systems rather than air conditioning, which means that onboard temperatures have come down by only two or three degrees during this year’s five heatwaves. On other such vehicles, it insists, the air-con is broken. The cabs where drivers sit are essentially compact greenhouses, and can easily reach 40C or higher. And there is another grim twist: union members complain of a shortage of toilets on too many routes, meaning they refrain from drinking water. Unite has been warning about all this since the phases of intense heat that began back in May; its members, the union says, have experienced “heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration”.
Arriva’s last financial figures showed a pre-tax profit of £133m. The company insists that it has “introduced short-term measures to protect drivers”, and is now also spending money on “longer-term fixes, including cab air-conditioning upgrades and our ongoing investment in new fleet”. But the root of its current problems seem clear. There is a longstanding failure, which runs across the UK’s public and private sectors – and also transcends national boundaries – to understand the mounting everyday effects of global heating, and to engage in what so many 21st-century companies and institutions remain so bad at: protective investment, with both eyes fixed not just on the searing inevitabilities of the future, but realities that are already here.
Arriva places tight restrictions on its drivers talking to the media, so Unite pointed me instead to Mo, who has worked for another London bus operator for over 15 years, and had come to a picket line to show the strikers his support. “When it’s very hot, it’s very difficult to concentrate,” he told me. “Imagine the heat you feel when you put your hand near an oven. That’s what it’s like.” What, I wondered, had happened when these problems were raised with management? “Sometimes, we don’t want to raise this stuff, because they don’t want to hear it. If you say, ‘I’ve got a hot cab, I want to come out,’ they’re like, ‘Well, we’re going to lose mileage; we’re going to get penalised by TfL [Transport for London].’ I know the mayor’s put the message out” – in June, Sadiq Khan said he was committed to improving working conditions for drivers – “but the company says, ‘He doesn’t employ you. We do.’”
There are no end of similarly unsettling reports from other occupations. The Royal College of Nursing says some of its members working in the health service have recently collapsed, while others have reported dizziness, nausea and dripping with sweat “from head to toe”, along with profound concerns about NHS patients’ most basic welfare. Recent research into the building trade from the University of Reading showed that 44% of the construction workers it contacted had experienced a heat-related illness, such as heatstroke, heat exhaustion or dehydration. Moreover, 57% said they had received no compulsory training on how to deal with heat.
Almost exactly a year ago, I wrote about the tragic story of Montse Aguilar, a 51-year-old woman who worked as a street cleaner in Barcelona, and returned home from a working day in which the city’s temperatures had reached 35C, only to collapse, hit her head and die. Soon after, people marched carrying banners that read “Extreme heat is also workplace violence”, and street cleaners demanded better summer workwear and more breaks. Much to her family’s distress, the city council has still not recognised her death as a workplace accident, and there has yet to be an autopsy.
This year, Barcelona’s authorities handed out about 1,400 bracelets for staff working outdoors – including street cleaners, park workers and refuse specialists – which measure workers’ body temperatures and go into alert mode if they sense that the wearer is at risk: as and when that happens, the person concerned has to stop working. But despite Spain’s reputation for comparatively stringent heat regulations, unions continue to draw attention to a supposed system of protection still full of gaps. Late last month, the CGT union filed official complaints with Barcelona’s labour inspectorate about what it deems deficient management of those wristbands, a lack of air-con in working vehicles and pledges from the city council being applied “late and halfway”.
Across the world, every hot season inevitably brings more victims. In the US, official figures suggest that more than 550 workers die annually from heat exposure across the country. One recent story is that of Umeshkumar Thakkar, a 58-year-old postal worker who lived in Little Elm, Texas – who, though the cause of his death has yet to be officially established, has been cited as the third such employee in three years to die in the Dallas area amid extreme heat. Amazingly, Texas has barred its cities and counties from passing local heat protections – while, to quote the New York Times, “The Trump administration is moving to rewrite Biden-era rules that would mandate breaks and access to water and shade for workers.” Hydration, it seems, is that bit too woke.
The UK’s position, it is a relief to say, is not nearly as dreadful, though there is still much work to do. For people working indoors, official guidance suggests a minimum temperature of 16C, which falls to 13C for “physical work”, but there are no maximum temperatures for either indoor or outdoor labour. Things do finally seem to be moving: last month, the Department for Work and Pensions said that the Health and Safety Executive will soon launch a public consultation on improvements to safety-at-work rules that will cover levels of heat at work. There again, the official line from the prime minister’s spokesperson sounds bleak: “We have no plans to introduce a mandatory maximum workplace temperature.”
In the wake of the Green MP Hannah Spencer’s private member’s bill to establish exactly that, Unite is loudly making the case – as are the TUC and the independent advisory Climate Change Committee, which wants employers to “ensure that workplaces and working practices are safe for employees, including for those working outside”. Meanwhile, having planned for a late summer talking about the cost of living, Burnham did not mention the climate crisis until last Friday, in a country where brown fields are so starved of water they are now turning a scorched yellow, homes have been engulfed by wildfires, and far too many workers are finding the once-simple business of earning a living physically impossible. Like many people – including, I would imagine, plenty of those north London bus drivers – my guarded optimism about the new prime minister and his government endures. But the last of those issues needs as much urgent action as the others, before another boiling summer takes an even grimmer toll.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

U.S. Coast Guard to convert new cargo planes into surveillance aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:31:59 UTC
20:31:59 KST

- The Coast Guard is seeking industry input to convert new C-130J aircraft into HC-130J surveillance planes for itself and Customs and Border Protection.
- The RFI covers a base of four aircraft with options for eight more, and includes a draft plan to add SpaceX Starshield satellite communications.
The U.S. Coast Guard is seeking companies capable of converting new C-130J transport aircraft into HC-130J surveillance planes, part of a program that will eventually cover 28 Coast Guard aircraft and 12 more for Customs and Border Protection.
The Coast Guard’s Office of Aviation Acquisition posted a request for information on August 14, asking industry for market research ahead of a future solicitation. Responses are due September 17. The notice covers what the service calls “missionization,” the process of installing its Minotaur Mission System Suite, known as MSS+, onto baseline C-130J aircraft built by Lockheed Martin Aeronautics. Once the system is installed, the aircraft is redesignated an HC-130J.
The upcoming contract covers a base of four aircraft, three for the Coast Guard and one for Customs and Border Protection’s Air and Marine Operations, with options for three more Coast Guard aircraft and five more CBP aircraft. The effort is a continuation of an existing missionization program and will begin with the Coast Guard’s 23rd HC-130J, according to the RFI. Work is expected to start in fiscal year 2030, with the four base aircraft ready for induction that year, and continued at a rate of one to two additional aircraft per year depending on funding.
A draft performance work statement attached to the RFI lays out the scope of the work in detail. The MSS+ package includes twin Minotaur Processors that serve as the system’s computational hub, two mission system operator stations installed on the flight deck, a turret-mounted high-definition electro-optical and forward-looking infrared sensor, and a multi-mode radar mounted in a radome under the aircraft’s belly, currently identified in program documents as the EL/M-2022A. The suite also adds a direction finder system, an automatic identification system transponder for tracking vessels, and a communications package built around two high-frequency radios, two RT-7000 radios and two ARC-210 radios capable of satellite communication.
The draft work statement also calls for installing a next-generation commercial satellite communications system built around SpaceX’s Starshield network, listed as an option in the current effort. The specification calls for a Starshield Aero Terminal Kit, Block 4 or higher, including an antenna, power supply, mounting tray and shell assembly, along with a minimum of 1 terabyte of monthly data service.
The Coast Guard currently supplies the multi-mode radar as government-furnished equipment. The RFI asks industry whether shifting that radar to contractor-furnished equipment would create obstacles, noting that the radar’s lead time may not support the timelines the Coast Guard is planning between contract award and aircraft induction.
The draft schedule attached to the RFI lists estimated induction and delivery windows for aircraft under the follow-on contract, running from an October 2029 induction for the first Coast Guard tail number through a 2037 to 2038 window for a sixth CBP aircraft under the contract’s later options. The RFI states the overall period of performance would run from April 2028, allowing time to order long-lead parts, through March 2038. The Coast Guard said it does not expect the period of performance to exceed 10 years and expects each individual aircraft modification to take no more than 12 months from induction.
The notice states that a formal solicitation may follow later this year based on feedback from the RFI, and that companies that do not respond may not be considered likely offerors if the service later decides to limit competition. Andrew Gordon and Mary Case are listed as points of contact for the notice.

Bam Khatoon ready for another Asian challenge
TEHRAN - Iranian women’s football champions Bam Khatoon are ready for another demanding campaign on the Asian stage as they return to the AFC Women’s Champions League, determined to build on their growing reputation as one of Iran’s leading clubs.
Khatoon have established themselves as the dominant force in Iranian women’s football. The Bam-based side have won the domestic league 12 times and have increasingly made their presence felt in continental competition. Their progress has been particularly notable in recent editions of the AFC’s premier women’s club tournament, where they have shown that Iranian women’s football can compete with some of Asia’s strongest teams.
The upcoming 2026/27 AFC Women’s Champions League presents a fresh test for Khatoon. The Iranian champions have been drawn in Group E of the Preliminary Stage alongside Al Nassr of Saudi Arabia, Jordan’s Etihad Club and FC CSKA Dushanbe of Tajikistan. The group will be played from Aug. 17 to 23, with only the group winners advancing to the next stage of the competition.
Khatoon’s opening match is scheduled against CSKA Dushanbe on Monday, before they face Al Nassr and Etihad Club. The format leaves little room for error, making every point and every goal potentially decisive. With only one team from each preliminary group progressing, Khatoon must maintain their focus throughout the tournament.
Jafari said Iran’s opponents have made significant investments ahead of the competition, highlighting the strength of Al Nassr of Saudi Arabia, which boast high-quality foreign players from Portugal, France, Brazil, Japan and several African countries.
She also pointed to Jordan’s Etihad, who have recruited several strong foreign players, while Tajikistan’s CSKA can rely on a number of internationals as well as four quality foreign-based players.
“All of our rivals have invested heavily and will enter the competition fully prepared, which makes our task even more difficult,” Jafari said.
However, she emphasized that Iran will compete with an almost entirely domestic squad. The team has added only Yasna Jafarzadeh as a reinforcement, while Mona Hamoudi and Negin Zandi will also be unavailable.
“Despite these challenges, we will give everything we have to return home with a positive result and represent Iranian women’s football with pride,” Jafari added.
Khatoon’s continental experience could prove crucial. In the 2024/25 AFC Women’s Champions League, the Iranian side reached the quarter-finals after finishing second in their group. They were eventually eliminated by Korea Republic’s Hyundai Steel Red Angels, who secured a narrow 1-0 victory.
That run represented a significant milestone for the club and Iranian women’s football. Khatoon had previously competed in the AFC Women’s Club Championship and have continued to strengthen their position as Iran’s leading representative on the continental stage. The club also became the first Iranian women’s side to obtain an AFC professional club license, an important step in their development.
Marziyeh Jafari, one of the most successful coaches in Iranian women’s football, remains a central figure in Khatoon’s success. She has been closely associated with the club for many years and guided the team to multiple domestic championships as well as continental achievements. Her experience at this level could once again be a decisive factor in navigating the demanding preliminary stage.

Burnham urged to crack down on gig economy firms to protect 4m workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:29:41 UTC
20:29:41 KST

Andy Burnham is being urged to protect 4 million gig economy workers by prosecuting companies that use widespread “bogus” self-employment practices to deny people their rights.
As the prime minister fleshes out his agenda, the Fabian Society and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation have warned that millions of workers are missing out on key statutory rights including parental leave, redundancy pay and protection against unfair dismissal.
Publishing a joint report calling on Burnham to take action, the Labour-linked thinktank and the anti-poverty charity said changes were essential to make work pay amid the cost of living crisis.
The report calls on the government’s Fair Work Agency – launched in April as a powerful watchdog for workers’ rights – to use its civil proceedings powers to prosecute companies suspected of engaging in “widespread bogus self-employment”.
It also urges ministers to push ahead with changes to employment law to combat longstanding misuse of the system.
Britain’s employment laws are unusual among leading economies for including three classifications of employment status. An employee has the most rights and responsibilities, while a self-employed person has limited protections but fewer obligations. There is also an intermediate “worker”, or “limb (b)” status, with fewer rights and obligations than a full employee.
According to the report, as many as 4 million workers – including hairdressers, personal trainers, delivery workers and drivers for gig economy platforms – work in this gap. Experts say many have been hired by gig economy companies in this way to avoid granting them employment rights.
Labour had promised to create a single “worker” status for all but the genuinely self-employed, before rowing back on the plan to fend off Conservative attacks on its approach to business before the 2024 general election.
Once in power, the policy was not included in Labour’s shake-up of employment rights, and though it promised to consult on “moving towards a single status of worker”, this has not materialised.
Labour faces intense lobbying from business over its sweeping Employment Rights Act, which includes a ban on exploitative zero-hours contracts and day-one rights to statutory sick pay.
Last week, official government analysis showed the planned changes would help to support economic growth and offer workers more protections, though they would cost businesses an estimated £350m to £2.9bn.
In his first week in office, Burnham spoke to business leaders to state his determination to push ahead with the plan for the biggest shake-up of employment rights in a generation.
However, the Fabian Society and Joseph Rowntree Foundation said changes to address employment status were needed to ensure gig economy workers would benefit from these upgraded protections.
The report calls for the burden of proof for whether someone is an employee, worker or self-employed to be shifted from the worker to the employer. This would help people to avoid fighting lengthy legal battles to secure basic rights such as the minimum wage and holiday pay.
Luke Raikes, the deputy general secretary of the Fabian Society, said: “The government must ensure those who play fast and loose with employment law can’t undercut the majority of good employers who play by the rules.
“If it looks like employment then employers should be treating people as employees by default and should expect enforcement action if they aren’t complying. Insecure workers should not have to take on a company’s lawyers – sometimes all the way to the supreme court – just to establish the basic rights they are owed.”
A government spokesperson said: “Our plan to make work pay will boost secure employment, improve job security and deliver stronger, higher living standards. The Fair Work Agency is already helping workers get the rights they are entitled to. We’ve committed to consult on employment status and will consider how the Fair Work Agency can use its civil proceedings power alongside that.”

Man under threat of deportation to Jamaica wins right to rejoin his British family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:27:22 UTC
20:27:22 KST

A Jamaican man who has lived more than half his life in the UK and was facing imminent deportation has been allowed to reunite with his British family after a legal challenge.
Mark Nelson, 47, came to the UK in 2000 and later set up his own car-mechanic business. He has five British children and a British partner. He faced deportation in 2022 after serving a four-year prison sentence for possession with intent to supply a class B drug, abstracting electricity and two offences of racially aggravated intentional harassment. He had not committed any further offences.
The deportation was later cancelled and instead he was tagged and told to report weekly at a Home Office centre. But last month – almost 10 years after his original conviction – Nelson was arrested, detained and told that the government again planned to deport him to Jamaica.
The Home Office gave him a ticket for a flight on 7 August, but after reading about his case in the Guardian, lawyers offered to represent him pro bono to challenge his deportation.
After they made an 11th-hour application for a judicial review the Home Office backed down on the deportation and cancelled his ticket. This week he was granted bail and can return to the home he shares with his partner, Rachel Derbyshire, in the north of England and see his children again.
Nelson said he was overjoyed to to have left the immigration detention centre near Heathrow where he had spent several weeks in hot and crowded conditions.
“I’ve spoken to my kids, my partner and my brother,” he said. “Everyone is so excited about my release. If it hadn’t been for the lawyers who got in touch after reading the Guardian article I would be back in Jamaica by now, separated from my family, not knowing when I would see them again.
“I have no family members there and believe my life would be at risk.”
Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors, who contacted Nelson after reading about his case, lodged the judicial review application. He has also lodged an appeal relating to his immigration case in the first-tier tribunal and a referral has been made for him to the national referral mechanism as a potential victim of modern slavery.
Kandiah said: “He committed his offences in 2017 and served his sentence. Yet nearly a decade later he continues to endure the threat of deportation, with the devastating possibility that he could be permanently torn away from his British children and partner. A prison sentence should not become a life sentence by another name.
“Vulnerable people can struggle to secure legal representation when they need it most. When a person facing removal cannot access timely legal advice, the risk is that the Home Office can remove them before their case has been properly scrutinised.”
Nelson wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian in 2022 about being under threat of deportation. He said Jamaica was a place where he no longer knew anyone after his great-grandparents, who brought him up there, died when he was 16.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “All foreign national offenders who receive a prison sentence in the UK are referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity.
“We have removed or deported almost 70,000 people who were here illegally since the last election, an increase of 41%.”

Why Bennett, Eisenkot, and Lapid privately asked Trump not to endorse Netanyahu - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:27:08 UTC
20:27:08 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political situation is further complicating the American calculus.
His current coalition is far from the 61 seats needed to form a government. From his perspective, preventing the opposing camp from securing a majority could also be enough: If no one succeeds in forming a government, he will remain in office as caretaker prime minister until another election. That possibility is particularly troubling to Washington because it could mean additional months in which Trump’s regional agenda is forced to wait for Israeli politics.
Trump also has personal political leverage over Netanyahu. So far, he has refrained from giving him the public election endorsement the prime minister had hoped for.
When they met at the White House about two weeks ago, Trump even asked him directly about his standing in the polls. Netanyahu hesitated, and one of his advisers quickly told the president that he was “winning.”
The data tell a different story. On four separate occasions in recent weeks, Trump was asked whether he supported Netanyahu, and each time he avoided offering an explicit endorsement.
Trump holding onto potential aid to Netanyahu before election
That reluctance carries additional significance because of the history between the two men. Trump has already demonstrated that he is willing to throw his full weight into an Israeli election campaign: Days before the April 2019 election, he recognized Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, a move he later boasted had helped Netanyahu. This time, at least for now, he is keeping that card in his hand.
The Israeli opposition also understands the value of that card. Figures close to Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and Yair Lapid have in recent months conveyed messages to Trump’s associates through acquaintances, donors, and political allies, asking him to remain neutral in the election. That activity demonstrates the extent to which Trump’s position has become a factor in the Israeli election campaign even before he has decided whether to intervene.
The personal relationship between the two men has not been severed. Senior American officials describe Trump as fond of Netanyahu but increasingly frustrated by his decisions. Trump was also recently quoted as saying in private conversations that Netanyahu is “his own worst enemy.”
At the same time, support in Israel for some of Trump’s policies has weakened following the agreement with Iran and the restrictions the administration imposed on Israel’s freedom of action in Iran, Gaza, Syria, and Lebanon. Trump also faces a political constraint of his own: Intervening too aggressively in Israel’s election could damage his standing among an Israeli public that once gave him almost automatic support.
US, Israel policies diverge
Lebanon is not the only arena where this gap is being tested. In Gaza, the White House wants to advance its Board of Peace plan; in Syria, Washington is investing in President Ahmed al-Sharaa, even as harsh statements against him are being voiced in Israel; and over Iran, the question remains whether the crisis will end in an agreement or another round of confrontation. Jared Kushner, Nickolay Mladenov, and Tony Blair are arriving in the region this week to advance the Gaza initiative. For them, it is expected to be the first issue on the agenda in their talks with Netanyahu. Israeli action in any one of these arenas could complicate an American initiative in another.
There is currently no basis for assessing that Trump is about to become an adversary of Israel or Netanyahu.
The risk for the prime minister is that an American president convinced that the time for deals has arrived will begin assigning Jerusalem an increasingly large share of the responsibility for delaying them. Trump still holds other cards that Netanyahu may need as the election approaches, from a public endorsement to another move involving President Isaac Herzog on the issue of a pardon. For now, he is not playing them. As the election draws closer, Netanyahu’s room to maneuver in the face of American demands is also narrowing.

What are Trump's options as he seeks to pile more economic pressure on Iran? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:26:48 UTC
20:26:48 KST

US President Donald Trump on Friday vowed to hit Iran hard economically, a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Washington would impose measures on Tehran that have "never been seen" as soon as next week.
The United States, the United Nations and the European Union have applied sanctions, implemented trade embargoes and frozen assets since the late 1970s over Iran's nuclear program, human rights violations and support for militant groups.
Since the Iran war began in February, Washington has levied additional maritime, energy and financial sanctions and started a naval blockade.
Data from the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) shows the agency has imposed sanctions on more than 1,000 people, vessels and aircraft since Trump began his second term.
Recent measures have targeted Iran's shadow oil fleet; shipping insurers; entities and people enabling Iran's acquisition of weapons; and digital exchanges, freezing an estimated $500 billion in Iran-linked cryptocurrency.
Experts say the Trump administration can also try these options:
Sanctions on Chinese 'Teapot' refineries
Chinese independent refineries known as "teapots" account for a quarter of Chinese refinery capacity. They operate with narrow and sometimes negative profit margins.
China buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Independent refiners absorb much of this trade, exposing them to so-called secondary measures that penalize entities helping a primary sanctions target.
Past US sanctions have deterred larger independent refiners from buying Iranian oil. But the independent refineries are somewhat immune since they have little exposure to the US financial system, sanctions experts say.
Sanctions on Chinese banks
OFAC has imposed secondary sanctions on smaller China- and Hong Kong-based entities accused of processing billions of dollars in Iranian oil and helping to fund weapons procurement.
Treasury has warned two larger Chinese banks they could face secondary sanctions if Iranian funds were found moving through their systems, but has stopped short of designating them.
Hitting those two banks, which US officials have not publicly identified, or imposing other sanctions could have a chilling effect on bigger financial institutions, sanctions experts said, although they warned it could also trigger retaliatory actions by Beijing.
Trump administration officials have sought to play down tensions between Washington and Beijing ahead of an expected meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping later this year. They worry that China could curtail exports of critical minerals that are essential to advanced technology production at a time when the US and Western allies are still trying to develop their own supplies.
'Whack-a-mole'
The United States could continue targeting Iranian individuals and entities, as well as others in China and the Gulf, that are helping Tehran evade sanctions to collect revenues for its war effort.
Treasury recently issued sanctions against firms that are springing up to facilitate Iran's trading of oil revenue for imports. But such measures amount to a "whack-a-mole" approach that has not altered Iran's behavior, said Brett Erickson, managing principal of Obsidian Risk Advisors, noting that Tehran simply creates new entities to replace them.
Miad Maleki, a sanctions expert with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Bessent was likely signaling a sharpened enforcement push against oil shippers, purchasers and currency exchangers who help Iran pay for its imports.
Further aviation sanctions were also possible, aimed at degrading Iran's ability to move trade now that the US has blockaded shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, he added.
Land blockade
Some US and Israeli officials have floated the prospect of a land blockade, which would require assistance from Iran's neighbors: Iraq, Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Armenia.
The Trump administration has varying degrees of closeness with all those countries except Afghanistan, but that border is mountainous and extremely difficult to patrol anyway.
Trump may have leverage over Pakistan, which recently sought a $10 billion currency swap line from Treasury, and Turkey, which is seeking to rejoin the US F-35 warplane program.
A land blockade could increase pressure on the Iranian people by halting their imports of food, energy, and textiles, but experts say such a move would be difficult to execute and might not result in protests or internal pressure.
Secondary tariffs
Trump has repeatedly threatened tariffs on goods from countries that do business with Iran, although the Supreme Court struck down the legal basis for such taxes.
The Senate passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill last week that included new Iran sanctions and would give Trump new tariff powers that he could potentially use against countries that aid Iran's commerce and weapons procurement.
That legislation must still pass the US House of Representatives, which could prove challenging given widespread concerns among Democrats and some Republicans about the tariff measures.

A major wildfire in eastern Belgium has burned around 27 square kilometres (2,700 hectares around 3,780 football fields) of natural land and forced hundreds of people from their homes, local media reported on Sunday.
The fire, which has been burning in the High Fens nature reserve since Friday, remained active in several locations, while heavy smoke continued to affect surrounding communities, according to Belgian public broadcaster VRT.
Residents evacuated from Sourbrodt and Butgenbach have not yet been allowed to return home.
Around 600 people were evacuated as a precaution.
More than 250 emergency personnel worked through the night to contain the blaze, including over 100 Belgian and German firefighters, 70 police officers, 40 soldiers and 20 civil protection personnel.
Two Dutch Chinook helicopters, each capable of carrying approximately 7,600 litres of water, were also dispatched to support firefighting operations.
Authorities said shifting winds and difficult terrain were hampering efforts to bring the blaze under control.
Peat beneath the heathland also continued to smoulder, causing repeated flare-ups.
As the fire spread towards Monschau, a German town near the Belgian border, residents of several neighbourhoods, including Plattevenn and Leyloch, were instructed to leave their homes on Sunday morning.
Authorities in Malmedy advised residents to remain indoors, close windows and doors, avoid outdoor physical activity and switch off ventilation systems because of the smoke.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever thanked emergency personnel and European partners for their assistance, saying his thoughts were with all those affected.

The Iran War Toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:26:00 UTC
20:26:00 KST

Trump’s war with Iran:
- Rallied the Iranian nation behind the regime and took oxygen away from the opposition, which had appeared to have the unpopular regime on the ropes earlier in the year with its demonstrations - perhaps by honoring pledges to support those demonstrating back in January 2026, lives could have been saved. As was, people seem to have died in vain.
- Failed at its initial aim for regime change but resulted in installing a new, more radical and uncompromising leadership in Iran, bent on revenge against the US and its allies
- Failed to completely take out Iran’s nuclear program, but perhaps made the regime more likely to go nuclear in the end. Maintaining a program on the threshold of going nuclear but not, failed to act as a deterrent but instead got the regime attacked. Perhaps the message is that only states armed with nukes are safe from attack, and the message to others is to proliferate. The irony is the intervention was aimed at countering nuclear proliferation, but it may well have the opposite effect.
- By making the war existential in talking about regime change it reduced the bar for the regime to escalate with attacks on Gulf states and closing the Straits. In so doing it has gifted the regime a new deterrence - its ability to cripple the Gulf states, the Straits and the global economy through the use of cheap/low tech drones and missiles;
- Through its control of the Straits, Iran is likely now to be able to toll/levy charges for passage, generating revenues for the regime. Prior to the war, the Straits offered free passage.
- Likely the Trump administration will cede a deal to Iran which eases sanctions, eases asset freezes and generates investment flows to further sustain the regime;
- Pushed oil and energy prices higher, stalling global growth and boosting inflation. Higher inflation will stall policy rate cuts, keeping rates higher for longer, further stalling global growth. Global GDP is going to be lower, meaning the global population is collectively poorer.
- Drawn-down global strategic oil reserves are increasing the chances of a systemic global shock in the future.
- Resulted in higher oil and energy prices, which boosted revenues to axis of evil states - Russia, Iran et al. Likely, they bolstered the Russian budget just at the time when in late 2025/early 2026 sanctions were beginning to impact with the Urals oil price discount running at one-third in the early part of 26’, the budget deficit by the end of February at the full year target with Urals down around the 40s a barrel. By bolstering Russia’s fiscal and BOP position it has extended the duration of the war in Ukraine, causing more deaths.
- The war has depleted finite stocks of critical US missiles, including Patriots and THAADs. These are expensive and time-consuming to replace and are now leaving Ukraine short of air defenses, and encouraging Putin to launch ballistic missile attacks and extend the war. The shortage of air defense missiles leaves the Gulf and the US vulnerable and Taiwan open to attack by China.
- The war has shown the limits of US military power and exposed a failure to learn from the recent conflict in Ukraine in the use of drones and military technology. The war will encourage enemies of the US, including China, which had already invested heavily in drone tech.
- The war has left the impression that the US is an unreliable partner and has furthered efforts by key allies to diversify defense ties away from the US This was seen this week with the signing of the Mecca Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. By such states hedging their bets this weakens US global leverage. Likely we will see similar efforts from allies in Europe – longer term this likely weakens the US network of global alliances and reduces long-term demand for US military kit - as countries move to develop autonomous military industrial capability which could ultimately serve as competition to US product.
- With the aim of diversifying away from the US, the Iran war will likely further the flight from the US dollar and US risk free assets. Nervousness around the latter move was probably highlighted by the US Treasury move to support the JPY, for fear of forced Japanese selling of US assets.
- The war has made a lasting peace in Gaza, the West Bank and even Lebanon appear less likely as suspicions on US and Israeli policy in the region have grown. It has made an extension of the Abraham Accords less likely.
- The war has further undermined US popular support for Israel and likely raises questions over the prior unlimited military and financial backing of Israel by the US.

The Times: Ukraine Used British Nyan Drones to Attack Oil Refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:22:26 UTC
20:22:26 KST

Ukraine used British-made Nyan attack drones to strike Russian oil refineries in Volgograd and Yaroslavl.
The Times reported the attacks.
The Nyan drone was developed by British company Callen-Lenz, which is part of FalconWorks, the technology division of BAE Systems.
The drone has a wingspan of 2.9 meters and a maximum takeoff weight of more than 75 kg. It is launched using a pneumatic catapult.
The aircraft is powered by a single gas turbine engine. It has a cruising speed of 120 knots, or about 222 km/h, and a reported range of more than 250 km.
The drone can carry up to 20 kg of payload. Its modular design allows different equipment to be installed depending on the mission.
Nyan drones have been in service with the Ukrainian Defense Forces for some time.
In late June 2024, an identical drone was found on Russian territory. At the time, it was mistakenly identified as a new Ukrainian kamikaze drone.
It later emerged that the drone is manufactured by British company Callen-Lenz at a facility in Wiltshire. In addition to Ukraine, Nyan drones have also entered service with the British Army.
The first unit to receive these drones was the 26th Regiment Royal Artillery, part of the 3rd Division. The British military uses Nyan as a long-range strike system and to complement the artillery capabilities of its units.
The drone was initially tested in Estonia during the annual Spring Storm exercises, where the Royal Artillery conducted test launches and practiced coordination. Following the trials, the regiment officially adopted the Nyan UAV into service.
Its use is expected to expand to other units in the future.
To expand the drone’s operational capabilities, the British Army, together with the Royal Navy, also tested launching it from a surface vessel.
In June 2026, a catapult was installed on the experimental vessel XV Patrick Blackett, from which a Nyan drone was launched.
Back in February 2026, Callen-Lenz was awarded a £4.99 million contract (approximately $6.7 million) by the UK Ministry of Defence to supply Nyan OWE systems to enhance deep-strike capabilities.
According to the official explanation, Nyan became the only mass-produced system of its class registered in the Military Aircraft Register. This was a key factor in selecting the system for rapid deployment.

First in 13 years: Ukraine's Onofriichuk crowned world champion in rhythmic gymnastics
Ukrainian gymnast Taisiia Onofriichuk has won gold in the hoop final at the 2026 Rhythmic Gymnastics World Championships currently taking place in Frankfurt am Main.
Source: Champion, a sports news platform within Ukrainska Pravda's holding company
Details: The judges awarded Onofriichuk's routine a score of 30.700. The Kyiv-born gymnast performed to Thriller by American singer Michael Jackson.
Onofriichuk received 8.300 points for artistry and 14.100 for difficulty, helping the Ukrainian gymnast finish ahead of all her rivals.
She beat Italy's 2022 Olympic bronze medallist Sofia Raffaeli to gold. Germany's Darja Varfolomeev, who was born in Russia, took bronze.
Final results:
- Taisiia Onofriichuk (Ukraine) – 30.700
- Sofia Raffaeli (Italy) – 30.500
- Darja Varfolomeev (Germany) – 30.400
- Daniela Munits (Israel) – 30.050
- Takhmina Ikromova (Uzbekistan) – 30.000
Notably, this is Ukraine's first gold medal at this year's World Championships.
The last time Ukraine won an individual event at the World Championships, which were held in Ukraine, was in 2013, when Hanna Rizatdinova claimed gold. She also won the hoop event.
This is Onofriichuk's first World Championship title. The Kyiv-born gymnast won two bronze medals at last year's World Championships in Rio de Janeiro.
Ukraine will contest two more finals on 16 August at this year's World Championships.
Onofriichuk will return to compete in the clubs final at 16:10, while Ukraine's group will battle for gold in the three hoops and two pairs of clubs final at 15:00.
Earlier, the Ukrainian team narrowly missed out on a medal in the five-ball final at the 2026 World Championships.

U.S. Air Force buys Chinese-made drones for nuclear missile base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
11:19:22 UTC
20:19:22 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is buying DJI drones for F.E. Warren AFB to train missile security forces against the type of foreign drones they are most likely to encounter.
- The brand-name justification cites DJI's 80 to 85 percent global market share and says the drones will run modified "RIZER" software to block data transfer before use.
The U.S. Air Force is buying Chinese-made DJI drones for a Wyoming nuclear missile base, using the foreign aircraft as stand-ins for the kind of drones security forces there are training to detect and shoot down.
The 90th Contracting Squadron posted a combined synopsis and solicitation on August 14 seeking a small business vendor to supply the drones for F.E. Warren Air Force Base, home to the 90th Missile Security Operations Squadron and part of Air Force Global Strike Command. Quotes are due August 24, with questions due five days earlier. The squadron says it needs the aircraft to run counter-small unmanned aircraft systems training, exercises meant to test radar, jamming and other defeat systems against real drone signals rather than simulated ones.
The order calls for two DJI Mavic 2 Pro quadcopters with Fly More kits, listed as refurbished, two DJI Mini 3 Pro drones with remote controllers, two DJI Avata 2 Fly More combos and six airdrop payload release devices, plus shipping. The government intends to award a firm fixed price contract to the lowest-priced offer that meets the technical requirements, according to the solicitation.
Contracting officials designated the purchase a brand-name requirement, meaning DJI specifically, rather than an open competition among drone makers. A justification document signed July 29 by Contracting Officer Chad A. Evans, a technical sergeant, states that DJI controls an estimated 80 to 85 percent of the global commercial drone market and that its “highly distinct, proprietary electronic protocols, radio frequency (RF) signatures, and flight capabilities” are not replicated by American-made drones or other manufacturers.
“To properly test our counter-systems and train our operators against the most statistically probable real-world threat, the 90 MSOS must utilize the exact devices adversaries are most likely to employ,” the justification states.
The document warns that without the specific DJI hardware, the squadron’s “no-fail nuclear security mission” would be degraded. Relying only on computer-simulated data or U.S.-made drones, the justification argues, would leave operators untested against DJI’s actual radio signatures and communication protocols, creating what it calls a critical blind spot in installation defense.
F.E. Warren is one of three U.S. Air Force bases that operates Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, and its security forces are responsible for defending that missile field against ground and airborne threats. The justification states that Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, another Global Strike Command missile base, is pursuing or using similar DJI platforms for its own counter-drone training, and frames the F.E. Warren purchase as bringing the two installations toward standardized threat replication across the command’s missile fields.
The document cites a Secretary of War memo titled “Unleashing U.S. Military Drone Dominance” as the legal authority permitting officers at the rank of O-6, or colonel, and equivalent to procure small quantities of foreign drone equipment for electronic warfare testing, training and counter-UAS development. That authority falls under 10 U.S.C. 2304(c)(1), which allows agencies to solicit from a single source under specific circumstances rather than through full and open competition.
To address cybersecurity concerns tied to Chinese-manufactured hardware, the justification says every DJI aircraft purchased will be loaded with software called RIZER before operational use. The document describes RIZER as overriding the drones’ native firmware to create what it calls “a completely air-gapped system that cannot transfer or download telemetry or imagery to foreign entities or DoW networks.”
The justification also states that the squadron identified multiple authorized DJI resellers and distributors capable of meeting the brand-name requirement, allowing the procurement to proceed as a 100 percent small business set-aside rather than a true single-source award to one company.

Khmara visited medical facilities where Ukrainian defenders are undergoing treatment and rehabilitation
Kyiv • UNN
Yevhen Khmara, together with the deputy head, visited medical facilities where defenders are receiving treatment. He promised to upgrade the infrastructure and attract international assistance.
Acting Minister of Defense Yevhen Khmara visited medical facilities where Ukrainian defenders are receiving treatment and rehabilitation. He discussed problematic issues with military personnel. The press service of the Ministry of Defense reports this, according to UNN.
Details
Together with Deputy Minister of Defense Liubov Halan, we visited military medical facilities where Ukrainian defenders are receiving treatment and rehabilitation. It was important to hear the soldiers in person. We spoke with military personnel undergoing treatment and recovery. We collected problematic issues requiring decisions by the ministry. We also spoke with medical staff and the management of the facilities
He noted that the ministry’s goals are clear: everything necessary must be done to protect the lives of soldiers at the front, provide quality medical care in the event of injury, and create conditions for military personnel to return to service after treatment and rehabilitation.
The lives and health of soldiers must be a priority for every commander. We will keep matters of medical training, timely evacuation, and the care of the wounded in military units under constant control. A separate focus will be updating the infrastructure of military medical facilities and supporting medical professionals. We will consider every possible way to direct additional resources. We will also more actively involve assistance from international partners for this purpose. The medical support of our defenders requires modern conditions and motivated, trained personnel
We remind you
Acting Minister of Defense Yevhen Khmara visited aviation and air defense units of the Air Force. They discussed maximum readiness to repel air attacks, the supply of ammunition, the development of interceptor drones, and other solutions for protecting the skies.

American actress Hayden Panettiere dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:16:55 UTC
20:16:55 KST

Hayden Panettiere’s family announced on the 16th of August that she had passed away shortly before her 37th birthday, Reuters reports.
The official statement did not mention the cause of death, but the actress’s publicist Kasey Kitchen told NBC News that an investigation is underway. The British broadcaster BBC writes that in one of her last interviews in May this year, Panettiere said that she still had a lot to experience, and that she felt as if she had finally shaken off all the dark and negative, and this meant that one door had closed and another had opened. During the interview, the actress shared her thoughts on postpartum depression, the persecution she experienced and her relationship with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko, the father of her daughter. In 2018, the actress handed over full custody of her daughter to Klitschko.
The actress’s father, Alan Panettiere, said the actress was bright and full of natural strength, and gave love and joy to everyone who knew her, as well as to the millions of viewers who watched her work.
Panettiere first gained fame for voicing the ant princess Dot in Pixar’s award-winning animated film A Bug’s Life.
The actress then starred in the NBC series Heroes from 2006, in which she played a high school cheerleader with superpowers.
The acting union SAG-AFTRA, of which Panettiere had been a member since 1994, expressed its condolences, adding that it was with the actress’s daughter, family, friends and admirers of her talent in this moment of sadness.
Panettiere received two Golden Globe nominations in 2013 and 2014 for her role as Juliet Burns in the musical drama Nashville. The actress also appeared in the satirical horror film franchise Scream. Her most recent role was in the psychological thriller Sleepwalker, which was released in 2026. In it, Panettiere played a grieving mother who suffers from sleepwalking.
In her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” published in May, the actress spoke about the traumatic experience of giving birth to her daughter in 2014, her struggle with postpartum depression, and her subsequent alcohol addiction. Her daughter Kaia and Klitschko currently live in Ukraine.
In 2023, the actress’s brother, Jensen Panettiere, passed away at the age of 28.
